course.introTranscript: Anti-racism is ordinary work at Minnesota DHS, not a poster. Privilege does the education — the people who hold the default learn the history and the present. Structure does the change — a hire, a rule, a public comment, a meeting. This title uses a published continuum as a map, not a score. You will not be ranked. You will place one live piece of work and name who owns it.

blocks.body:
Institutional and structural racism is not a personal failing you fix in the hallway. It is everyone’s work. It can be perpetrated by anyone of any race. Dismantling it is predominantly the work of people who hold racial privilege and power inside the institution.

BIPOC staff already live the harm. They are then asked to prove it happened and to teach the room how racism works. That double shift is not Inclusion. It is extraction.

blocks.body:
Organizational culture is a pattern of basic behaviors, espoused values, and assumptions that shape how people perceive, think, and feel — until those patterns become shared meaning. Values that never become practice are theater.

Managers and leaders are responsible for programs and practices that advance a diverse, equitable, and inclusive workplace. Sustainable change means: break barriers that constrain BIPOC staff engagement and effectiveness; improve structures, policies, and practices; then the culture follows. Representation without that work is a photo.

blocks.body:
Tokenism is including a person as a symbolic effort — to prevent criticism — so the group can look diverse. The invitation is often not about the work. It is about the identity the institution wants to display: race, ethnicity, gender, disability.

It shows up as: diversity at the entry level, not in leadership. Events without policies. Black and Latinx faces in marketing for an organization that does not retain them. A diversity council with no diversity at the table that decides. Hiring without retention. Asking one person to be the voice of the agency when a DEI problem hits the news. Heritage-month branding as the year’s racial-equity work.
blocks.heading: What tokenism is

blocks.body: One person is not a people. One seat is not Adaptation. One campaign is not a structure.

blocks.heading: Questions that separate optics from infrastructure

items.body: Or only in the photo and the listening session after the lock?
items.title: Are marginalized staff in the strategy?

items.body: If past hiring did not change retention, a new poster is not a new effort.
items.title: Is this the beginning, or a repeat of a failed initiative?

items.body: If the only product is a council, an event, or a month, you are looking at tokenism until a rule, a budget, or a gate moves.
items.title: Are there policies?

blocks.body: Being the only one is isolating. Support may not appear when a microaggression happens. Visibility becomes pressure to represent an entire group — or invisibility as a figurehead. Stress, depression, and anxiety are not a private failing. They are a predictable result of a structural setup.
blocks.heading: Cost to the person used as proof

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Intention beyond optics is the distinction.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The guide names this pattern. Presence is not power.

options.text: Representation. The flyer is the outcome.
Tokenism until hiring, retention, and decision rights move.
Flyers are forbidden.
Marketing owns racial equity.

blocks.body:
As an institution improves anti-racist effort, it moves along an action continuum toward an anti-racist, multicultural organization. The map runs: monocultural → multicultural → anti-racist → anti-racist multicultural. Differences seen as deficits → tolerated → seen as assets.

This program does not score employees. The continuum is a reading of systems — policies, teaching, decision-making, who holds power. An agency can be in different stages toward different communities at the same time. Ask: what is this unit actually doing? Whom did we consult?
blocks.heading: Crossroads, rebuilt for an agency that defaults to sameness-as-fairness

blocks.body: You do not IDI the building. You read the decision, the hire, and the rule.

events.body: Open exclusion or segregation. Racist status quo as policy. Dominant-group power maintained in the open.
events.title: Exclusive

events.body: A limited number of “token” people allowed in with the “right” views. “We don’t have a problem.” Business as usual is the White norm.
events.title: Club

events.body: Official multicultural policy. Open doors. Recruitment onto committees. Little change in culture, policy, or decision-making. Tokens must assimilate.
events.title: Compliance

events.body: Names systemic racism. Trains. Recruits. Builds some accountability. Identity as anti-racist. White advantage in structure still largely intact.
events.title: Affirming

events.body: Audits and restructures institutional life. Inclusive decision-making and power-sharing. Anti-racist diversity as an asset, not a program.
events.title: Transforming

events.body: A future vision — not a claim. Full participation and shared power. Allies against other oppressions. Work beyond the building.
events.title: Fully inclusive

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Voluntary. No scores. The map is for the work in front of you.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: This program does not sit people. It sits work.

options.text: Score colleagues and publish a ranking.

Declare the agency Stage 6 because the Equity Policy exists.
Ignore it. Continuums are academic.

blocks.body:
A Club institution tolerates a few people with the “proper” credentials, may still exclude in practice, and treats dominant-culture norms as the right way. Diversity is engaged only on club members’ terms and inside their comfort zone.

A Compliance organization makes pronouncements, recruits onto committees, expands the list of groups it names, and remains relatively unaware of privilege, paternalism, and control. Tokens must assimilate. That is Minimization with a policy cover sheet.
blocks.heading: Where Minimization sits on this map
Three failure modes that look like fairness

tabs.body: “We don’t have a problem.” A limited number of people allowed in. Business as usual is unnamed Whiteness. Issues taken up only inside comfort.
tabs.label: Club

tabs.body: Open-door language. Committee seats. Little contextual change. Assimilation still required. Unaware of continuing control.
tabs.label: Compliance

tabs.body: Process that does not sting. Sameness-as-fairness. A values sentence that never enters the eligibility engine, the posting, or the 90-day.
tabs.label: Minnesota Nice

items.text: “We hired two people of color onto the council. The bylaws are unchanged.”
Toolkit before the lock; owner named; who is affected is written.
A staff person reports racial harassment.
Heritage-month branding with no retention plan.
Tribal consultation when a Nation is affected.
The posting no longer dresses extras as requirements.

blocks.body:
An Affirming institution develops an analysis of systemic racism, sponsors anti-racism training, recruits and promotes people historically denied access, and begins accountability to racially oppressed communities. It still often leaves the structures that maintain White power and privilege relatively untouched.

A Transforming institution commits to intentional restructuring. It audits institutional life so People of Color participate fully — including worldview, culture, and how power is shared. Anti-racist multicultural diversity becomes an asset of the institution, not a side program.

Stage 6 is a future vision of a transformed society. It is not a banner you hang after a training cycle.
blocks.heading: The split the guide will not let you blur

blocks.body: Awareness is the on-ramp. Structure is the work. Training is not a substitute for a changed operating environment.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The guide names this: structures remain intact.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Affirming work is real. It is not the same as transforming the gates.

options.text: Stage 6. Training is transformation.
Affirming at best. Identity and training without restructuring the gates.
Exclusive. Training is segregation.
You cannot place work on a continuum.

blocks.body:
The guide asks: What work is the institution doing, and where would you place it? Which communities are supported, and which are not? Did you consult those communities?

For this title, pick one live piece of work — a hire, a policy, a public comment, a meeting. Name the community it lands on. Place that object on the continuum. If you cannot name a structural move, you are still in compliance or club, whatever the poster says.
blocks.heading: Do not diagnose the whole agency in an hour

items.body: Policy, budget, hire, IT change, comment period — something that will lock.
items.title: 1. Name the object

items.body: Not “diverse communities.” A people, a Nation, a language, a disability group. Variation inside the group still applies.
items.title: 2. Name who it lands on

items.body: Exclusive, Club, Compliance, Affirming, Transforming — for this object. Not for the employee’s soul.
items.title: 3. Place it

items.body: A gate, a default, a consult, a formal door. If you will not move it, write that. Theater is the unnamed skip.
items.title: 4. Move or write why not

blocks.body: Hearts and Minds through institutional and structural equity. Awareness is the on-ramp. Structure is the work. No scores.

course.introTranscript: This is a brief, not a capsule. Somali Minnesota is not one person, not a festival poster, and not a racial module. An iceberg will show you what a Tuesday usually sees, and what sits under it. Ethnography, here, means Minnesota, dated, named sources, and variation inside the community. Unvarnished means we will not soften clan, disability stigma, or fear of child protection into a press release. You will still ask this family. You will still book the interpreter. Voluntary. No score.

blocks.body: Most of this building will not have sat with Somali Minnesota families. Sameness-as-fairness will write one English exception and call it fair. This brief is operations: unvarnished group dynamics so who a process was built for can be seen. It is still a hypothesis. Ask this family. Book the interpreter. Date the gate. Offense is not the metric.

A racial module. Somali Minnesotans are Black, mostly Muslim, and many are immigrants — that triple is structure (the racial record still exists). Culture does not replace the record.
A Tribal Nation. Do not file this next to consultation.

blocks.body:
Somalia’s civil war after the 1991 collapse of the Siad Barre government displaced hundreds of thousands. Early arrivals to Minnesota included students; the larger refugee movement in the 1990s found work first in places like Marshall, then in the Twin Cities (Ahmed Ismail Yusuf; MNopedia). Cedar-Riverside became a hub — businesses, mosques, organizations — sometimes called Little Mogadishu. Karmel Mall on Lake Street is a statewide gathering place, including a mosque (UMN Somali Culture and Foods, updated May 2025, Huda Gass and Idil Hassan).

A “welcoming state” is part of the story. Jobs, housing, and chain migration are the rest. It is not a compliment you are owed for showing up to work.
blocks.heading: How they got here — not a myth of welcome
Counts — they do not match, so we date them
items: Minnesota Compass (recent ACS-based profile): about 79,500 people of Somali ancestry; 78% Twin Cities, 22% Greater Minnesota; about 47% age 17 or younger; 56% foreign-born; 37% of those 5+ speak English less than “very well”; median household income about $43,600; 36% below poverty.
Census Bureau ACS cited in 2025 reporting: about 107,000 people of Somali descent in Minnesota in 2024; ~84,000 in the metro; ~58% born in the U.S.; of the foreign-born, ~87% naturalized.
Older UCare (2020) figure: “over 52,000.” MNopedia (2010s) ranged 30,000–100,000.
Write “about” and the year. Do not pick the number that makes a grant easier.

blocks.body: Standard Somali is the majority official variety. Maay and Benadiri are also spoken; clan and region matter for dialect (UMN 2025). Arabic is used for religion. Second-generation Somali Minnesotans widely use English. A “Somali interpreter” who does not speak Maay is still a closed gate for that family. Gender match for interpreters is often requested in maternal and intimate care (MDH interpreter chapter; UMN 2025).
blocks.heading: Language — “Somali” is not one channel

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ethnography here is dated.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Compass, ACS, and older health-plan slides are all evidence — with a year.

options.text: Close enough. The count is fine.
Date it or write missing. Counts moved. A blend of years is a blend of who.
Only Census may be cited.
Numbers do not belong in a culture brief.

blocks.heading: Deep culture — as a hypothesis, not a rule

tabs.body: Traditionally large, close, respect for elders. Status has often included many children (UMN 2025). Decisions may be family decisions. That can look like “the uncle speaks” — or like a strength you need in a waiver meeting. Ask who should be in the room. Do not assume a nuclear two-parent English form matches the household.
tabs.label: Family

tabs.body: Most Somali Minnesotans are Muslim. Prayer, fasting, gender space, and what is discussed in mixed company can shape a DHS appointment. Islam is not a monolith and not a diagnosis. Some families are more observant than others. Second generation may differ from parents. Do not make the imam your case plan unless the family asked.
tabs.label: Islam

tabs.body: Households have often been described as male-centered in public and female-centered in the running of the house — “the man is the head, the woman is the neck” (UMN 2025). Civil war and resettlement also pushed many Somali women into work, business, and household finance. A woman may be the decision-maker and still want a female interpreter. Both can be true.
tabs.label: Gender

tabs.body: Clan is real in Somali history. The civil war was organized partly along clan lines. In Minnesota, asking someone’s clan is often off-limits except in marriage or among intimates; people may refuse it because it divides (UMN 2025). You will not use clan as an icebreaker, a risk score, or a “cultural insight” in the file. If it shows up because the family named it, you listen. You do not go looking.
tabs.label: Clan

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Unvarnished is not invasive.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Real ≠ yours to extract.

options.text: That is good ethnography.
Off-limits as an icebreaker. Clan is deep, and it is not yours to extract. Ask about the process in front of you.
Only Somali staff may ask.
Clan is a myth and should not be named.

blocks.body: UCare’s Circles of Health work with Somali women in Minnesota: good health as being productive, in relation with family and with God, in a community that watches children. Ill health as insomnia, fatigue, spiritual dissonance, isolation, sadness. Women named Minnesota isolation — “in Somalia we knew each other; here we have depression” (UCare 2020, citing Cedar-Riverside cultural-assets work).
blocks.heading: Health is not only the absence of a disease

blocks.body:
MDH’s qualitative study with Somali, Hmong, and Latino families of children with autism (University of Minnesota School of Public Health, Confederation of Somali Community in Minnesota, SoLaHmo): shame and blame from family; stigma around cognitive and mental-health labels; isolation; fear of housing loss; grief; not knowing what to ask in English; doctors who said nothing was wrong; wait lists; schools that felt disrespectful; a preference for support from people who share language and values. Parents also supported each other in the room. That is not “Somalis don’t believe in autism.” It is a system plus a meaning.

Community concern about high autism identification in Minneapolis Somali children has been public since the 2000s. Fear of MMR clustered with age of diagnosis (UMN 2025). Studies have not shown a vaccine-autism link. Unvarnished: the fear is real, the science is not on that link, and the system also dismissed parents and, in documented cases, turned a help-seeking visit toward child protection (community advocates, including public testimony). Both are true.
blocks.heading: Disability and autism — MDH 2014, in their words

blocks.body: Mental-health stigma is real. War and displacement trauma is real. A hallway diagnosis of PTSD is not humility. Book the interpreter. Do not make the parent the curriculum.

blocks.caption: Triple jeopardy named in the UMN guide: Black, Muslim, immigrant. That is not a foodway.

blocks.heading: What the iceberg chart usually skips
items: Poverty and income: Compass median household ~$43,600; more than a third below poverty. That hits housing, food support, who can wait unpaid.
Language access failure: 37% of those 5+ speak English less than “very well” (Compass). An English portal is a who.
Discrimination and surveillance: after public attacks on the community, families may read a DHS badge as risk, not help. That is history in the room, not “paranoia.”
Child-welfare fear: asking for disability help and meeting a report. The gate was built for someone who already trusts the county.
Workforce: bilingual Somali staff pulled off their caseload as interpreters and “cultural brokers” without a role (see those titles).

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. That is why this brief has a layer under the ice.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The racial record still exists. This brief does not replace it.

options.text: The culture work is done.
Travelogue. The iceberg without structure is a poster. Change the wait or write unfunded.

blocks.body: Unvarnished is not a deficit pile. The object is still the gate. Intra-community power is real. So is the agency’s power.
blocks.heading: How to say a hard thing
Say it — then stay on the work

tabs.body: Some families carry female genital cutting as a practice from regions of origin. It is a health and, for minors, a child-protection and criminal-law matter in the U.S. It is not “Somali culture” as a whole, not an icebreaker, and not a reason to treat every Somali girl as a case. If it is in front of you, use the health and legal doors. Do not workshop it as a story circle. Do not make a mother the curriculum.
tabs.label: FGC / FGM

tabs.body: Stigma around LGBTQ+ people is real in many conservative Muslim families — and not only there. A brief does not tell you to out a young person to their parents. Use the person’s name. LGBTQ+ inclusion in services still applies. Family rejection is a safety issue, not a cultural excuse to deadname.
tabs.label: Queerness

tabs.body: Imams, businessmen, men of a certain clan, a handful of nonprofits, a handful of elected officials — none of them are the whole. Women, Maay speakers, people with disabilities, youth, and people who left the mosque also live here. If your only Somali voice is one broker used as the whole community, you have a capsule with a name.
tabs.label: Who speaks for “the community”

tabs.body: Parents in the MDH study and in public advocacy described being unheard, then punished. Unvarnished includes that fear. It does not mean you never report. It means you know what a knock at the door already means, you use an interpreter, and you do not treat a missed appointment as proof of neglect without a who.
tabs.label: Help-seeking vs. CPS

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Unvarnished is both layers.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Erasing stigma is a press release. Erasing the system is a villain story about a people.

options.text: Keep it. Unvarnished.
Shame is named in Somali parents’ own MDH interviews — and so are wait lists, dismissed concerns, and English-only meetings. Write both. Then change a gate.
Never mention shame.
Only Somali trainers may speak.

blocks.body:
Most Somali Minnesotans are Sunni Muslim. Prayer times, Friday jumu’ah, Ramadan, Eid, halal food, and modest dress can shape a DHS appointment. Arabic is used for religion; Somali is the language of the home. Islam is not a diagnosis and not a racial module.

Variation is the point: some families are more observant; some youth are not; some women lead; some people left the mosque and still eat halal. Ask this family. The calendar (Ramadan, Eid, Mawlid, Independence Day) is a breadcrumb back here — not a quiz.
blocks.heading: What is common — as a hypothesis
At the desk
items: Do not schedule a mandatory meeting at sundown in Ramadan if you can help it.
A female interpreter for maternal and intimate care is often requested — book it.
Do not make an imam the case plan unless the family asked.
Leave on Eid is reasonable. Extracting Somali staff to “explain Islam” is not.

tabs.body: Salaam / as-salamu alaykum is common. Many people will not shake a hand of another gender outside family (UMN 2025). The right hand is preferred. Do not force a handshake as “professionalism.” Wait for what they offer.
tabs.label: Greetings

tabs.body: Somali naming is often given name + father’s name + grandfather’s name — not a U.S. first/middle/last. Forms that demand a “last name” already have a who. Write the names they use. Do not invent a surname because the database wants one without saying so.
tabs.label: Naming

tabs.body: Honour (sharaf) and modesty (xishood) show up in dress, volume, and who sits in the room. Elders first. Hospitality is a value — tea is not a delay tactic. Do not call frank talk about the body “rude” if that is how they speak; do not assume frankness about clan.
tabs.label: Etiquette

tabs.body: Oral culture: news travels in the mosque, the mall, the family. Directness can be high among men who know each other; a government office is not that room. English-only voicemail is a closed gate. Maay is not Standard Somali. Book the dialect.
tabs.label: Communication

blocks.body:
MDH’s 2014 report to the legislature is a qualitative study of families of children with autism in the Somali community, compared with other immigrant groups (University of Minnesota, Confederation of Somali Community, SoLaHmo). Families named how they meet systems — language, delay, who is believed. That is evidence of gates.

It is not a personality profile. Do not teach “Somali beliefs about disability” as a module. Ask this family what they need, book the interpreter, and run the disability door. Hmong, Karen, and Latino guides are the same: evidence, not a capsule.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Evidence, not a course on a people.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Naming a community in data is allowed. Reducing that community to a briefing is theater.

options.text: Hold the briefing. That is cultural competence.
No capsule. Read the report as evidence of barriers. Change the wait, the interpreter, and who is believed — or write that you will not.
Only MDH may serve Somali families.
Never mention Somali in a packet.

blocks.body:
The National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) are a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services blueprint (Office of Minority Health). Enhanced 2013. Fifteen standards. The principal standard is quality that responds to language and culture — not a festival. Standards 5–8 are the language cluster: assistance at no cost; tell people it exists, in writing and orally, in English and other languages; qualified interpreters, not untrained people or minors; easy-to-understand materials in the languages commonly used in the service area.

A poster of the fifteen is not practice. Practice is a channel that a person can actually use. After the nested lists: open From the list to the household — each language opens the right cultural intelligence, or says there is not one yet and you still book the interpreter.
blocks.heading: What CLAS is

blocks.body:
Two layers, not one poster.

Law and grants (2021). Minnesota Laws 2021, First Special Session, Chapter 7, Article 11, Section 40 directed DHS to develop a statewide implementation and transition plan for the national CLAS standards, including technical assistance so providers can transition and so disparate treatment outcomes move. Article 16 funded grants to disability services, mental health, and substance use disorder treatment providers to implement CLAS. Effective July 1, 2021. The department’s CLAS page names six action areas from the national implementation framework: foster cultural competence; reflect and respect diversity; ensure language access; build community partnerships; collect diversity data; benchmark, plan, and evaluate. That is a provider-and-system job — not a cultural-competence certificate.

Operations (Equal Opportunity and Access). Spoken and written language assistance is run as Limited English Proficiency work. Translations have been coordinated centrally since 2000. Languages on the standing lists come from a periodic analysis of DHS program participants plus division input — not from a lobby anecdote and not from a census checkbox. Other languages may be available based on need. A language missing from the standing five is not a finding that the household does not exist.

Minnesota Statute 15.441 is a separate state duty: agencies that serve a substantial number of non-English-speaking people must staff public-contact work so information and services can be provided in those languages, and should give highest priority to materials that notify people of legal rights, duties, or privileges.
blocks.heading: How Minnesota DHS practices it
The nested lists — date them; they are not the person

tabs.body:
DHS Equal Opportunity and Access, LEP resources (current public list): translations of selected documents are available in five primary languages. Other languages may be available based on need.

Hmong (pronounced mung). Russian. Somali. Spanish. Vietnamese.

That is the standing written list. It is not Maay. It is not White Hmong versus Mong Leng. It is not ASL. A vital notice still has to reach this household.
tabs.label: Five — primary translation

tabs.body:
Most public DHS documents carry a language block: the right to free help interpreting the document, in ten languages.

Arabic. Hmong. Khmer (Cambodian). Lao. Oromo. Russian. Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian). Somali. Spanish. Vietnamese.

The block is notice (CLAS 6). It is not the interpreter. Staff who answer the number on the block must be ready for a non-English call and must have an LEP plan.
tabs.label: Ten — language block

tabs.body:
DHS-4374 cards, fifteen languages:

Amharic. Arabic. Burmese. Cantonese. French. Hmong. Karen. Korean. Khmer (Cambodian). Laotian. Oromo. Russian. Somali. Spanish. Vietnamese.

The person points. You still book a qualified interpreter for this dialect and this appointment. Cantonese is not “Chinese.” Karen is not Burmese as a synonym.
tabs.label: Fifteen — “I need an interpreter”

tabs.body: DHS-4059, Catalogue of Languages: Notice of Rights to Language Assistance in seventy-five languages. Use it to identify the language. Do not treat a catalogue page as a completed interview.
tabs.label: Seventy-five — catalogue

blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A list is how the building batches translation. It is not a finding that Karen households are optional.

Book a qualified interpreter now. The five are the standing written list, not the ceiling — DHS says other languages may be available based on need. A vital notice is still a vital notice. Confirm dialect.
Hand them the language block and close the file.

course.introTranscript: Language access is a design, not a favor. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, who can use the door, the form, and the phone is already decided — in English, in one channel, at one hour. Title VI and Minnesota law are legal doors. CLAS is a standard. This course is the Tuesday: name who the channel was built for, then change it or write why it stays. Voluntary. No score.

blocks.alt: The counter is already a language design.
blocks.caption: If the form, the voicemail, and the portal are English-only, the gate already chose.

blocks.body: Minimization: we treat everyone the same — in English. Adaptation: name who this channel was built for, then add a language or write why you will not.

Title VI of the Civil Rights Act: no person shall, on the ground of race, color, or national origin, be denied the benefits of a federally funded program. The Supreme Court in Lau v. Nichols (1974) treated language as one form of national-origin discrimination. DOJ: recipients must take reasonable steps so people with limited English proficiency have meaningful access.

Minnesota Department of Health’s interpreter chapter: Minnesota law also requires public health care institutions to provide services to people with limited English proficiency. Minnesota Statute 15.441 is the state-agency duty on public-contact capacity when a substantial number of people are non-English-speaking.

CLAS (HHS, enhanced 2013) is the blueprint: language assistance at no cost; tell people it exists; do not use untrained people or minors as interpreters; materials in the languages commonly used in the service area. At this department that is not a mystery list. Equal Opportunity and Access publishes nested lists — date them: five primary translation languages (Hmong — pronounced mung — Russian, Somali, Spanish, Vietnamese; other languages by need); a ten-language block on most public documents; fifteen “I need an interpreter” cards; a 75-language catalogue. The five are the standing written list, not the ceiling and not the dialect. A Language Access Plan you can walk is the next title.

course.introTranscript: Equal opportunity is both a door and a lens. The door is Equal Opportunity and Access when someone is harmed. The lens is the posting, the panel, the ninety-day, before anyone has to complain. This course teaches you to tell them apart, and not to merge them in a hallway. You will not be the investigator. Voluntary. For every employee.

course.introTranscript: The employee life cycle is a system, not a poster. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, equity lives in the posting, the panel, the first ninety days, the survey blend, who gets a sponsor, and who leaves. This course is the map for every employee — classified staff, intern, contractor, appointee. Voluntary. No score. You will name which gate you actually touch, who it was built for, and which doors you will not improvise.

blocks.alt: Ordinary work — the people system is already running.

blocks.body:
People, Access and Culture already has three spines: intercultural development, racial equity and anti-racism, and access in service practice. The shared method is the toolkit. What was missing is the people system — the gates every employee walks, whether they hire anyone or not.

The Equity Policy asks for a lens on actions. Hiring, onboarding, who is visible, who leaves — those are actions. This course is the map. Later courses go gate by gate. You do not have to take them in order. You do not get a score for taking them.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: we treat every employee the same, so the people system is fair. Adaptation: name who a gate was built for, then change it or leave it identical on purpose.

blocks.heading: What sameness-as-fairness sounds like here
items: “We use the same posting template.”
“Everyone gets the same 90-day.”
“The survey says we are at 72 percent engaged.”
“Fit.”
“We don’t see race in hiring — that’s how we stay legal.”

blocks.body: Some workdays, identical treatment is the law or the contract: veterans’ preference, a bargaining rule, a required qualification. That is a constraint. Write it. Do not use it as blindness. The lens still asks who the remaining channel was built for — hours, language, unpaid homework, who is on the panel.
Polarization in this work: ranking who “gets it” on the panel or in the stay interview. The object is the gate, not a soul.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Constraint is not blindness.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not improvise a racial rule. Do not skip the who.

options.text: Correct. Sameness is the legal safe harbor for every workday.
Sometimes identical is required. That still is not a pass on naming who the posting and panel were built for. Toolkit before the lock, or write the constraint.
Invent a different rubric by race.
Only EOAD may look at a hire.

Statute. Use the door. The lens still looks at channels you control around it.
Reasonable accommodation is a legal process. Do not replace it with a hallway favor. Do not skip it because “we treat everyone the same.”

This curriculum. Toolkit. Date.

course.introTranscript: Seeing the system does not mean a higher score. It means you can see the budget, the IT default, the contract — not only the sentence. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, equity lives in budgets, IT defaults, contracts, hiring pipelines, and who is in the room when a rule is written. This course is for people who lead or design those systems. Voluntary. No ranking. You will name where a process was built for one kind of workday, and what a leader of a system actually changes.

course.introTranscript: Acceptance is the next step after Minimization. Not a score. A work habit: you can notice difference without ranking people, and without pretending everyone is the same. Sameness-as-fairness hid who a process was built for. Polarization ranks who is evolved. Acceptance names the who. It does not yet change the channel. This course stays there long enough to get good at noticing. Voluntary. The continuum is a map. You choose the next move.

blocks.alt: A table where people are listening — noticing starts here.
blocks.caption: Minimization said we are all the same. Acceptance says difference is real, and ranking people is still the wrong move.

blocks.body:
The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDI, LLC) is a published map of how people and groups orient to difference. This program uses it as a map. It does not test you. Minnesota DHS, as diagnosed, defaults to Minimization: sameness-as-fairness. The organizational aim is a pathway toward Adaptation: change the work.

You do not skip a step by hanging a poster. Acceptance is the orientation in between: you can see that people are not the same, you can be curious, you can name who a process was built for — without making colleagues into good and bad people.

blocks.caption: Acceptance is a way of looking. It is not a personality. It is not a loyalty test.

blocks.body:
On the continuum, Acceptance is an orientation in which difference is seen as real and complex, and people can hold more than one cultural frame without needing everyone to be “basically the same.” In DHS work, we use a plain-language version:

You can name who a process was built for, and who it was not, without ranking colleagues and without pretending the process is universal.
blocks.heading: A work definition

cards.back: Minimization says difference is mostly surface; the same rule is fairness. Acceptance says the same rule can still sort people.
Polarization makes difference a contest: us/them, woke/not, evolved/behind. Acceptance refuses the ranking.
You can notice the English-only after-hours line and still ship it. That is Acceptance without a shift. Incomplete — and still a real step.
This course will not tell you your stage. You practice a habit. You choose the next course.

blocks.body: Acceptance can hear a hard sentence about impact without turning it into a character trial — of you or of them.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Named the who. No ranking. Not yet the design change — that is the next course.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: First is Minimization. Third is Polarization. Fourth is Adaptation. Acceptance is the noticing sentence.

blocks.body:
Minimization is not always hostile. It is often kind. “We all want the same things.” “A good process is a good process.” Kindness that erases who cannot use the default is still erasure.

Acceptance does not require you to become an expert in every culture. It requires you to stop using “same” as a substitute for looking.
blocks.heading: What Minimization treated as surface

tabs.body: A 15-minute call-back window in English is not the same process for a person who needs an interpreter booked two days out.
tabs.label: Language

tabs.body: A PDF that cannot be read by a screen reader is not “the same application.” It is a closed door with a stamp.
tabs.label: Disability

tabs.body: A metro in-person only hearing is not the same access in greater Minnesota. Distance is not a personality trait.
tabs.label: Place

tabs.body: A blended wait of 21 days can hide a longer wait. Naming that is intercultural noticing and it is also racial-equity work. Keep the doors labeled. Do not collapse them.
tabs.label: Race

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Peace that erases the who is Minimization. Ranking people is Polarization. Acceptance names the process.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The object stays the process. That is how you notice without a fight.

blocks.caption: “What does this step assume?” is Acceptance. “You’re our expert because of who you are” is theater. Culture without theater is a later course. The habit starts here.

blocks.body:
Curiosity about difference can turn into extraction: one Somali staff person asked to “explain the community,” one disabled staff person asked to fix access, one Native staff person treated as consultation. That is not Acceptance. That is using a person as a module.

Acceptance asks the process: What does this form assume. Who can complete it at 7 p.m. Who cannot travel. What language is the default. Lived experience may be offered. It is not extracted in the hallway.
blocks.heading: How noticing asks

items.body: Who was this built for. Who waits. Who drops. What would a second channel be.
items.title: Ask the process

items.body: Do not look at one colleague and say “can you speak for.” If a Nation is affected, that is consultation — a government door.
items.title: Do not ask a person to be a people

items.body: You can write down an impact sentence without agreeing with every remedy. That is still noticing.
items.title: Hear without converting

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Curiosity aims at the design, not at a colleague’s identity as unpaid labor.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Extraction is not noticing. It is theater. This course refuses it.

options.text: Useful curiosity. That is inclusion.

blocks.body:
Complete it without a villain:

This process was built for someone who can ________. It is harder for someone who ________.

If you cannot fill the blanks, you are still in Minimization — not because you are a bad person, because the who is still invisible to you.
blocks.heading: The pattern sentence

tabs.body: Built for: daytime, English, a printer, a stable login. Harder for: language access, shift work, no broadband, a screen reader.
tabs.label: Front desk / portal

tabs.body: Built for: people who hear in the room, read the night-before deck, speak over each other. Harder for: captions, processing time, remote greater Minnesota.
tabs.label: Meeting

tabs.body: Built for: people who already know the acronyms, can write a 48-hour sample unpaid, can wait for a delayed posting. Harder for: everyone else. Name the skill. “Fit” is not a who.
tabs.label: Hire

blocks.body:
The Equity Policy named an intercultural organization and an antiracist organization. They are related. They are not the same skill. Acceptance (this curriculum) is how you notice difference without ranking. Racial equity (Curriculum II) is the record, Minnesota numbers, and measurable change by race.

If you treat every racial gap as “cultural preference,” you Minimized race. If you treat every language or disability barrier as only racism, you blended the who the other way.
blocks.heading: Why this lesson exists

cards.back: How a group orients to difference — language, culture, disability, place, role. This course.
History, wealth, justice, Minnesota child welfare and waits by race. The record and Minnesota courses. Disparity still is not automatically discrimination.
Governments. Consultation. Not a cultural module and not a racial stakeholder bullet.
A legal duty and a design fact. Not a diversity icebreaker.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Acceptance is honest about what you do not know. It does not invent a culture story to protect the default.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Guessing “culture” to avoid race is still not looking.

options.text: Accept the cultural explanation. That is noticing.
Notice that you do not yet know. A preference story without a breakout is Minimization with anthropology. Ask who waits, in which channel. Race stays on the table until you look.

course.introTranscript: Noticing difference without ranking people is Acceptance. Changing the work is Adaptation. Sameness-as-fairness says we treat everyone the same and calls that fairness. This course is more practice: a form, a hire, a meeting. Voluntary. No score. The continuum is a map. You choose the next move.

course.introTranscript: Good intentions are not the test. The Equity Policy asks for measurable change. A disparity is an observation. Discrimination is a causal claim. They are related, and they are not the same sentence. This course shows how a blended average hides who a process was built for, how to look without a courtroom, and how the Equity Analysis Toolkit is the method before the lock. You will not be scored. You will be asked to measure.

course.introTranscript: This is Minnesota, not a national seminar. At the Department of Human Services, the record lands as who waits, who is removed, who is hired, and who is believed. American Indian children in out-of-home care at many times the white rate. African American and Hispanic children at about twice. Greater Minnesota is not a footnote. Tribal Nations are governments. A blended average is not a finding. This course does not score you. It shows the Minnesota numbers, names the doors that are already law, and asks what your process does on a Tuesday.

blocks.caption: Curriculum II after The record. Charts without a Minnesota desk are still a seminar.

blocks.body:
The record named history, wealth, justice, and health as national evidence. This title asks the same discipline of this state’s human services: who waits, who is removed, who is hired, who is believed. People of color and American Indians are both in the picture. They are not the same story. Tribal Nations are governments.

Child welfare operations now sit with the Department of Children, Youth, and Families. DHS staff still meet those families in MA, behavioral health, disability, cash, and child care. A number published by the state is still a number you may not ignore.

blocks.alt: Bar chart: Minnesota out-of-home care relative rates, 2023.
blocks.caption: 2023 public reporting of DHS-5408PA-ENG: Black and Hispanic youth about twice as likely as white children to be in out-of-home care; American Indian / Native youth about sixteen times as likely.

blocks.alt: Grouped bars: share of child population versus share of child-protection cases, 2025.
blocks.caption: DCYF summary in the MAAFPCWDA context (2025): African American children 16% of child population and 29% of cases; American Indian 4% of population and 20% of cases; Hispanic / Latine 10% and 12%. A gap is a disparity.

blocks.body: These are observations the state already prints. They do not, by themselves, prove a particular worker discriminated. They also do not get to be “national politics.” Minnesota has named the pattern in statute (the 2024 African American Family Preservation and Child Welfare Disproportionality Act). Implementation has been contested. A law can name a gap. A process still has to be looked at.

blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A large published gap is not a verdict and not ignorable.

blocks.body:
The Minnesota African American Family Preservation and Child Welfare Disproportionality Act (2024) named longstanding unequal outcomes for African American, American Indian, and other disproportionately represented children. It required annual identification of disproportionality and active efforts for covered children.

This title does not litigate the rollout. Courts and counties have argued about how it was applied. Your job as a DHS employee is not to pick a team on that fight. It is to notice that the state already said the gap is real, and to look at adjacent processes you do own.
blocks.heading: What the Act is — and is not

blocks.body: A statute can name a disparity. Tuesday still has to be designed.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Observation, statute, and implementation are three sentences.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Politics does not erase a published gap. Cause still has to be argued.

options.text: Agree. Statute is only politics.
The numbers were published before the Act. The Act named them. Implementation is contested. Ignoring the observation is Minimization.
The Act settled cause.
Only attorneys may look.

blocks.alt: Two colleagues with a packet — hiring is a legal process.
blocks.caption: This title asks who applies, who is interviewed, who stays. It does not replace affirmative action, labor, or civil rights.

blocks.body:
Workforce composition is a legitimate equity question under the Equity Policy. Hiring is also a regulated process. This program will not teach you to invent a shortcut, pick a team on a federal investigation, or convert a meeting into a racial ranking of candidates.

What you can do: look at the posting language, the unpaid extra steps, “culture fit,” who is on the panel, who gets a developmental assignment, who leaves in year one. If a complaint or a legal review is live, stop and use EOAD and HR.
blocks.heading: Keep the doors labeled

blocks.body: Culture-fit without a skill is Minimization with a smile — or Polarization with a score. Name the skill.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Process, skill, legal door. Not a team.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Improvising a racial rule is not Adaptation. Neither is “fit” with no content.

options.text: Agree. Fit is enough.
Ask which skill or behavior is missing. Write it. If they cannot, the phrase is doing work it cannot defend. Use HR process. Do not hold a racial seminar in the panel.
Override HR with an equity vote.
Drop race from all hiring talk forever.

course.introTranscript: This briefing is the national record on racism in America — one of the largest and most argued-about subjects in American life. The aim is not to win an argument. It is to lay out what scholars mean by the term, what the historical record shows, what the evidence says, and where serious people genuinely disagree. That last part matters, because racism gets used to mean several different things in one breath, and people end up talking past each other. Start with definitions. The field has gotten precise about this. The familiar one is individual racism: prejudice, an individual acting with hostile intent. But in 1967, in the book Black Power, Stokely Carmichael and Charles Hamilton named a second thing: institutional racism, the idea that an institution can produce racially unequal outcomes even when no single person intended harm. That scales up to structural racism: policies across housing, schools, jobs, health care, and the justice system that interlock so that opportunity and risk fall along racial lines over generations. The key move is from intent to outcome - not who's the villain, but what does the machine produce year after year. That's the central analytic move in modern scholarship. One more: implicit bias, those automatic unconscious associations. How much they predict real behavior is itself debated, so even inside the field, not everything is settled. None of these mechanisms make sense without the history. It begins with race-based chattel slavery established in the colonies in the 1600s, written into the Constitution itself: the three-fifths clause, the fugitive slave clause. By 1860, about four million people were enslaved. Then the Civil War, and what looked like a turning point. Three amendments: the Thirteenth abolishing slavery, the Fourteenth guaranteeing equal protection, the Fifteenth barring racial barriers to voting. And for a brief window in Reconstruction, Black Americans voted and held office, which is the part people skip. There was real multiracial democracy in the 1870s South, and it was deliberately dismantled. Federal troops withdrew in 1877, and in rushed disenfranchisement and racial terror, Jim Crow: an entire legal system of segregation, blessed by the Supreme Court in Plessy versus Ferguson in 1896, the separate-but-equal doctrine, enforced by poll taxes, sharecropping, and lynching. Millions left in the Great Migration and often met new tools of segregation in northern cities. Then the chapter most people know: the Civil Rights Movement. Brown versus Board in 1954 overturned Plessy. Then the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the Fair Housing Act of 1968, outlawing discrimination by law - genuinely world changing. And here's where modern disagreement lives. One view: the legal barriers fell, so the job was substantially done - a serious position. The counter, for much of the scholarship: ending legal segregation didn't undo the material inequalities it had already produced. If a group was barred for centuries from building wealth, saying now it's equal on a Tuesday doesn't move the starting lines. So the disagreement isn't really about whether the past was unjust. It's about how much the past still operates in the present. And the strongest case that it still operates is housing. The key text is Richard Rothstein's 2017 book, The Color of Law. His argument: it was not merely private prejudice; it was federal policy. New Deal and FHA mortgage programs, and a federal agency that literally drew maps coloring Black neighborhoods red - redlining - denying them federally backed mortgages, plus racial covenants in deeds. So in the very decades the government was building the middle class through homeownership, Black families were largely locked out by design. That's the bridge to the racial wealth gap. For most families, home equity is the single largest source of wealth. Give one group a multi-decade government-backed head start and exclude another, and you'd predict an enormous wealth gap that persists across generations even after the discrimination ends. That's exactly what the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows: median white household wealth several times that of median Black household wealth. Not income. Wealth. The accumulated cushion. The most contested domain in public debate is the criminal legal system. Separate evidence from interpretation. The foundational popular text is Michelle Alexander's 2010 The New Jim Crow, arguing mass incarceration works as racialized social control. Start with undisputed facts: the U.S. incarcerates a larger share of its population than almost any nation, and Black Americans are incarcerated at several times the white rate. That's straight from the Bureau of Justice Statistics and the Sentencing Project. Where's the debate then? Cause. How much of the disparity reflects differences in offending versus disparities in enforcement - who gets policed, stopped, charged, sentenced. Honest researchers say it's genuinely both, in proportions that vary and that people argue about. What's well documented is that at discretionary points - drug enforcement is classic, where usage rates are similar across groups but arrest rates aren't - the system produces disparate outcomes. So you can accept the disparities without every interpretation being settled. That's the discipline. Here's the disparity, which is measurable, versus here's the full causal story, which is contested. Disparity is an observation. Discrimination is a causal claim. Related, but not the same, and good scholarship never collapses them. And that discipline pays off when you find the clean causal evidence. In 2004, the economists Bertrand and Mullainathan sent thousands of identical resumes to real jobs, randomly assigning white-sounding or Black-sounding names. The white-sounding names got significantly more callbacks. Same qualifications. The name is the only thing that could explain the gap. That's an audit study. It isolates the causal effect of perceived race, one of the strongest tools we have. And the pattern recurs in health: Black maternal mortality is markedly higher than white, and the gap persists even adjusting for income and education, which rules out the simple class-only story. Researchers point to differential treatment and chronic stress against a backdrop like the Tuskegee study that still shapes trust today. How do we actually know any of this? How do you measure something as slippery as racism? It's genuinely hard, and the skepticism is the right instinct. Main tools: audit studies, big administrative datasets, and attitude surveys, each with limits. The big one: disparities alone don't prove discrimination, because a gap can come from current discrimination or accumulated history or other intertwined factors. Audit studies isolate causal discrimination cleanly but only in narrow settings. So no single method is decisive. The rigorous move is to triangulate and look for where independent methods point the same way. And across housing, lending, and hiring, they converge. Which is why these are mainstream empirical findings, not fringe claims. Be equally disciplined about the frameworks. This is where it gets heated. Represent different views fairly. Do not pick a team. These are genuinely contested. Critical race theory started as a technical legal framework - Bell, Crenshaw - arguing racism is embedded in structures, not merely individual prejudice. In public it's become a much broader and disputed term, especially about K-12 classrooms. Colorblindness is the principle that policy shouldn't classify by race at all. Proponents say any official use of race risks new unfairness. Critics say ignoring race while past effects persist still locks in inequality. There's race versus class: William Julius Wilson emphasizing economic class, others arguing race retains independent power. Most now say it's an interaction, but the emphasis is debated. And the one people feel most strongly about: remedies. Honesty requires saying plainly there's no scholarly consensus, and this shades into values, not only evidence. The options include affirmative action, which the Supreme Court sharply constrained in 2023 in Students for Fair Admissions versus Harvard; reparations; place-based investment; and the debate between universal and targeted policy. You can accept the entire historical and empirical record and still land in different places on those remedies. Many thoughtful people do. Draw this toward something usable, especially for people in public service. There's a practical implication that doesn't depend on resolving the politics: if unequal outcomes can be produced by processes and defaults, not merely bad intentions, then good intentions alone don't guarantee fair results. You have to look at the outcomes your processes actually produce. Examine outcomes by group. Test for unintended barriers. Is a step screening people out for reasons unrelated to what you care about? Design processes that are transparent and accessible by default. None of that requires adopting any particular position on the contested remedies. That is ordinary institutional practice, and it connects to humility as a working stance. You can't introspect your way to fairness. You measure. Sincerity isn't a substitute for evidence. You check. Racism in America is best understood not as a collection of individual villains, but as a long documented history that built structures in housing, wealth, justice, health, education, whose effects compound across generations and are measurable today. That record is strong and mainstream. And what we should do about it is a genuine democratic debate where people of good faith disagree. Holding both at once - taking the evidence seriously and the disagreement seriously - is what a mature understanding looks like. Take the evidence seriously and take the disagreement seriously. A good place to end.

blocks.body:
People talk past each other because they are not talking about the same object. Individual racism is prejudice and hostile intent. Institutional racism, named in 1967 by Stokely Carmichael and Charles Hamilton in Black Power, is an institution producing racially unequal outcomes even when no single person intended harm. Structural racism is those processes interlocking across housing, schools, jobs, health care, and justice so that opportunity and risk fall along racial lines over generations.

blocks.caption: The Constitution named slavery. Later maps named credit. History here is law and policy, not a feeling.

blocks.body: If you do not know that Reconstruction included Black officeholding and that it was dismantled on purpose, you will think 1964 was the first try. If you do not know Jim Crow was a legal system blessed by the Supreme Court, you will think the past was only private meanness. Starting lines in wealth, housing, and who is believed were built in public.
blocks.heading: Why a DHS employee needs this, not as trivia
In this lesson you will
items: Place slavery in law, not only in memory.
Name Reconstruction as a real, then destroyed, multiracial democracy.
See Jim Crow as statute, court, terror, and labor.
Carry one DHS close: “the past is over” is a claim you still have to check against outcomes.

events.body: Race-based slavery in the colonies; Constitution: three-fifths clause, fugitive slave clause. About four million enslaved by 1860.
events.title: Chattel slavery in law

events.body: 13th abolishes slavery; 14th equal protection; 15th bars racial barriers to voting.
events.title: Three amendments

events.body: Black Americans voted and held office. Real multiracial democracy in the South. The part people skip.
events.title: Reconstruction

events.body: Federal troops withdrawn. Disenfranchisement, racial terror, Jim Crow.
events.title: Dismantling

events.body: Supreme Court blesses “separate but equal.” Segregation as doctrine, enforced by poll taxes, sharecropping, lynching.
events.title: Plessy v. Ferguson

events.body: Millions leave the South and meet new tools of segregation in northern cities — including the housing machine in lesson 5.
events.title: Great Migration

blocks.heading: A short spine — not the whole library

blocks.body: The disagreement later is not whether this was unjust. It is how much of it still operates in a present-tense process.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Reconstruction is the skipped chapter that makes 1964 look like a first attempt instead of a second.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: History here is about starting lines, not a magic proof that every present gap is current discrimination.

options.text: Nothing. 1964 is the only date that matters.

You will think equal-protection language was never tried, or that Jim Crow was only custom. You will miss that a democracy was built and then taken apart on purpose — which is how starting lines get reset.
It only matters for historians.
It proves every present gap is discrimination.

blocks.alt: An empty hearing room — law can change in a day; starting lines do not.
blocks.caption: Brown, 1964, 1965, 1968: world changing. The modern disagreement is not whether they mattered. It is whether they finished the job.

blocks.body:
Brown v. Board (1954) overturned Plessy. The Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965), and Fair Housing Act (1968) outlawed discrimination by law. Genuinely world changing.

Position A (serious): the legal barriers fell, so the job was substantially done. Remaining gaps are mostly culture, class, or behavior.

Position B (much of the scholarship): ending legal segregation did not undo the wealth, housing, and health inequalities already produced. If a group was barred for centuries from building assets, “now it’s equal on a Tuesday” does not move the starting line.

This title will not make you pick A or B as a loyalty test. It will make you look at present outcomes anyway — because the Equity Policy already does.
blocks.heading: Two serious positions
In this lesson you will
items: Give the civil-rights statutes their due.
State the live disagreement without mocking either side.
See why a DHS dashboard is how you refuse to settle it by slogan.

blocks.body: The disagreement is not whether the past was unjust. It is how much the past still operates in the present.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Hold the disagreement. Check the process. That is public-service practice.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Ranking colleagues is Polarization. The record can be shared while remedies stay contested.

options.text: End the meeting until they agree on remedies.
Agree the statutes mattered. Then look at who your process currently serves and burdens — the outcome — without requiring them to join a team.
Declare position A racist.
Declare position B unpatriotic.

blocks.question: Which move matches this title when two colleagues hold position A and position B?

blocks.alt: A modest Minnesota street — home equity is how most families store a cushion.
blocks.caption: In the decades the government built a middle class through homeownership, federal policy locked many Black families out by design. Rothstein, The Color of Law.

blocks.body:
Richard Rothstein’s argument in The Color of Law (2017): it was not only private prejudice. New Deal and FHA mortgage programs, official maps that colored Black neighborhoods red (redlining), racial covenants in deeds. In the years the federal government subsidized white homeownership, Black families were largely excluded from that machine.

Home equity is, for most families, the largest store of wealth — what you pass on, borrow against, use for tuition. A multi-decade head start predicts a gap that lasts after the formal discrimination ends. That is a mechanism, not a metaphor.
blocks.heading: Why housing is the linchpin

blocks.alt: Bar chart of 2022 median family wealth: White about 285 thousand dollars, Black about 45 thousand, Hispanic about 62 thousand.
blocks.caption: Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022. Median White family wealth about $285,000; Black about $44,900; Hispanic about $61,600. Median, not mean. Not income — wealth.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Separate income from wealth.
See federal housing policy as a public machine.
Read a median as “typical family,” not an average pulled by the top.
Land it: DHS does not run FHA, but DHS runs eligibility, waivers, and who can stay housed enough to use a service.

blocks.body: A wealth gap is not a proof that your Tuesday hire was biased. It is a reason “treat everyone the same” starts on different floors.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Race versus class is a real debate about emphasis. It does not erase the median gap or the housing mechanism.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not collapse the chart into a legal verdict, and do not throw the chart out because class exists.

options.text: Class is irrelevant.

Class is in the story. The SCF still shows a racial gap in the typical family’s cushion. Housing policy was racialized on purpose. You can hold class and race together. Wilson and others argue about emphasis. The chart is still the chart.
The chart proves every DHS decision is discrimination.
Medians are meaningless.

blocks.question: Someone says the wealth chart is “just class.” Strongest disciplined reply?

blocks.heading: DHS close — your turn
items: Where does housing stability show up in your work (eligibility, address, portal access, keeping a child at home)?
If a typical cushion differs by a factor of six, what identical requirement might land differently?

blocks.alt: A hearing room — enforcement is a system with discretion points.
blocks.caption: Michelle Alexander’s The New Jim Crow is a popular interpretation. BJS and the Sentencing Project are the counts. Keep them labeled.

blocks.alt: Bar chart: Black share of U.S. population about 14 percent versus Black share of sentenced prisoners 32 percent in 2022.
blocks.caption: BJS, Prisoners in 2022: about 32% of sentenced state and federal prisoners were Black. Black Americans are about 14% of the U.S. population. The Sentencing Project’s U.S. imprisonment-rate ratio is about 4.8 to 1, Black to white. A gap is a disparity.

blocks.body:
Undisputed: the U.S. incarcerates a larger share of its people than almost any nation; Black Americans are imprisoned at several times the white rate. Contested: how much of that is differences in offending versus differences in who is policed, stopped, charged, sentenced. Honest researchers say both, in proportions people argue about.

Where the system is well documented: discretionary points such as drug enforcement, where usage is similar across groups and arrest is not. You can accept the disparity without settling the full causal story. Disparity is an observation. Discrimination is a causal claim. Good scholarship does not collapse them.
blocks.heading: The discipline
In this lesson you will
items: Read a population-versus-prison chart without turning it into a verdict.
Keep Alexander as interpretation and BJS as count.
See Minnesota’s child-welfare numbers as DHS’s own house — still as disparity until cause is shown.

blocks.alt: Bar chart of Minnesota out-of-home care relative rates: white baseline 1, Black and Hispanic about 2, American Indian about 16.
blocks.caption: Minnesota DHS child-welfare reporting as publicly summarized for 2023 (DHS-5408PA-ENG): Black and Hispanic youth about twice as likely as white children to be in out-of-home care; American Indian / Native youth about sixteen times as likely. ICWA is a government-to-government path, not a diversity module.

blocks.body: A sixteen-times gap in your own agency’s data is not “national politics.” It is a Minnesota human-services outcome. Cause still has to be argued. The number does not get to be ignored.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Publish, examine the process, keep Tribal sovereignty. Do not collapse the ratio into a courtroom.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A large published gap is not a verdict and not ignorable. Consultation is a door, not a module.

options.text: The ratio proves every removal was discrimination.

The ratio is a disparity this agency already publishes. Ask what the process does at each step. Use ICWA as government-to-government, not as a racial seminar. Do not treat “we mean well” as the analysis.
Native numbers are too small to mention.
This belongs only in Curriculum I.

blocks.question: The Minnesota chart shows Native children far more likely to be in out-of-home care. Strongest next sentence?

blocks.alt: A clinic waiting area — health outcomes are produced in systems, not only in households.
blocks.caption: Researchers point to differential treatment and chronic stress, against a history that includes Tuskegee and still shapes trust. Cause is studied. The rate is not a rumor.

blocks.alt: Bar chart of 2023 U.S. maternal mortality: Black 50.3, White 14.5, Hispanic 12.4, Asian 10.7 deaths per 100,000 live births.
blocks.caption: CDC NCHS, Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2023. Black 50.3 per 100,000 live births; White 14.5; Hispanic 12.4; Asian 10.7. The 2021 peak was higher (Black 69.9; White 26.6). The gap is not new.

blocks.body: If a gap vanished after you controlled for income and education, “it’s just poverty” would be a stronger sentence. In Black maternal mortality, the gap persists after those adjustments. That does not name a single doctor as a villain. It does mean the simple class-only story is incomplete. Differential treatment, weathering, and trust built by documented abuse are among the mechanisms researchers study.
blocks.heading: What the adjustment does
In this lesson you will
items: Read a rate per 100,000 without turning it into a morality play.
See why “adjusting for income” is the honest test of a class-only story.
Land it on MA, behavioral health, and who is believed at a desk.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Test the class-only story. Do not skip race because class exists, and do not skip class because race exists.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The disciplined move is the adjustment. Maternal mortality is a case where the gap survives it.

options.text: Agree. Income explains all health gaps.
Ask whether the gap remains after income and education. In maternal mortality it does. Class can still matter. Race is not therefore off the table.
Income data is biased, so ignore it.
Only CDC staff may speak.

blocks.question: A packet says a health gap is “socioeconomic, so race is off the table.” Strongest reply?

items: Where does “who is believed” show up in your health, MA, or behavioral-health work?

blocks.alt: Documents on a table — method is how a claim earns the word evidence.
blocks.caption: Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004): identical resumes, names randomized. White-sounding names got significantly more callbacks. That isolates perceived race in one setting. It does not settle a legislature.

blocks.body:
Audit studies randomize a racial signal (a name, an appearance) and hold the rest constant. Clean causal evidence in a narrow market (hiring, housing). Not a picture of a whole life.

Administrative data (wait times, removals, imprisonment) can show large disparities. They rarely isolate a single cause. A gap can be current discrimination, accumulated history, offending, eligibility, or a mix.

Attitude surveys measure what people say they believe. They do not measure what a portal does at 7 p.m.

No single method is decisive. The rigorous move is to triangulate: where independent methods point the same way — housing, lending, hiring — the finding is mainstream, not fringe.
blocks.heading: Three tools, each with limits
In this lesson you will
items: Give skepticism its due.
Know what an audit study can and cannot do.
Refuse to treat a dashboard gap as a completed causal story — and refuse to treat it as noise.

blocks.body: You cannot introspect your way to fairness. You measure. Sincerity is not a substitute for evidence.

blocks.heading: DHS close — how this changes a packet

items.body: You do not yet have a disparity. Ask for the breakout. “We don’t have it” is a finding.
items.title: You have a blended average

items.body: You have a disparity. You still need a story about mechanism before you write “discrimination” as if a court had spoken.
items.title: You have a breakout

items.body: Now you are triangulating. Change the design. That is Adaptation. That is also the toolkit.
items.title: You have an audit or a lived-experience pattern plus a number

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. That is the briefing’s method in a packet.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not collapse, and do not vanish, the number. Method is how you stay out of both traps.

options.text: Any racial gap in our data is discrimination.

A gap is a disparity. Discrimination is a causal claim. Audit evidence can isolate cause in a narrow setting. Dashboards need breakouts. Triangulate before you either freeze the design or name a villain.
Gaps are too confounded to mention.
Surveys of feelings are the gold standard.

blocks.question: Which sentence is the most disciplined?

items: On one live metric: do you have a blend, a breakout, or both?
What would triangulation look like this month (a number plus who you hear plus one design test)?

blocks.alt: Study, not a rally — frameworks are tools, not teams.
blocks.caption: This lesson represents views fairly. It does not pick a team. The Supreme Court constrained race-based admissions in 2023. Values enter at remedies.

blocks.body:
Critical race theory began as a legal framework (Bell, Crenshaw): racism as embedded in structures, not only individual prejudice. In public it became a much broader, disputed slogan, especially about schools. Use the technical meaning or you will talk past people.

Colorblindness: policy should not classify by race. Proponents: official race risks new unfairness. Critics: ignoring race while past effects persist locks the gap in.

Race versus class: William Julius Wilson emphasized class; others argue race retains independent power. Most serious work now treats an interaction. Emphasis is still debated.

Remedies: no scholarly consensus. Affirmative action was sharply constrained in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023). Reparations, place-based investment, universal versus targeted policy — you can accept the entire record and still disagree. Many thoughtful people do.
blocks.heading: Contested on purpose
In this lesson you will
items: Describe each framework without a sneer.
See where values enter (remedies) versus where evidence already sits (the record).
Know what a DHS employee can do without resolving the politics.

blocks.body: Good intentions and fair processes can still produce unequal outcomes. Looking at those outcomes does not require you to adopt a contested remedy.

blocks.heading: What does not depend on picking a team

tabs.body: Break out who waits, who is removed, who is hired, who completes. The Equity Policy already asks this.
tabs.label: Examine by group

tabs.body: Is a step screening people out for reasons unrelated to the goal? Change or defend it with a reason.
tabs.label: Test barriers

tabs.body: Transparent criteria. More than one channel. Language. Disability. Not a slogan — a design.
tabs.label: Accessible by default

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Institutional practice can proceed while remedies stay contested.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The briefing’s usable implication does not depend on resolving the politics. Look at outcomes. Test barriers.

options.text: They must pick one remedy before any process can change.
They can keep the disagreement. The packet still names who is affected, looks at the data, and tests barriers. That work does not wait on a national consensus.
Colorblind process forbids any breakout.
CRT requires a race-only remedy.

blocks.question: Two directors accept the SCF wealth chart and disagree about targeted versus universal policy. What does this title require of the packet?

blocks.body:
You now have definitions that stop people talking past each other; a history of starting lines; civil-rights statutes and the live argument about what they finished; housing and wealth as a public machine; justice and Minnesota child welfare as disparities that still need cause; health gaps that survive income; a method (triangulate); and frameworks you are not required to join.

The Equity Policy already named racial equity as measurable change in the lives of people of color, and named DHS an antiracist organization in an outcome sense. The toolkit is how a packet does that. Curriculum I is how you notice difference without ranking the room. This title was the record those two stand on.

course.introTranscript: Minimization is not a personal verdict. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, it is a work habit: we treat everyone the same, and we call that fairness. The Equity Policy asks for something else — an equity lens, and an organization that is intercultural as well as antiracist. This course does not score you. It shows what sameness-as-fairness does in a packet, a hire, and a front desk — and what it looks like to notice difference without ranking people, then to change the work. You choose how far to go. The continuum is a map, not a test.

blocks.alt: A working table — this program starts with the work, not a verdict.
blocks.caption: You choose this title. Nothing here grades you. The test, if there is one, is whether Tuesday’s packet still treats everyone as the same person.

blocks.body:
People, Access and Culture is a voluntary developmental program for DHS employees. It is a resource for the Equity Policy duty: analyze actions through an equity lens so disparities shrink and access improves. It is not a test, a ranking, or a required stage.

This title is the floor of Curriculum I — Intercultural development. It teaches a published map of how people and groups orient to difference — the Intercultural Development Continuum (IDI, LLC) — and then it stays in the work: a front desk, a hire, a dashboard, a toolkit attached after the vote.
blocks.heading: Why this title exists
In this lesson you will
items: Know what this program will and will not do with you.
Hold three policy values as related, not identical.
See where this title sits among the others.
Decide whether to continue — that decision stays yours.

blocks.body: This course does not score you. If a word names something you recognize in the work, that recognition is yours.

blocks.heading: Three values the Equity Policy names — kept distinct

tabs.body: Capability to shift perspective and adapt behavior across cultural differences and commonalities. This title lives here. The continuum is the map.
tabs.label: Intercultural

tabs.body: The policy commits DHS to operating as an antiracist organization and defines racial equity as measurable change in the lives of people of color. That is Curriculum II — the record, Minnesota human services, culture without theater. Not this title’s whole job.
tabs.label: Antiracist

tabs.body: Many cultures in a common space; disability, language, LGBTQIA2S+, veterans, place. Curriculum III is Adaptation in a specific practice — accessibility, family, employment, health. The toolkit is the shared method across all three.
tabs.label: Multicultural / access

blocks.heading: What this title will not do

items.body: No badge, no report, no homemade inventory. We describe Minimization as a work habit DHS culture often uses. We do not announce who you are.
items.title: It will not assign you a stage

items.body: Civil rights, labor relations, Tribal consultation, and any assessment you already completed stay where they belong.
items.title: It will not replace HR or a complaint door

items.body: Intercultural competence without racial structure is Minimization in nicer clothes. We will say when a habit hides race. The deep record is another title.
items.title: It will not mash race into “just culture”

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Sameness-as-fairness is the habit this title names. It is not a verdict and not the whole policy.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Treating everyone the same is the Minimization habit, not the finish line — and not a person to report. The policy asks for a lens, not sameness.
