blocks.alt: Chart of the Intercultural Development Continuum from Denial through Adaptation, with Minimization highlighted.
blocks.caption: Conceptual source: Intercultural Development Continuum, IDI, LLC. This image is original One DHS explanation. It is not an assessment.

blocks.body:
The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC) describes orientations toward cultural difference. On the left, monocultural mindsets: difference is missed (Denial) or judged (Polarization). In the middle, a transitional mindset: difference is de-emphasized (Minimization). On the right, intercultural mindsets: difference is comprehended (Acceptance) and bridged in thought and behavior (Adaptation).

Moving right is not a promotion. It is a change in what you do with difference. This course will not place you on the line. It will ask what the work does with difference.
blocks.heading: What you are looking at
In this lesson you will
items: Name all five orientations in plain language.
See Minimization as transitional — not the worst, not the goal.
Separate Polarization (us/them) from Acceptance (difference without ranking).
Hold Adaptation as behavior change, not a feeling.

blocks.body: Minimization is often an achievement out of us-versus-them. It is also where “we’re all the same” hides who the form was built for.

blocks.heading: Five orientations — in the work, not as a score

items.body: The process assumes one kind of person. Other ways of living, speaking, deciding, or moving through a building do not register as relevant. “We don’t have those clients.”
items.title: Denial — misses difference

items.body: Us and them. Defense: our way is the right way. Reversal: their way is the only virtuous way. Either way, ranking. A DHS meeting that becomes a fight about who is the problem is often Polarization, not analysis.
items.title: Polarization — judges difference

items.body: Common humanity is real and useful. The trap is using it to skip structure: language, disability, race, Tribe as government, who has a portal. “We treat everyone the same” is the signature sentence.
items.title: Minimization — de-emphasizes difference

items.body: You can describe how this process lands differently without ranking the people it lands on. Curiosity without a costume. You may still not have changed the form.
items.title: Acceptance — comprehends difference

items.body: Two moves: shift the frame (see it as they live it) and shift the behavior (change the script, the channel, the meeting, the packet). The Equity Analysis Toolkit is an Adaptation method when it is used before the lock.
items.title: Adaptation — bridges across difference

cards.back: Minimization signature. Personhood is real. Erasing how the process lands is the habit.
cards.front: “We don’t see color / disability / language. We see people.”

cards.back: Polarization. Difference is judged. The form is never the object.
cards.front: “Those people don’t want what we offer.”

cards.back: Toward Acceptance and Adaptation. The process is the object.
cards.front: “What would have to be true for this to work on the language line at 7 p.m.?”

cards.back: Often Minimization with a dashboard. The design stayed the same.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Adaptation is the behavior in the design, not the sentence in the deck.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A values line or a lunch is not a shifted process. Adaptation changes the path someone has to walk.

options.text: “We value diversity and inclusion.”
Keeping a staffed phone path because the portal assumes English, daytime, and a private device.
“I don’t see difference; I see the human.”
A lunch-and-learn about culture.

blocks.question: Which sentence is Adaptation rather than a better speech?

blocks.heading: Which orientation is the work using?

items.text: One form, one channel, “fair because identical.”
“If they wanted services they’d figure it out like we did.”
Break out wait times by language and add a channel the data said people already use.
A blended statewide average as proof the change is fine.
The meeting becomes who is “for equity” and who is “against.”

blocks.alt: An empty table after a meeting that treated everyone as the same person.
blocks.caption: A decision can be sincere and still built for one kind of Tuesday.

blocks.body:
Many DHS employees arrived at “treat everyone the same” for decent reasons: they watched Polarization harm people; they believe in equal protection; they do not want to be the person who sorts human beings. Minimization is often an achievement. The IDC names it as transitional — between monocultural and intercultural — for that reason.

The Equity Policy still asks for an equity lens: who is affected, what the data show, who you heard, what you will change. Identical treatment on an unequal starting line is how a disparity lasts. That is not a theory you have to love. It is how a portal, a hire, and a visit-request form actually behave.
blocks.heading: Give Minimization its due
In this lesson you will
items: Separate common humanity from sameness-as-process.
See why Minimization is stable in government work.
Name the cost: who the “same” process was built for.
Hold the policy’s lens without treating Minimization as a sin.

blocks.body: Equal protection is not the same thing as one form, one channel, one average.

blocks.heading: Why this habit sticks in a human-services agency

items.body: “Treat everyone the same” sounds like the Civil Rights Act. Sometimes identical treatment is required. Sometimes identical treatment is how a group already behind never gets in. The lens is how you tell which Tuesday you are on — not a vibe.
items.title: It feels legally safe

items.body: One script. One dashboard. One launch date. Noticing difference takes time. Minimization is a speed strategy that calls itself fairness.
items.title: It is fast

items.body: Talking about race, disability, language, or Tribe as government can pull a room into Polarization. Minimization keeps the peace. The packet still ships.
items.title: It avoids a fight

items.body: Don’t stare. Don’t name. Don’t make it a thing. That was manners. It is not analysis.
items.title: It matches how many of us were taught to be good

blocks.cite: This lesson, to take with you
blocks.text: Common humanity is real. Using it to skip who the form was built for is the habit.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Naming impact is analysis. Ranking people is Polarization. The policy wants the first.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The lens names groups to see impact, not to crown virtue. Sameness-as-process can be the unfairness.

options.text: Never name groups. Sameness is the only fair process.
Naming who a process helps and who it burdens is how you check fairness. The Equity Policy requires that look. It is not a ranking of human worth.
Name groups only in a values statement, never in the data.
Turn the meeting into who is evolved enough.

Tell a legal identical requirement from a lazy identical process.

blocks.body: A blended average that looks fine can hide the group this change will hit first. That is Minimization with a chart.

tabs.body: One greeting, one ID rule, English-only signage, a portal kiosk with no staffed phone. Fair because identical. Unusable for language, disability, or someone who cannot stand in that line.
tabs.label: Front desk

tabs.body: Statewide wait improved. No race, language, disability, or county breakout. “We don’t have that data” is a finding. Using the blend as proof is Minimization.
tabs.label: Data

tabs.body: The same interview, the same unpaid extra step, the same “culture fit.” Identical. Built for people who already look like the unit.
tabs.label: Hiring

tabs.body: “Families will handle nights” as if every household were the same household. Some are already carrying three jobs. Some are not safe. Some are a Tribal kin network the form cannot see.
tabs.label: Family / unpaid work

tabs.body: Attached after the vote, or filled with “all Minnesotans will benefit.” That is not analysis. That is Minimization wearing the Equity Policy.
tabs.label: The toolkit

blocks.alt: Printed pages on a desk — a chart that may be hiding a group.
blocks.caption: If the packet cannot name a group, it cannot see a disparity. The policy already defined disparity that way.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A blend plus a blank form is the habit. Adaptation would break it out and change the path.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Mentioning a group is not Polarization. A dashboard without a who is Minimization, not proof.

options.text: Average wait is the fairness measure. Ship it.
The blend may hide who got slower. The blank toolkit is sameness-as-process with a cover sheet. Ask for the breakout and a design change before the lock.
Only Equity staff may question a dashboard.
This is Polarization because someone mentioned race.

blocks.question: A launch packet shows average wait time down and a blank equity toolkit. Strongest read?

items.text: Portal-only visit requests; phone retired as “inefficient.”
“No disparate impact anticipated” and no groups named.
“Culture fit” as the tie-breaker.
Statewide average as the only performance slide.
Mom will do nights — no yes, no backup.

blocks.alt: A table after a meeting that became a fight.
blocks.caption: A room that splits into “for equity” and “against” has left analysis. It is ranking people.

blocks.body:
People leave Minimization two ways. One is Acceptance: we can describe how this lands differently without crowning saints. The other is Polarization: now there is an us and a them. Government rooms are good at the second. The program’s job is to make the first more likely.

That is why this title will not score you, will not stage you, and will not turn a packet review into a character trial. The object is the process.
blocks.heading: Why this lesson is here
In this lesson you will
items: Hear Polarization in both directions (defense and reversal).
Keep the process as the object when someone makes it personal.
See why “confront” without a method creates backlash.
Practice one sentence that names impact without ranking the room.

blocks.body: If the meeting is about who is evolved, you are not doing an equity analysis. You are sorting colleagues.

items.body: “This is America.” “They have to learn the system.” “We’re lowering the bar.” Difference is a threat to the default.
items.title: Defense — our way is the real way

items.body: “Anyone who questions this is the problem.” “If you don’t already know, you don’t belong in the room.” Difference is a moral ranking. Still Polarization.
items.title: Reversal — their way is the only virtuous way

items.body: “This channel assumes daytime English and a private device. Here is who already uses the phone. What do we change before Friday?” The people in the room are not the object. The channel is.
items.title: What Acceptance sounds like instead

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Adaptation work stays on the design. Ranking the speaker is Polarization.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A character trial is not analysis. Sameness-as-default is the habit this title named. Change the path or defend it with data — don’t sort the room.

options.text: Argue about who is biased until the hour is gone.
Return to the process: who already uses the phone, what the policy requires, what we will change or not change before the date — keep the channel as the object.
Agree, because identical treatment is always fairest.
Label them publicly so the team learns.

blocks.question: Someone says, “If we add a phone path we’re catering to people who won’t adapt.” Strongest next move?

items: Write a sentence about your process that names an impact and does not rank a colleague.
Pattern: “This step assumes ____. The people who already ____ will feel it first. I want us to look at ____ before we lock it.”

blocks.alt: Two colleagues looking at a form together — the process is the object.
blocks.caption: Acceptance is being able to say how this form lands. Adaptation is changing the form, the channel, or the date.

blocks.body:
Acceptance: you can describe difference without ranking it. You know the portal is easy for someone with a private device at noon, and hard for someone on a language line at 7 p.m. You have not necessarily fixed it.

Adaptation: you shift the frame (see it as they live it) and you shift the behavior (keep the phone, change the hours, break out the data, use the toolkit before the lock). The Equity Policy’s toolkit is an Adaptation method when it is not a cover sheet.
blocks.heading: Two moves, in order
In this lesson you will
items: Tell Acceptance from a nicer Minimization speech.
Tell Adaptation from a lunch-and-learn.
Connect the toolkit to this map without making it a test.
Choose one Adaptation move on your live process.

blocks.body: A values sentence is Minimization in better clothes if the channel did not change.

events.body: Online-only. “Everyone has a phone.” Language, disability, greater Minnesota do not appear.
events.title: Miss it

events.body: “If they cared they’d use the portal.” Or: “Only a bigot would launch a portal.” The people are the object.
events.title: Judge it

events.body: One portal for all. Toolkit blank. Average wait improves. “Fair because identical.”
events.title: Same path

events.body: Name who already uses the phone. Name who has no private device. The room can say this without a fight.
events.title: See it

events.body: Keep a staffed phone and in-person path. Translate the script. Delay the launch until that is funded. Date an owner.
events.title: Change it

blocks.alt: Two people walking — a process that can travel with more than one kind of body.
blocks.caption: Adaptation is visible in the path someone can actually walk — not in the poster in the lobby.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The policy asks for a lens that changes actions. Noticing without a design change is incomplete.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Seeing the burden and shipping the same path is not Adaptation. The toolkit’s job is a modification, not a later dashboard.

options.text: Adaptation — they noticed.
They reached noticing (Acceptance) and stayed in Minimization on the design. Monitoring is not the behavior change.
Denial — they never saw it.
The Equity Policy is satisfied by noticing.

blocks.question: The team can describe who the portal will fail. They ship it anyway and “monitor.” Where is the work?

items.text: We can name who lacks a private device.
We keep a staffed phone path and fund it.
“All Minnesotans will benefit” in the impact statement.
Break out wait time by language this quarter.
A diversity sentence at the top of the memo, same form below.

course.introTranscript: An equity analysis is not a cover sheet you attach after the decision is already made. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, the Equity Analysis Toolkit is the method: name who is affected, look at the data, hear the people who live with the result, write the benefits and the burdens, and put a date on who is accountable. This course teaches the toolkit, then walks it one step at a time. Bring a real piece of work — a policy, a budget line, a hiring process, an IT change. If you cannot name who is harmed and who benefits, you are not done.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: a blank toolkit after the vote. Adaptation: name who, look at the data, date an owner — before the lock. This course does not assign a score.

Minnesota DHS expects staff to use the Equity Analysis Toolkit when work will last and needs leadership approval — policy, budget, hiring, IT, contracting, service delivery, community engagement. Teams still treat it as a cover sheet. This course teaches what the toolkit is for. Then each lesson makes you write against one live piece of work.

The official toolkit and User Guide remain the form you file. This is original One DHS instructional content so a working unit can actually run it.
blocks.heading: Why this is a course and a walkthrough
In this lesson
items: Separate a method from a slogan.
Name when a full analysis is required and when a scan is enough.
Hold education and practice on the same page: learn it, then write it.
Pick the live work you will walk for the rest of this course.

blocks.body: If the decision is already made and the toolkit is a cover sheet, you are not doing an analysis. You are decorating a choice.

cards.back: A written look at how a decision will reduce or grow disparities — before you lock it. Not a values statement. A method.
The official DHS / enterprise steps: results, data, engagement, benefits and burdens, impact statement, accountability, alignment, sustainability.
A shorter honest page when time is tight. Still names outcome, groups, data, benefits/burdens, what you will change, and who you will tell. A scan is not a skip.
Every lesson ends with writing on your live work. If you skip those prompts, you took a course. You did not use the toolkit.

blocks.body: Toolkit step 1 asks for desired results and who is disproportionately affected — race and ethnicity, LGBTQIA2S+, disability, veterans, language, place, Tribal Nations, intersections. Teams write “all Minnesotans” because it feels fair. It hides the people who already wait, already cannot use the portal, already do the unpaid night. If your analysis has no empty chair, you have not started step 1.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either we slow everything for a 40-page analysis, or we ship and “keep equity in mind.” The toolkit is neither. Cover-sheet fills a form after the vote. Walk-the-tool uses data and engagement to change the work, then writes who owns the rest. A scan can still be walk-the-tool if it is honest. A long toolkit can still be a cover sheet if nothing moved.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters
In this lesson
items: Tell a cover sheet from a walkthrough.
Keep speed without skipping the people in lesson 3.
Run toolkit steps 2 and 3 — data and engagement — on your work.
Know when civil rights or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: If the only people in the room already have the access this proposal assumes, you engaged the wrong room.

items.body: Decision first. Form later. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a failed launch. Looks compliant. Changes nothing.
items.title: Cover-sheet

items.body: Groups first. Data and who you heard. A design change before approval. Dates and names. The packet can still say no to an unfunded mitigation.
items.title: Walk-the-tool

items.body: EOAD, Tribal consultation, labor relations. Use those doors. Do not paste them into a stakeholder bullet.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

tabs.body: Online-only visit requests, starting in October. Staff want less phone tag. Leadership wants a launch date.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: “Improves access.” Statewide average. Webinar of supervisors. Monitor after go-live. Phone line “year two.”
tabs.label: Cover-sheet

tabs.body: Groups named (disability, language, greater Minnesota). Data: those groups already use the phone. Engagement with people who call from a lobby. Keep a staffed phone and translated path. Launch slips until that is real.
tabs.label: Walk-the-tool

tabs.body: If a Nation’s program is affected, consultation. If the change is a civil-rights access issue, EOAD. Do not workshop those as “feedback.”
tabs.label: Formal path

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Write who you actually heard. Supervisors are not a substitute for the people in step 1.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Engagement is who lived it, not who could make a noon webinar. Name the gap.

options.text: A webinar counts. Move on.
You heard supervisors. Write that. Then hear the groups you named — people who use the service, and the staff who will carry the change — before you call it engagement.
Engagement is optional if the data is strong.
Send the slide deck and call it complete.

blocks.alt: The worksheet — the loop has to survive an ordinary packet.
blocks.caption: If the method needs a 40-page binder, the cover sheet will win. Write short, specific lines.

blocks.body: You already did steps 1–3 (results, data, engagement). The rest of the official toolkit is: benefits and burdens plus a design change; a short impact statement; accountability with names and dates; alignment with equity people and policy; sustainability — is this funded and able to collect the data you promised.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?
In this lesson
items: Run toolkit steps 4–8 on the same piece of work.
Treat “we will monitor” as not a modification.
Write a statement only this proposal could wear.
Refuse an unfunded mitigation.

blocks.body: A mitigation that lives only in a “we will monitor” sentence is not a modification. Change the design. If it is not funded, write that.

items.body: Who is better off. Who pays in time, money, access, dignity, or risk. What you will change in the design before approval. Does this still match step 1?
items.title: 4. Benefits, burdens, unintended consequences

items.body: Six to ten sentences: action, groups, what data and engagement showed, main benefit, main burden, design change, remaining risk. No slogan.
items.title: 5. Equity impact statement

items.body: Three rows: impact review (who, when); outcome review (who, when); communication (who, when, which audience — including people who carry the burden).
items.title: 6. Accountability

items.body: Sit with the equity director or committee before the freeze. Match equity policy and the strategic plan. Do not bcc after the packet is locked.
items.title: 7. Alignment

items.body: Personnel, money, data collection, engagement. If the phone line in your mitigation has no FTE, you did not mitigate. You wrote fiction.
items.title: 8. Sustainability

blocks.cite: A statement that could only belong to this proposal
blocks.text: We are moving visit requests online. People with disabilities, limited English, and greater-Minnesota households without reliable internet will feel this first. Data shows phone requests are already how those groups reach us. We will keep a staffed phone and in-person path, in plain language and the languages we already fail. The remaining risk is night and weekend coverage — named, dated, and owned.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Unfunded mitigation is not mitigation. Change the work or change the date.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Step 8 is whether it can actually run. A press line is not a phone line.

options.text: Approve and hope a vacancy appears.
Write that the mitigation is unfunded, delay or change the launch until the line is real, and sit with the equity director and the budget owner before Friday.
Put the phone line in “year two” and launch anyway.
Ask Communications to announce both the portal and a future phone line.

blocks.question: The analysis is complete. The mitigation (a staffed phone line) has no budget. Approval is Friday. Strongest move?

items.text: Keep a translated phone path because the burden is already visible.
Six sentences only this proposal could wear.
Sit with the equity director before the approval date.
Impact owner + date; communication owner + audience.
No FTE for the mitigation — delay the launch.

items: Two benefits (who). Two burdens (who). One design change — not a monitoring promise.
Draft the six-to-ten sentence impact statement. Read it out loud. If it could fit any other project, rewrite.
Three dated rows: impact, outcome, communication (name + audience).
Who in the equity role you will sit with, and whether the mitigation is actually funded.

blocks.heading: From evidence to ordinary work
In this lesson
items: Finish or repair one live packet.
Practice a repair that does not make Equity staff the author of your miss.
Set a seven-day practice transfer.
Know the job aid and the formal doors you must not skip.

blocks.cite: The intro, to take with you
blocks.text: If you cannot name who is harmed and who benefits, you are not done.

items.body: Apply the job aid to the work you named. Short lines. Groups. Design change. Dates. Small and complete.
items.title: Fix the next packet

items.body: The unit’s decision memo or leadership cover. If it cannot hold groups, a burden, and an owner, every future packet will be a cover sheet.
items.title: Fix one template

items.body: If “we’ll monitor” is the applause line, interrupt it. If a blank toolkit is praised as on time, stop praising it.
items.title: Fix the culture tell

blocks.body: You will have shipped a cover sheet. Repair is: name the miss, name the groups, change the design or the date, put owners on the calendar, sit with the equity director, and skip the speech that makes them comfort you. “We should have named who pays before the vote. We are naming it now. We can still change the launch.”
blocks.heading: Repair without theater

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Repair is the channel restored plus a method change. It is not a sharing circle they did not ask to lead.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Drop-off is data. Restore access. Do not make the people who paid the burden the trainers for your skip.

options.text: Ask them to tell the team how it felt, as a learning moment, then move on.
Name the miss, restore another channel now, write groups and owners, and change the template so the next launch does not ship a cover sheet.
Leave it — they will adapt, so the analysis no longer applies.
Add an equity poster to the intranet.

items: Finish steps 1–8 on the work you named in lesson 1 — or repair the packet that already moved.

sections.heading: Steps 1–4 — see it
items: 1. Desired results: action, 12-month change, who is disproportionately affected, which DHS areas.
2. Data: workforce and community, breakouts, what is missing, how you will get it.
3. Engagement: who you heard, how, what they said, who is still missing. Tribal consultation is not a stakeholder workshop.
4. Benefits, burdens, unintended consequences, and a design change — not a monitoring promise.

sections.heading: Steps 5–8 — write it and own it
items: 5. Impact statement: six to ten sentences only this proposal could wear.
6. Accountability: impact owner + date; outcome owner + date; communication owner + date + audience.
7. Alignment: equity director / committee before the freeze; equity policy and strategic plan.
8. Sustainability: funded, staffed, able to collect the data. Unfunded mitigation is not mitigation.

course.introTranscript: Family is not a staffing plan. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, natural supports are the people a person already has — family, friends, neighbors, faith — and they are chosen, not assumed. If we write a mother's nights into the plan without asking her, we did not honor family. We used her. If we shut out the people the person wants in the room, we did not protect them. We isolated them. This course is a staff guide: ask who they want. Name what unpaid people actually do. Do not treat family as free labor, or as a veto. And put respite on the page before someone burns out.

blocks.alt: A kitchen-table planning meeting with family, the person, and a case manager.
blocks.caption: The person is at the table. Family is at the table because they were asked — not because they are the default staff.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: family is a staffing plan. Adaptation: ask who they want, name unpaid hours, put paid support on the page. This course does not assign a score.

Minnesota person-centered practice says we build and keep relationships with family and friends, and we use natural supports so a person can live the life they want. Teams still write “mom will do nights” without asking mom. Teams still leave a friend out of the meeting because they are “not legal.” Teams still treat a guardian as the only relative who counts.

If family is only named when we need unpaid hours, we did not honor a circle. We used it. This course is the staff job: ask who they want, name what unpaid people actually do, and put paid support and respite on the page before someone burns out.
blocks.heading: Why this is a leadership course
In this lesson
items: Separate a chosen circle from a staffing assumption.
Name unpaid work as work — not love that never needs rest.
Hold family as support without handing them a veto.
Own the staff job: ask, name, and do not dump.

blocks.body: If we write a mother’s nights into the plan without asking her, we did not honor family. We used her.

cards.back: People already in the life — family, friends, neighbors, faith, chosen family. Unpaid. Chosen. Not a vendor. Not a default night shift.
Who they want in the meeting, on the call, at the hospital. Blood is not automatic. A roommate or a friend can be closer than a parent they do not want in the room.
Nights, rides, meds, translation, the 2 a.m. call. If it is in the plan, it is work. Work needs a yes, a limit, and a rest.
Paid time so unpaid people can stop. If respite is “we’ll see,” the plan is hoping a relative never gets sick.

items.body: A circle is not a prize for compliance. Isolation is not a teaching method.
items.title: They should not have to earn their people

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A circle is asked, not assumed. Unpaid nights without a yes are a dump.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not assume. Do not erase. Ask both people. Name the work. Fund what they cannot do.

blocks.question: A plan says “family provides overnight support.” No one asked the sister who lives there. What is the Family and Natural Supports move?

blocks.caption: If the calendar only works because someone unpaid never sleeps, the plan is not a plan. It is a hope.

tabs.body: “Mom will do it.” Mom was not in the meeting. The nights were not counted. That is staffing by silence.

tabs.body: A friend they want is “not family.” A sibling is “too involved.” The person named them. We left them in the hallway.

tabs.label: The veto

tabs.body: No family. We write “no natural supports” and stop looking. Neighbors, faith, chosen family, a coworker still exist — or paid support has to be real, not a shrug.

blocks.body: If we shut out the people the person wants in the room, we did not protect them. We isolated them.

events.body: Build and keep family and friends. Natural supports help a person toward what is important to them — not toward cheaper staffing.
events.title: Relationships are the work

events.body: The person (and, if there is a guardian, supported decision-making) chooses who helps decide. A default relative is not informed choice.

events.body: Family caregiver coaching and respite are real services. If they never make the page, we are still using people.
events.title: Coaching and respite exist

events.body: Visitors, relationships, and privacy are not house favors. A restriction has to be justified.
events.title: Rights still apply

events.body: Staff still write “family will handle it.” The protocol did not finish the work. The yes and the respite are the work.
events.title: This course

items.body: Unpaid hours appear as if they were a service. No yes. No limit. No backup. When the relative gets sick, the “plan” was never a plan.
items.title: The dump

items.body: A friend, a partner, a sibling the person wants. We call them extra. We keep the meeting small. The person is lonelier and we call it clean.
items.title: The shutout

items.body: A parent or guardian speaks over the adult. We take that as the circle. Legal authority is real. It is not a reason to skip the person’s people.
items.title: The veto

blocks.alt: A father and daughter look at a paper together; a worker sits aside, not between them.
blocks.caption: Sit beside. Do not sit between. The paper is theirs to see.

cards.back: Love is not a shift. Nights are a shift. Shifts need a yes and a rest.
cards.front: If they love them, they can do the nights

cards.back: Friends, neighbors, faith, chosen family. Or paid support has to be honest. An empty line is not an assessment.
cards.front: No family means no natural supports

cards.back: Guardianship is a legal door. The circle can still include people the guardian does not prefer — if the person wants them, and the law allows the role.
cards.front: A guardian is the whole family

cards.back: Not asking makes a later crisis. A named limit is kinder than a silent dump.

blocks.alt: Two people walking together on a Minnesota sidewalk.
blocks.caption: Ask who never gets named: fathers, siblings, friends, chosen family, neighbors, people with no living relatives.

blocks.body: Who we count and who we dump on are not even. Mothers and daughters-in-law carry silent nights. Fathers and brothers are often not asked. Chosen family and friends are treated as unofficial. People of color and immigrant families get used as interpreters. Tribal kinship gets flattened into “mom.” People with no family get written as empty — then isolated.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows
In this lesson
items: Map who is overused and who is never invited.
Treat chosen family as family when the person says so.
See how race, language, and kinship stack in the note.
Name the harm of “no natural supports” as a closed file.

blocks.body: If only one tired relative is on the page, you do not have a circle. You have a single point of failure.

items.body: Write the truth. Then look for friends, faith, neighbors, and paid support that is real. Do not leave a blank and call it assessment.
items.title: People with no living family — or no safe family

items.body: A partner, a roommate, a church friend. If the person wants them, they are natural supports. “Not legal” is not a reason to leave them in the hall.
items.title: Chosen family and friends

items.body: We default to the woman who already said yes once. Ask the whole set. Some will say no. That no is useful.
items.title: Fathers, brothers, and people we do not ask

items.body: Kinship may not match a metro nuclear-family form. Ask. Consult. Do not use a child as the interpreter and the night shift.
items.title: Tribal kinship and immigrant families

blocks.alt: A staff person listens while a young man explains who he wants at his meeting.
blocks.caption: The people we call “too involved” are often the people they already chose.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Natural supports are the people they already have. The form’s “family” box is not the whole map.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: An empty line is not neutrality. Ask. Name. Backup. Do not wait for a vendor to notice a neighbor.

options.text: Neighbors are not family. The line can stay.
Ask the person about the neighbor. If they want them, name the meals as unpaid support with a yes and a backup — do not leave the file empty because the form said “family.”
Pay the neighbor immediately or drop them.
Wait for a social-network vendor assessment.

A chosen partner left out of planning.

blocks.alt: An empty kitchen — what the week looks like when unpaid people are the whole plan.
blocks.caption: Family-as-staff ends at “they’ll handle it.” Person-names-circle designs the week after they say what they can actually do.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either family does everything unpaid, or professionals shut family out. Natural supports are neither. Some relatives want a role. Some cannot. Some are the risk. Person-names-circle asks who they want and what each person can do. Family-as-staff writes nights into the plan because it is cheaper.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters
In this lesson
items: Tell a chosen role from an assumed shift.
Keep family in without handing them a veto.
Hold guardianship without erasing the rest of the circle.
Know when maltreatment, 245D, or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: A guardian can hold some legal doors. They do not own the whole circle, and they are not a night shift unless they say yes.

items.body: Lead with who is unpaid. Fill gaps with a relative. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a year. Use family when they say yes. Do not use them as the budget.
items.title: Family-as-staff

items.body: They name who. Each person names what they can do. Paid support and respite fill the rest. Family can still be central. They are not silent labor.
items.title: Person-names-circle

items.body: Maltreatment, a 245D visitor restriction, guardianship changes, and Tribal consultation are not informal family conflict. Use the proper door.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

blocks.alt: A community walk with someone they chose.
blocks.caption: Person-names-circle is visible: they are outside with someone they want. The plan did not invent a relative, and it did not ban one.

tabs.body: An adult wants more community. A sister is exhausted. A friend is willing on Saturdays. Staffing is thin. A parent wants to decide.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: Sister keeps doing evenings. Friend is unofficial. Parent’s preference overwrites the adult. Respite is “later.”
tabs.label: Family-as-staff

tabs.body: Adult names sister, friend, not every evening. Sister’s limit is written. Saturday friend is named with a backup. Respite and paid hours cover the gap. Parent is in a conversation, not the vote on the friend.
tabs.label: Person-names-circle

tabs.body: If a visitor ban is actually a restriction, use 245D. If maltreatment is suspected, report. If a Tribal program is involved, ask consultation leads.
tabs.label: Formal path

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Rest is how a circle lasts. Withholding respite to keep free labor is the dump.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not erase family. Do not withhold rest. A yes with a limit lasts longer than a silent night shift.

options.text: Agree. Keep unpaid nights so family stays involved.
Drop family from the plan to keep it clean.
Respite is how unpaid people stay in the life. Name the yes, name the limit, put rest on the page, and stop using burnout as a staffing strategy.
Write “family declined respite” without asking.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “If we offer respite they’ll stop helping.” What is the strongest response?

items.text: Write the friend’s Saturday with a backup and the sister’s limit.
Fill every gap with “mom” because the budget is tight.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of treating it as family conflict.
Assume a Tribal citizen’s kin should not be in the meeting.

blocks.body: Six moves: ask who they want; ask each person what they can actually do; write unpaid work as work; put paid support and respite in the gaps; keep legal doors in their lane; review when someone is tired or a yes changes.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?
In this lesson
items: Run the circle-and-respite loop on one person you already serve.
Write a yes, a limit, and a backup.
Use questions that do not force a relative to perform love.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one silent night shift, a hallway friend, and a frozen “family will handle it.”

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write the circle so you still ask for a yes.

items.body: Privately first. Family, friends, neighbors, faith, chosen family. Who is in the meeting. Who is not. Do not start with the loudest relative.
items.title: 1. Ask who they want

items.body: A yes with a limit. Sunday rides, not every night. Translation, not the only voice. If they cannot say no in the room, ask again without the audience.
items.title: 2. Ask what they can actually do

items.body: Hours, days, what happens if they are sick. If you cannot write it, it is not a plan. It is a hope.
items.title: 3. Name unpaid work as work

items.body: Paid hours, respite, CFSS/CDCS, a neighbor who said yes on Saturdays with a backup. The gap is staff work, not a moral test for family.
items.title: 4. Fund the gap

items.body: Guardianship, 245D restrictions, maltreatment. Use them. Do not let them become the whole circle.
items.title: 5. Keep legal doors in their lane

items.body: When someone looks exhausted, when a yes changes, when a friend moves. An undated “family will handle it” is a future crisis.
items.title: 6. Review — tired is a finding

blocks.alt: Listening with the laptop closed — who they want at the meeting.
blocks.caption: The circle is a control, like a med pass. If it is not written, the dump will win at 10 p.m.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A no is data. The gap is ours to fund. She can still be family without being the night shift.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named a limit. Your job is to fund the gap, not to talk her back into unpaid nights.

options.text: Ask her to try a little longer. The waiver waitlist is long.
Thank her, take weeknights off her line, put paid support or respite in the gap this week, and date a review — honor the no.
Remove her from the person’s life to keep boundaries clean.
Ask the person to convince her in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A sister says, “I cannot do weeknights anymore.” The plan still lists her. Best next step?

items.text: Ask privately who they want in the meeting.
Write Sunday rides with a backup driver.
Authorize respite after a sister names exhaustion.
Use 245D if visitors are actually being restricted.
Ask again when a friend moves away.

items: Choose one person and run the chair test.

Set a seven-day practice transfer.

blocks.cite: Lesson 1, to take with you
blocks.text: If we write a mother’s nights into the plan without asking her, we did not honor family. We used her.

items.body: Apply the job aid to one person. Ask who, ask what they can do, name the work, fund the gap. Small and complete.
items.title: Fix the next meeting

items.body: The unit’s planning form. If it cannot hold a friend, a limit, and respite, every future meeting will dump or shut out.
items.title: Fix one template

items.body: If “good families handle it unpaid” is the applause line, interrupt it. If a quiet unpaid night is praised as loyalty, stop praising it.
items.title: Fix the culture tell

blocks.body: You will have written unpaid nights without a yes, or left a friend in the hall. Repair is: name the miss, ask now, write the limit, put respite or paid hours in the gap, invite the person they named, and skip the speech that makes them comfort you. “We should have asked you months ago. We are asking now. You can say no. We will fund the gap.”
blocks.heading: Repair without theater

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Repair is the yes restored plus a gap funded. It is not a sharing circle she did not ask to lead.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Coping is not a yes. Fund the gap. Do not make her the trainer for your dump.

options.text: Ask her to tell the team how it felt, as a learning moment, then move on.
Name the miss, ask what she can still do, take nights off her line if that is the no, put paid support or respite in the gap, and change the template so the next family is asked.
Leave it — they have coped, so natural supports are working.
Add a poster about family in the hallway.

blocks.question: You realize a plan has said “family overnight” for two years. The sister is tired and not angry. What is the strongest repair?

blocks.heading: Seven-day list
items: Pick one person whose plan says “family” without a named yes. Ask them who they want. Ask the unpaid person what they can actually do.
Write one limit and one backup — or take the unpaid line off and fund the gap.
Invite one person they named who has been in the hallway.
Tell your team that unpaid nights are not the applause line — then follow it when the first no is inconvenient.

items.text: Ask one unpaid person what they can actually do, with a chance to say no.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of calling it family conflict.
Write “family will handle nights” without a yes.
Put respite or paid hours in one gap you heard this week.
Leave a chosen partner in the lobby to keep the meeting small.

course.introTranscript: A name is not a lifestyle. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, people with disabilities are also LGBTQ — and they do not have to earn that by looking ready, or by asking a guardian's permission. If we write the wrong name on the door, or tell the house who they are dating, we did not keep them safe. We outed them. This course is a staff guide: use the name they use. Ask who may know. Do not let a form, a roommate, or a family veto become the plan. And stop treating identity as extra.

blocks.alt: A living-room planning meeting where the person is in the conversation, not the topic of it.
blocks.caption: Inclusion looks like the name they use already on the page — before anyone asks permission.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: identity as extra, same form for everyone. Adaptation: the name they use is already on the page. No score.

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act protects sexual orientation and gender identity in public services. Person-centered practice says we listen to what is important to someone. Teams still treat LGBTQ identity as a “family issue,” a roommate problem, or something to wait on until the person “understands.” Names get overwritten on doors. Dating gets announced at the house meeting. Forms still force a box that is not their life.

If inclusion is a poster in the hallway and the wrong name on the file, we did not include anyone. This course is the staff job: use the name they use, ask who may know, and stop treating identity as extra.
blocks.heading: Why this is a leadership course

blocks.body: This lesson names the terms. Later lessons show how we still out and overwrite, whose identity we skip, two honest frames, and a Tuesday-sized method — the name-and-privacy loop.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Separate identity from a lifestyle you get to approve.
Name outing as a safety failure, not a care update.
Hold disability and LGBTQ on the same page without a ranking.
Own the staff job: the name and the circle of who knows.

blocks.body: If we write the wrong name on the door, or tell the house who they are dating, we did not keep them safe. We outed them.

cards.back: The name and pronouns they tell you. Not the birth certificate, not the guardian’s preference, not the form’s first box. Ask. Write it. Use it.
Telling someone else their sexual orientation or gender identity without their say. A house meeting, a family call, a roommate “update.” Safety is not a reason to broadcast.
A circle they name: which staff, which family, which housemates. Different people may get different information. That is privacy, not secrecy from you.
It is not a specialty caseload. It is not after the waiver goals. Relationships, names, and bodies are already the plan — or the plan is incomplete.

blocks.heading: What sits with you versus specialists

items.body: You decide whether the door, the MAR, and the meeting use their name; whether a family veto is allowed to stand; and whether “the house should know” is actually outing.
items.title: You own the name and the circle

items.body: Use Equal Opportunity and Access, mental health, and community LGBTQ resources they choose. Bring them in when asked. Do not out someone in order to get a referral.
items.title: Specialists support the path

items.body: A correct name is not a prize for compliance, insight, or guardian approval. It is the minimum.
items.title: They should not have to earn a correct name

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Daily name is theirs. Legal name is a document. Broadcasting to the house is outing.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A guardian does not own a name. Insight is not a ticket. Telling the house is not consistency. It is outing.

options.text: The guardian decides. Keep the legal name everywhere.
Use the name they use in daily life and on the door; keep legal name only where the law requires it; do not let a veto overwrite how they are called.
Wait until they can explain their identity in a team meeting.
Tell the whole house so staff are “consistent.”

blocks.question: A person asks to be called by a name that is not on the birth certificate. A guardian says no. Staff keep the old name on the door. What is the LGBTQ+ Inclusion move?

events.body: Minnesota Human Rights Act: sexual orientation and gender identity are protected in public services. A DHS meeting is not exempt because it is “just the house.”

items.title: Overwrite the name

items.body: A staff huddle, a roommate update, a family call. Framed as safety. Lived as outing. Ask who may know. Write the circle.
items.title: Broadcast to the house

items.body: A parent says no pronouns, no dating, no “phase.” The adult is in the room. Guardianship is not ownership of identity.
items.title: Family veto

cards.back: Disability does not cancel identity. Capacity to name a preference is not the same as a term paper. Ask. Listen. Use it.
cards.front: They don’t understand enough to be LGBTQ

cards.back: All adults take relationship risk. LGBTQ dating is not a special danger category. Support around safety. Do not ban the life.
cards.front: Dating is a risk we should pause

cards.back: Then train the staff who need to know. A roster of every roommate is not a training plan.
cards.front: Staff will slip if we don’t tell everyone

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Bathroom privacy is architecture and staffing. It is not a license to out someone.

options.text: Safety first. The house needs to know.

blocks.question: Night staff tell the whole house a person is trans “so nobody is surprised in the bathroom.” Strongest read?

blocks.alt: A clinic counter — the first place a name is said out loud.
blocks.caption: Ask who never gets asked: people with high support needs, people who do not use speech, people of color, people in greater Minnesota.

blocks.body: Being asked and being believed are not evenly distributed. People with intellectual disabilities, people who use devices, people of color, Two-Spirit and Native people, and people in greater Minnesota are more likely to be treated as “not really” LGBTQ and less likely to get a correct name, a private circle, or a relationship that is allowed to exist. If your “open” homes are all people who already look like a metro clinic’s idea of out, your practice has a queue you have not named.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows
In this lesson you will
items: Map who is not asked and who is over-exposed.
Treat communication access as part of identity, not a later translation.
See how race, disability, and place stack in the note.
Name the harm of writing a relationship as a behavior.

blocks.body: If only the people who already look “out” get a correct name, you do not have inclusion. You have a sorting hat.

items.body: A device left at home is a missed name and a missed “don’t tell my dad.” Meetings without the device are guesses we write as plans.
items.title: People who do not use speech the way we do

items.body: A crush, a kiss, a late-night text. We write risk. We do not ask what they want, who may know, and what support would make it safer.
items.title: People whose dating is called behavior

items.body: An English-only identity conversation and a family interpreter who is also the veto are access failures dressed as culture.
items.title: People of color and people who need another language

items.body: Do not paste a clinic label over a word they did not choose. Ask. Consult. Do not treat Two-Spirit as a synonym you get to assign.
items.title: Tribal citizens and Two-Spirit people

blocks.alt: A staff person listens while a young man explains who should be called and how.
blocks.caption: The people we call “not ready to know who they are” are often the people we have not asked in a format they can use.

cards.back: Staff skip the question because it feels complicated. Skipping is a decision. It writes them as straight and cis by default.
The person who translates also shuts the identity down. Get a real interpreter. Ask the person separately.
Greater Minnesota has people, partners, and privacy needs. Distance is not a reason to skip the name or broadcast it to the only grocery in town.
No community, no dating, no internet “for their own good.” Protection that removes a life is still a smaller life.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Not asking is how you write a default. The device is how you ask.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Skipping is not neutrality. A specialist can help. It cannot be the reason you never ask.

options.text: They would tell us if it mattered. Stay the course.
Identity questions are too abstract for device users.
The people who need communication access are missing from the question. Ask with the device, extra time, and a private room — do not skip them.
Wait for a specialist vendor that handles “sexuality and IDD.”

blocks.question: Your “inclusive” files are mostly people who already used LGBTQ words. Device users were never asked. What does the empty-chair test say?

items.text: A person with high support needs who has never been asked what name they want.
A relationship announced to roommates without their say.
A Tribal member whose word for themselves was overwritten as a clinic label.
Family used as the only interpreter for an identity conversation.
A greater-Minnesota adult told to “keep it quiet in this town.”

blocks.alt: A closed door — privacy as a real practice, not a rumor.
blocks.caption: Family-veto ends at the relative’s no. Person-names-self designs the circle after they speak.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either we tell everyone, or we hide the person from their own life. LGBTQ inclusion is neither. Some people need family in the circle. Some families are the risk. Person-names-self asks who they are and who may know. Family-veto lets the loudest relative write the door.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters
In this lesson you will
items: Tell a needed legal name from a daily overwrite.
Keep privacy real when a guardian or a house is loud.
Hold safety without using it to isolate.
Know when civil rights, maltreatment, or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: A guardian can hold some legal doors. They do not own a name, a pronoun, or a private circle.

items.body: Lead with who will be upset. Pause the name. Hide the dating. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a life. Family can be support. They are not the author of identity.
items.title: Family veto

items.body: They say the name. They name the circle. Staff use it. Legal name stays where the law requires it. Safety is designed, not broadcast.
items.title: Person-names-self

items.body: EOAD complaints, maltreatment, a 245D restriction on relationships, and Tribal consultation are not “team vibes.” Use the proper door.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

blocks.alt: Two people walking in a Minnesota park — a community life that includes who they are.
blocks.caption: Person-names-self is visible: they are outside. Someone is with them. The identity was not a hallway rumor. It was supported.

tabs.body: An adult wants to date. They use a name that is not on the birth certificate. A parent is angry. Staffing is thin. Housemates gossip.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: No dating. Old name on the door. “We’ll revisit when the family is ready.” The person is not the author.
tabs.label: Family veto

tabs.body: Daily name in use. Circle written: which staff, which family, not the house meeting. Dating supported with ordinary safety. Parent is in a conversation, not the vote.
tabs.label: Person-names-self

tabs.body: If a rights restriction is actually being used, use 245D. If maltreatment or harassment is happening, report. If EOAD is the door, call it. If a Tribal program is involved, ask consultation leads.
tabs.label: Formal path

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Documents have rules. Daily speech has the person. Those are not the same sentence.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not erase required documents. Do not erase the daily name. A guardian’s no is not a house style guide.

options.text: Agree. Legal name everywhere is the safe play.
Ignore the guardian completely in every document.
Use the name they use in daily life; keep legal name only where required; write the circle of who knows; do not treat a guardian’s comfort as the whole plan.
Write “family declined identity” and close the topic.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “Until the guardian agrees, we use the legal name so we don’t get in trouble.” What is the strongest response?

items.text: Daily name on the door; legal name on the billing form only.
Pronouns paused until a parent is comfortable.
Call EOAD when a program refuses a name as a civil-rights issue.
Assume a Tribal citizen will use metro clinic labels.
Use the 245D process if you are actually restricting relationships.

blocks.alt: A community walk that includes who they are, not a hallway briefing.
blocks.caption: The method has to survive a Tuesday shift change. If it needs a binder, the old name on the door will win.

blocks.body: Six moves: ask the name they use; ask who may know; put it on the door and the meeting; fix the form; support relationships without broadcasting; review when someone new is hired or a family wants a veto.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?
In this lesson you will
items: Run the name-and-privacy loop on one person you already serve.
Write a circle that a night shift can actually follow.
Use questions that do not force a coming-out speech.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one house briefing, a frozen legal name, and a family veto.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the shift changes. Write the name and the circle so Tuesday-night staff do not invent a briefing.

items.body: Privately, with the device if they need it. Name, pronouns, how to say it. Do not require a speech. Do not correct their word.
items.title: 1. Ask — the name they use

items.body: Which staff, which family, which housemates, which clinic. Different people may get different information. Write it.
items.title: 2. Ask who may know

items.body: Door, meeting, MAR-as-used, how we call them in the waiting room. Legal name only where the document requires it.
items.title: 3. Put it where daily life happens

items.body: If the form cannot hold the name, add a line. If the waiting-room script deadnames, change the script. The form is staff work.
items.title: 4. Fix the form

items.body: Dating, community, clothes, a partner at the table. Ordinary safety. Not a house announcement.
items.title: 5. Support the life without broadcasting

items.body: When someone is hired, when a family pushes, when they change the circle. An undated “everyone knows” is outing waiting to happen.
items.title: 6. Review — new staff, new veto, new ask

blocks.alt: Listening with the laptop closed — who should be called, and how.
blocks.caption: The circle is a control, like a med pass. If it is not written, the house meeting will invent one.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Don’t-tell is the circle. New staff are a review trigger. The house is not the briefing list.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named a privacy line. Your job is a written circle, not a broadcast and not a family override.

options.text: Tell the whole house so nobody slips.
Write the circle (dad is out), brief only the staff who need it, put the daily name where they live, and review when the new staff start — honor don’t-tell as far as the real duty allows.
Call dad anyway because guardianship.
Ask them to present the request in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A person says, “Don’t tell my dad.” New staff start next week. Best next step?

items.text: Ask privately what name they use.
Change the waiting-room call so it matches.
Support a date without a house announcement.
Write which family members are not to be told.
Rebrief when a new DSP starts.

blocks.body: Last lesson: practice on one person already on your caseload, and how to repair a name or an outing that outlived their say.

blocks.alt: The living-room meeting from the start of the course.
blocks.caption: The course ends when one wrong name or one house briefing that outlived their say gets fixed.

blocks.body: You now have a definition of name and circle, a pattern for outing and overwrite, a chair test, two frames, and a six-move loop. This lesson turns that into one person you already serve — not a special “LGBTQ project.”
blocks.heading: From evidence to Tuesday
In this lesson you will
items: Choose one person and run the chair test.
Practice a repair that does not make them manage your embarrassment.
Set a seven-day practice transfer.
Know the job aid and the formal doors you must not skip.

blocks.cite: Lesson 1, to take with you
blocks.text: If we write the wrong name on the door, or tell the house who they are dating, we did not keep them safe. We outed them.

items.body: Apply the job aid to one person. Ask the name, write the circle, fix the door, support the life. Small and complete.
items.title: Fix the next meeting

items.body: The unit’s intake, MAR-as-used, or waiting-room script. If the template can hold the name they use, every future person inherits the method.
items.title: Fix one template

items.body: If staff joke about names or gossip about dating, interrupt it. If a quiet closet is praised as keeping the peace, stop praising it.
items.title: Fix the culture tell

blocks.body: You will have used the wrong name or briefed the house. Repair is: name the miss, use the correct name now, rewrite the circle, change the door and the script, and skip the speech that makes them comfort you. “We should have used this name months ago. We are using it now. We will not tell the people you named as out. You can say stop.”
blocks.heading: Repair without theater

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Repair is the name restored plus a method change. It is not a sharing circle they did not ask to lead.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Getting used to a wrong name is not consent. Change the door. Do not make them the trainer for your miss.

options.text: Ask them to tell the team how it felt, as a learning moment, then move on.
Name the miss, change the door and the daily scripts now, write the circle, and change the template so the next person does not wait two years.
Leave it — they seem used to it, so inclusion does not apply.
Add a poster about names in the hallway.

blocks.question: You realize a door still has a name they asked you to stop using two years ago. They are not angry. What is the strongest repair?

blocks.heading: Your seven-day list
items: Pick one person whose name or circle you have never asked — or asked once and never written. Ask privately, with access they can use.
Fix one daily place: door, MAR-as-used, waiting-room script.
Write who may know. If you cannot name the circle, you are one briefing away from outing.
Tell your team that a house announcement is not the applause line — then follow it when the first don’t-tell is inconvenient.

items.text: Ask one person the name they use and who may know.
Call EOAD when a program refuses a name as a civil-rights issue.
Brief the whole house so “nobody slips.”
Change one door or waiting-room script this week.
Pause pronouns because a parent objected.

blocks.cite: Lesson 2, to take with you
blocks.text: “The house should know” is often “I do not want to track who may know.”

blocks.body: Open the Name-and-Privacy Job Aid and keep it beside your next intake. This course is original One DHS instructional content for staff practice. course.introTranscript: The person you met last year may not be the person in the room today. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, brain injury is often invisible — fatigue, memory, mood, and a life that got smaller without a scar you can point to. If we quiz them on what they should remember, we did not assess. We shamed. This course is a staff guide: slow down. Write it down. Do not treat a tired brain as noncompliance. And review the plan when the injury is still changing.

blocks.alt: A kitchen-table planning meeting with mixed staff and a person who does not look “injured.”
blocks.caption: If you are waiting for a scar, you will miss the injury sitting at the table.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: they seemed fine, so same meeting. Adaptation: pace, write, do not quiz. This course does not assign a score.

Minnesota’s Brain Injury Waiver funds home and community-based services for children and adults with an acquired or traumatic brain injury. That is a program. This course is the staff job: the person in front of you may look fine, forget the appointment you set moments ago, crash after a 40-minute meeting, and still be telling the truth. Teams still write “no-show,” “noncompliant,” and “they seemed fine last year.” Those sentences are often the injury, not the character.

Complex disability here means the injury stacked with pain, mental health, substance use, housing, and a life that got smaller. If we treat only the waiver checkbox, we will miss the person.
blocks.heading: Why this is a leadership course

blocks.body: This lesson names the terms. Later lessons show how we still quiz and shame, whose injury we skip, two honest frames, and a method that fits ordinary work — the pace-and-write loop.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Separate an invisible injury from an attitude.
Name fatigue and memory as the injury, not the excuse.
Hold more than one disability on the same page.
Own the staff job: slow down and write it down.

blocks.body: If we quiz them on what they should remember, we did not assess. We shamed.
Government pages are evidence, not the staff-facing deliverable.
blocks.heading: Terms used with care

cards.back: Injury after birth — crash, stroke, assault, oxygen loss, tumor, overdose. Not the same as a lifelong developmental disability, though a person can have both.
No scar, no wheelchair, a face that “looks fine.” Fatigue, word-finding, light, mood, and memory do the work. Looking fine is not a clinical finding.
The battery runs out. A good morning is not proof they can do a three-hour meeting. After the crash they may look angry, shut down, or gone. That is the injury.
Brain injury plus mental health, pain, substance use, housing, or another disability. One program lane is not a whole person. The plan has to hold more than one story.

blocks.body: Assessors own waiver eligibility. Clinicians own medical orders. The Brain Injury Alliance and resource facilitation are partners. None of that removes the person in the planning meeting from slowing down, writing things down, and not treating a missed bus as a character test.
blocks.heading: Who holds which part
What sits with you versus specialists

items.body: You decide whether “no-show” is allowed to stand for “the morning battery was gone,” whether the plan is written in their hands, and whether last year’s person is allowed to overwrite this year’s brain.
items.title: You own the pace and the note

items.body: Use neurology, rehab, mental health, BI Waiver, and resource facilitation. Bring them in early. Do not hand them a person you already labeled as unmotivated.
items.title: Specialists support the path

items.body: A scar is not the eligibility for dignity. Looking fine is not consent to a faster meeting.
items.title: They should not have to prove they are injured

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Looking fine is not capacity. A missed appointment can be the injury. Change the method.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A tired, forgetting brain is the injury. Quizzing them or closing the file is not assessment.

options.text: Tighten the rules. If they looked fine, they could have come.
Treat memory and fatigue as the injury: shorten the meeting, write the next step in their hands, and stop using a no-show as a character finding.
Close the case. They are not ready for waiver supports.
Wait for a neuropsych report before you change how you meet.

blocks.question: A person looks well, misses the follow-up, and cannot recall the goals from last month. Staff write “noncompliant.” What is the Brain Injury move?

blocks.alt: A planning table with a pill organizer, a calendar, a house key, and a bus pass.
blocks.caption: If the next step is only in our notes, it is not in their week.

blocks.body: Move from “why didn’t they follow through?” to “what would make follow-through possible for this brain this week?” A perfect attendance record can be a success metric for a clinic. It is a poor metric for a changing injury.
blocks.heading: The shift this course asks for

blocks.body: The BI Waiver, person-centered protocol, and the Minnesota Brain Injury Alliance are public evidence. They are not the staff course. Minnesota DHS work also lands on counties, 245D homes, clinics that quiz, and people whose “noncompliance” started when nobody wrote the next bus time on paper. That is the practice context.
blocks.heading: DHS-wide, not a vendor script

tabs.body: They hear “you seemed fine last time.” They spend the meeting proving they are hurt. The energy for the actual goal is gone.
tabs.label: The person

tabs.body: Light, overlapping talk, a long agenda. We call it a meeting. Their battery calls it empty.
tabs.label: The brain

tabs.body: “No-show.” “Unmotivated.” “They remember when they want to.” Memory is missing from the sentence, so the person becomes the problem.
tabs.label: The note

tabs.body: We pick one lane — waiver, mental health, or housing — and the other stories fall off the page. Complex means all of them stay.
tabs.label: The stack

blocks.heading: Injury, support, or a character finding?

items.text: They cannot recall last month’s goals.
Write the next step on a card they take with them.
“They remember when they want to.”
A 40-minute meeting instead of two hours.
Closing the file after two no-shows with no other offer.

blocks.alt: An empty living room, TV off, one lamp on — a life that got smaller.
blocks.caption: A smaller week is often the injury doing its work. It is not proof they do not care.

blocks.body: Minnesota wrote a Brain Injury Waiver and person-centered practice into the work. Teams still start with a memory test. Clinics still run long. Notes still compare this Tuesday to a person who existed before the crash. Direct support still gets blamed when a plan required a battery the person did not have at 4 p.m.
blocks.heading: The pattern is older than the waiver
In this lesson
items: Name quiz-as-assessment as a practice, not a one-off.
See how “they seemed fine” erases fatigue.
Separate a needed review from a shame test.
Spot the three usual shrinks: quiz, overbook, freeze last year.

blocks.body: “They seemed fine” is often “I did not look long enough to see the battery.”

events.body: Home and community-based services for acquired or traumatic brain injury. A funding path. Not a personality test.
events.title: A community life after injury

events.body: Planning is not last year’s goals copied forward. The injury may still be changing.
events.title: This year’s person

events.body: Minnesota Brain Injury Alliance and partners help people and families navigate. Use them. Do not replace them with a quiz.
events.title: Resource facilitation

events.body: Memory loss does not cancel dignity, informed choice, or a community life.
events.title: Rights still apply

events.body: Staff still write “unmotivated.” The waiver did not finish the work. The note is the work.
events.title: This course

items.body: “Do you remember what we said last time?” If they fail, we doubt the injury. Memory is the finding. It is not a character score.
items.title: The pop quiz

items.body: A two-hour meeting with three topics. They nod. They crash in the parking lot. We call the hour a success because they stayed.
items.title: The overbooked hour

items.body: We plan for who they were before the crash, or for the best Tuesday last spring. A changing brain needs a dated review, not a frozen photo.
items.title: Last year’s person

blocks.alt: A clinic waiting room: a woman holds an appointment card, a support worker sits beside her.
blocks.caption: Getting there was already work. The meeting still has to fit the battery that is left.

cards.back: Humor and a good hour are not a full tank. Fatigue can drop after they leave your sight.
cards.front: If they can laugh, they can follow through

cards.back: Brain injury is often inconsistent. A good day is data. A blank day is also data. Both can be true.
cards.front: Inconsistent memory means they are lying

cards.back: Try-harder is not a rehab plan. A reminder, a ride, a shorter visit, and a written next step are.
cards.front: They need to try harder to attend

cards.back: A funding stream is not a Tuesday method. The plan still has to fit this brain this week.
cards.front: Waiver means they are already supported

blocks.heading: Myths that still sit in the room

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Bring the paper. Do not make memory the ticket into their own plan.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Recall is the injury. Quizzing them at the door is not person-centered. It is a test they already failed because of the injury.

options.text: They are not invested. Document and move on.
A pop quiz is a shame test. Put last time’s notes in front of them, ask what still fits, and stop using recall as the door to the meeting.
They need a harder neuropsych battery before we continue.
Family should answer for them from now on.

blocks.question: A team opens every review with “Tell us your goals from last time.” The person fails and shuts down. Strongest read?

tabs.body: “They no-showed. Unmotivated. They remember when they want to.” The brain is not in the sentence.
tabs.label: Character

tabs.body: “Prove you remember last month, then we will talk about work.” Access as a prize.
tabs.label: Quiz

tabs.body: “Here is last month on paper. What still fits. Here is a 30-minute visit. Here is the next step in your pocket.”
tabs.label: Pace and write

items.text: Opening with “What did we decide last time?” with no notes in front of them.
A two-hour meeting after they already used the morning at a clinic.
Copying pre-injury work goals without asking this year’s energy.
Three topics in one visit because “we might not get them back.”
Treating a good Tuesday last spring as the new baseline forever.

blocks.alt: Clinic waiting room with a support worker sitting beside, not talking over.
blocks.caption: Ask who never gets believed: women, people of color, people without a dramatic crash story, people whose English is not the meeting’s English.

blocks.body: Belief and support are not evenly distributed. Women, people of color, people with “mild” labels, people injured by assault or overdose, and people in greater Minnesota are more likely to be told they look fine and less likely to get a shorter meeting, a written next step, or a BI Waiver path. If your lowest-effort cases are all people with a visible story and a family who can retell it, your practice has a queue you have not named.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows
In this lesson
items: Map who is not believed and who is over-managed.
Treat “mild” as a label, not a small life.
See how race, gender, and language stack in the note.
Name the harm of writing fatigue as attitude.

blocks.body: If only the people with a dramatic story get believed, you do not have a brain-injury practice. You have a sorting practice that decides who counts.

items.body: No scar, no wheelchair, a job they are failing. We wait for them to “try harder” until the job is gone. Invisible is not mild.
items.title: People who look fine

items.body: Concussion, intimate-partner violence, medical events. Notes say anxiety. The brain is in the room. The note is not.
items.title: Women and people whose injury is doubted

items.body: A missed appointment plus an interpreter who was never booked becomes “they don’t care.” That is an access finding dressed as character.
items.title: People of color and people who need another language

items.body: Injury, ceremony, family, and how memory is held may not match a metro clinic script. Consultation is not a stakeholder workshop.
items.title: Tribal citizens and Urban Indian communities

blocks.alt: A staff person listens while a man with a cane explains what he remembers this week.
blocks.caption: The people we call “unreliable historians” are often the people we have not given a paper trail.

cards.back: The scan was “mild.” The week is not. Labels do not measure a Tuesday.
We talk only to the relative who can retell. The person is in the room. Put paper in their hands too.
How they were injured is not a reason to give a smaller plan. The brain still needs the same pace and the same writing.
cards.front: Overdose or assault as moral story

cards.back: Greater Minnesota has kitchens, sidewalks, and shorter visits. Distance is a design problem. It is not proof that brain injury pauses at the metro belt.
cards.front: Rural = no rehab, so no support

blocks.heading: Reading the same caseload three ways

tabs.body: Who missed. Useful. Blind to who never got a reminder they could use, and who never got believed.
tabs.label: No-show map

tabs.body: Who had a meeting that fit the battery. This is the map that predicts follow-through.
tabs.label: Energy map

tabs.body: Who has to prove they are hurt every time. Those people are doing extra work before the actual goal starts.
tabs.label: Belief map

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A full waiting room of people with spokespersons is not proof the practice works for people who come alone.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Coming alone is a design problem. A specialist can help. It cannot be the reason you stop offering a usable meeting.

options.text: That is how motivation works. Stay the course.
People without family are not ready for waiver supports.
The people without a spokesperson are missing from the method. Change reminders, length, and written next steps — do not change the presumption they belong.
Wait for a specialist vendor that handles “mild TBI.”

blocks.question: Your “engaged” clients all have a family member who retells the story. Your “no-shows” are mostly people who look fine and come alone. What does the empty-chair test say?

items.text: A woman with post-concussion symptoms written as anxiety only.
A meeting without an interpreter, then a no-show note.
A Tribal member whose family memory practices were written as “poor historian.”
No written next step, only a voicemail they will not recall.
A greater-Minnesota adult whose only offer is a three-hour metro clinic.
