blocks.alt: An empty living room — what a life looks like when the week was too long.
blocks.caption: Quiz-and-catch ends at the missed answer. Pace-and-support designs the hour after you put paper in their hands.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either we never check understanding, or we quiz until they fail. Brain injury practice is neither. Some reviews are required. Some “checks” are shame with a form attached. Pace-and-support names the battery, writes the step, and shortens the visit. Quiz-and-catch names our doubt and puts it on their memory.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters
In this lesson
items: Tell a needed review from a shame test.
Keep support real when a guardian or a prior no-show is loud.
Hold medical care without making last year’s person the destination.
Know when maltreatment, licensing, or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: A hard medical fact does not cancel the person. It changes the pace. A real review still requires paper in their hands.

items.body: Lead with what they forgot. Catch the inconsistency. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a life. Use questions when you are teaching a skill they asked for. Do not use a pop quiz as the door.
items.title: Quiz-and-catch

items.body: The life is on the table first. Last time is on paper. The visit is short enough to survive. The next step leaves in their pocket. You will still check understanding. That is not the same as a trap.
items.title: Pace-and-support

items.body: Maltreatment, a 245D process, a physician order, emergency hold, and Tribal consultation are not informal team judgments. Use the proper door.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

blocks.alt: Two people on a Minnesota sidewalk — a community hour that had to be paced.
blocks.caption: Pace-and-support is visible: they are outside. Someone is with them. The curb was not imaginary. It was designed around.

tabs.body: An adult wants to go back to work. They forget appointments. The guardian is afraid. Staffing is thin. They look fine.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: No work until they prove they can remember a weekly meeting. Looking fine is used against them.
tabs.label: Quiz-and-catch

tabs.body: Written reminders, a shorter try, a job-site with breaks, guardian in the conversation not the only voice. Review date on energy, not a freeze until they look like last year.
tabs.label: Pace-and-support

tabs.body: If a rights restriction is actually being used, use 245D. If maltreatment is suspected, report. If a Tribal program is involved, ask consultation leads.
tabs.label: Formal path

cards.back: Should mean they can use information with support. If the only test is a pop quiz, it is shame with better branding.
Needs a written step, a reminder, and a battery that was not already spent. A no-show is data for design, not a closed file.
A medical label. Not a small life. Not permission to skip accommodations.
Needs information they can still hold after they leave. If it only lived in our speech, it was not informed.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Paper is not cheating. Withholding the tool is practice at being unsupported.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not erase the goal. Do not erase the paper. Memory is the injury. The tool is the method.

options.text: Agree. Withhold paper so they practice memory.
Ignore work altogether until memory returns.
Writing it down is the accommodation. Practice with the tool, name the life they want, and stop using “they’ll never learn” as a reason to withhold support.
Write “family will remember for them” and close the goal.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “If we write everything down they will never learn to remember.” What is the strongest response?

items.text: Put last visit’s notes in front of them and ask what still fits.
Open with a memory test before any other business.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of handling it as a house issue.
Assume a Tribal citizen will not want family in the memory support.
Use the 245D process if you are actually restricting a right.

blocks.alt: A paced walk — a community hour that had to be designed.
blocks.caption: The method has to survive a busy caseload. If it needs a 40-page rehab binder, the pop quiz will win.

blocks.body: Staff need a loop that survives a full caseload. Six moves: ask this week’s energy; put last time on paper; shorten the visit; write the next step in their hands; keep the stacked stories on the page; review when the injury is still changing.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?
In this lesson
items: Run the pace-and-write loop on one person you already serve.
Write the next step so it survives the parking lot.
Use questions that do not start with a trap.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one long meeting, a frozen last year, and a no-show as character.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write it down so you still offer a short visit and a card in the pocket.

items.body: Open with how the battery is, not with a quiz. Sleep, pain, lights, what already happened this morning. If they have been tested before, say you are not testing them now.
items.title: 1. Ask — this week’s energy

items.body: Do not ask them to perform recall. Show last time. Ask what still fits. Memory is the injury. Paper is the method.
items.title: 2. Put last time on paper

items.body: One or two topics. A visit they can leave with energy left. A long success in the room can be a crash in the car.
items.title: 3. Shorten

items.body: A card, a text they can find, a calendar they actually use. If it only lives in SSIS, it does not live in their week.
items.title: 4. Write the next step in their hands

items.body: Pain, mental health, housing, substance use, another disability. If the plan is only “BI Waiver,” the rest will ambush the week.
items.title: 5. Keep the stack

items.body: A goal can be real. An undated copy of last year is a freeze. Put the next look on the plan. They can still want work. You cannot hide from the calendar.
items.title: 6. Review — the injury is still changing

blocks.alt: Listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like a med pass. If it is not on the plan, the pop quiz will win at 10 a.m.

tabs.body: A checkbox that says “goals reviewed.” A quiz. A two-hour meeting. A voicemail they will not recall. Leaders learn about harm from a no-show they cannot explain.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: Energy first, last time on paper, a short visit, a card in the pocket, stacked stories, a dated review.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page cognitive profile nobody opens on Saturday. If the method takes longer than the meeting, the quiz will win. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. They named the battery. You have a visit to design. Last month’s face is not this week’s tank.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named fatigue. Your job is pace and paper, not a longer meeting and not a pep talk.

options.text: Push through. Looking fine means they can do it.
Thank them, shorten today, put last time on paper, write one next step in their hands, and date a review of length — honor the battery they named.
Cancel all contact to honor the injury.
Ask them to present their limits in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A person says, “I cannot do a long meeting.” They looked fine last month. Best next step?

items.text: Ask how this morning already used their energy.
Leave one next step on a card they take.
Keep housing and pain on the same page as the BI goal.
Cut the visit to 30 minutes.
Show last month’s notes instead of quizzing.

Practice a repair that does not blame them for our quiz.
Set a seven-day practice transfer.

blocks.cite: Lesson 1, to take with you
blocks.text: If we quiz them on what they should remember, we did not assess. We shamed.

items.body: Apply the job aid to one person. Ask energy, paper, shorten, write, stack, review. Small and complete.
items.title: Fix the next meeting

items.body: The unit’s review agenda. If the template starts with paper in their hands instead of a quiz, every future meeting inherits the method.
items.title: Fix one template

items.body: If people who no-show are called unmotivated, interrupt it. If a long meeting is praised as thorough, stop praising it. Culture is what gets applause.
items.title: Fix the culture tell

blocks.alt: A paced community walk — the destination of pace-and-support.
blocks.caption: Return to the sidewalk. The question is whether the people we serve get this kind of hour before we congratulate ourselves for a full two-hour meeting.

blocks.body: You will have written no-show as character. Repair is: name the miss, offer a shorter visit now, put last time on paper, write the next step in their hands, change the agenda so energy comes before the quiz, and skip the speech that makes them manage your embarrassment. “We should have written this down months ago. I am writing it now. You can say stop. We will come back on a date we name.”
blocks.heading: Repair without theater

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Repair is the method restored plus a note change. It is not a sharing circle they did not ask to lead.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Looking fine is not a closed file. Restore the method. Do not make them the trainer for your miss.

options.text: Ask them to tell the team how it felt, as a learning moment, then move on.
Name the miss, offer a shorter visit, put paper in their hands, and change the agenda so energy and writing come before a character finding.
Leave it — they seemed fine, so brain injury does not apply.
Add a poster about invisible injury in the hallway.

blocks.question: You realize a file says “unmotivated” after two no-shows. The person is not angry. What is the strongest repair?

blocks.heading: Seven-day list
items: Pick one person you would usually quiz or mark as a no-show. Write a half-page: this week’s energy, what last time actually was, what “unmotivated” is doing in the file.
Offer a shorter visit and put last time on paper — or schedule that access now.
Write one next step they can take with them. If you cannot, the plan is not in their week.
Tell your team that a long meeting is not the applause line — then follow it when the first short visit is inconvenient.

items.text: Put last visit on paper instead of opening with a quiz.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of handling it as a house issue.
Write “unmotivated” after a no-show with no other offer.
Leave one next step on a card they take.
Copy last year’s goals because the meeting ran long.

course.introTranscript: Difference is not a deficit to fix. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, neurodiversity is how brains actually work — not a behavior to train out of someone. If we measure success by eye contact, stillness, and looking ready, we did not support a person. We made them perform our comfort. This course is a staff guide: change the environment first. Ask how they communicate. Honor the words they choose for themselves. And stop treating compliance as the goal.

blocks.alt: A mixed planning meeting where someone uses headphones and a tablet instead of forced eye contact.
blocks.caption: Support looks like a room that already works for more than one kind of brain.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: one kind of ready room. Adaptation: change the environment before you change the person. No score.

Minnesota person-centered practice and positive supports say we start with the person, not the program. Teams still treat stimming, silence, a device, or a need for a quiet room as something to train out. Notes say “noncompliant,” “poor eye contact,” “refused group.” Those sentences are often about our room, our pace, and our idea of ready — not about the person’s worth.

If success is stillness and looking at our face, we will keep writing people as problems. This course is the staff job: change the environment first, ask how they communicate, and stop making compliance the goal.
blocks.heading: Why this is a leadership course

blocks.body: This lesson names the terms. Later lessons show how we still treat difference as deficit, whose communication we skip, two honest frames, and a Tuesday-sized method — the environment-first loop.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Separate neurodiversity from a diagnosis to be managed away.
Name compliance-as-success as a practice, not a personality.
Ask how someone communicates before you write “won’t engage.”
Own the staff job: the room is yours to change.

blocks.body: If we measure success by eye contact, stillness, and looking ready, we did not support a person. We made them perform our comfort.
Flip each card. Government pages are evidence, not the staff-facing deliverable. These are the terms this course uses on purpose.
blocks.heading: Four words used carefully

cards.back: Human brains vary. Autism, ADHD, intellectual disability, learning difference, and more are part of that variation — not a single “normal” to restore people to.
A person whose mind works outside the majority pattern. Ask how they name themselves. Do not correct “autistic” into “person with autism” if that is not their word.
Light, noise, time, surprise, how we ask, whether the device is in the room. Change those before you write a behavior. Many “behaviors” are a body saying the room is wrong.
Eye contact, sitting still, answering on our clock, looking grateful. Useful for our meeting. A poor measure of a life. Skill-building is real. Performing neurotypical is not the same thing.

blocks.body: EIDBI and clinical teams own medically necessary intervention when a family chooses it. Positive supports own the floor against coercive practices. Licensing and 245D own rights. None of that removes the person in the planning meeting from asking, first, “What does a good day look like in this brain — and what in our process makes it worse?”
blocks.heading: Who holds which part
What sits with you versus specialists

items.body: You decide whether “noncompliant” is allowed to stand for “needed a quieter room,” whether the device came to the meeting, and whether surprise is still how we run the day.
items.title: You own the room and the note

items.body: Use speech, occupational therapy, EIDBI, positive supports, and trauma-informed clinicians. Bring them in early. Do not hand them a person you already labeled as refusing.
items.title: Specialists support the path

items.body: Access that has to be deserved after compliance is not access. It is a token economy with better letterhead.
items.title: The person should not have to earn a quieter room

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The device is speech. The rocking may be regulation. The note was about our comfort.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Engagement is not eye contact. A device is communication. Change the room before you change the person.

options.text: Train eye contact first. Then we can talk about goals.
Read the tablet as communication, stop requiring eye contact as proof, and change the room (light, noise, time) before you write a behavior.
End the meeting. They are not ready.
Wait for a specialist to translate. Planning cannot use a device.

blocks.question: A person looks at the floor, rocks, and answers on a tablet. Staff write “poor engagement.” What is the Neurodiversity move?

blocks.alt: A planning table with headphones, a communication device, a visual schedule, and a house key.
blocks.caption: If the device and the headphones never make the page, the plan was written for a different brain.

blocks.body: Move from “how do we make them look ready?” to “what environment makes a good day possible, and what communication already works?” Quiet compliance can be a success metric for a clinic hour. It is a poor metric for a human life.
blocks.heading: The shift this course asks for

blocks.body: Person-centered protocol, positive supports, and EIDBI policy are public evidence. They are not the staff course. Minnesota DHS work also lands on lead agencies, 245D homes, classrooms that punish stimming, and people whose “behavior plan” started when nobody brought the device. That is the practice context.
blocks.heading: DHS-wide, not a vendor script

tabs.body: They hear “use your words” when they already are — on a device, in movement, in silence. They are trained to look at eyes they cannot stand.
tabs.label: The person

tabs.body: Fluorescent lights, overlapping talk, surprise schedule changes. We call it a meeting. Their nervous system calls it an attack.
tabs.label: The room

tabs.body: “Noncompliant.” “Refused group.” “Poor eye contact.” The environment is missing from the sentence, so the person becomes the problem.
tabs.label: The note

tabs.body: We correct “autistic” or refuse “person with autism.” Their name for themselves is data. Ours is not a policy.
tabs.label: The words

blocks.body: Tap a statement, then tap the bucket. The point is not to attack skill-building. It is to stop hiding a smaller person inside a compliance form.
blocks.heading: Sort the work

items.text: Bringing the communication device to every meeting.
They asked to learn to ride the bus.
No community time until they sit still for 20 minutes.
Headphones allowed in the waiting room.
Eye contact required before we “know they are listening.”

blocks.alt: An open office under fluorescent light; one person covers an ear, another works at the next desk.
blocks.caption: If the only tool is “try harder,” we have already decided the room is fine and the person is not.

blocks.body: Minnesota wrote person-centered practice and positive supports into the work. Homes still treat stimming as disruption. Clinics still skip the device. Teams still use group as the only offer. Direct support still gets blamed when a plan required a person to look neurotypical on a Tuesday night.
blocks.heading: The pattern is older than the protocol

blocks.body: This lesson is the history and the habit — so you can see your own note in it.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Name compliance-as-success as a practice, not a one-off.
See how “use your words” erases a device.
Separate a skill someone asked for from a performance we demanded.
Spot the three usual shrinks: train the face, skip the device, punish the stim.

blocks.body: “Noncompliant” is often “the room was wrong, and we wrote it on the person.”

events.body: Listen to what is important to someone. A plan driven by professional comfort is not person-centered, even with the header.
events.title: People, not programs

events.body: Respect, choice, and feeling safe are the floor. Coercive practices are not a teaching method with better branding.
events.title: Not a hold as the plan

events.body: Early intensive developmental and behavioral intervention is a Medical Assistance benefit. It is not a mandate to make a child look typical. Families choose. The person is still a person.
events.title: Intensive support is a choice

events.body: A behavior program does not cancel dignity, communication access, or the right to a community life.
events.title: Rights still apply

events.body: Staff still write “poor eye contact.” The protocol did not finish the work. The note is the work.
events.title: This course

items.body: Eye contact, a still body, a “calm” voice. Some people can do that for an hour and crash after. We call the hour success and never see the crash.
items.title: Train the face

items.body: Left in the van. Battery dead. “We’ll just talk.” Then the note says they would not answer. Access failed before the question.
items.title: Skip the device

items.body: Rocking, flapping, humming, pacing. Sometimes it is joy. Sometimes it is regulation. Treating it as disruption is how we make the next incident.
items.title: Punish the stim

blocks.alt: A young person uses a communication tablet while a support worker sits beside them at the same height.
blocks.caption: If the device is in the room, they already used their words. Write that down.

blocks.body: If you do not put communication on the paper, “won’t talk” will. If you do not name the lights, “behavior” will. If you do not ask what they call themselves, our labels will. Shrinks are usually omissions, not villains.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: our comfort fills the vacuum

cards.back: Many people listen better when they are not performing a face. Listening is not an eyeball position.
cards.front: They understand more if they look at me

cards.back: Sometimes. Sometimes it is thinking. Sometimes it is joy. Ask, look at context, and do not make stillness the only allowed body.
Speech is not more real than a tablet. If the device is how they talk, it is the first tool, every time, including the clinic.
cards.front: A device is a last resort

cards.back: Some supports help skills a person wants. Erasing autism is not a DHS outcome. Quality of life is.
cards.front: Intensive therapy will make them typical

blocks.heading: Myths that still sit in the room

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Safety is a check-in design problem. It is not a reason to run a nervous system without a tool that already works.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Hearing them is real. Taking the only regulation tool is not the only way to hear them. Design around it.

options.text: Safety first. Headphones come off.
They will get used to the noise. That is skill-building.
The environment is the intervention. Design a way to check in that does not require taking the headphones — do not make sensory pain the house rule.
Wait for OT to write a letter.

blocks.question: A home forbids headphones “because we need to hear if they need us.” The person is more distressed without them. Strongest read?

tabs.body: “They rock, avoid eyes, and won’t do group. Increase social skills hours.” The room is not in the sentence.
tabs.label: Deficit

tabs.body: “When they sit still, they can have community.” Access as a prize.
tabs.label: Compliance

tabs.body: “Group is loud. They communicate on a device. Here is a quieter offer, the device in the bag, and a community hour that does not require a performance.”
tabs.label: Environment first

items.text: Community time cancelled until they stop flapping.
Meeting held without the tablet “to work on talking.”
A goal that is only “maintain eye contact for 10 seconds.”
Staff answer for them because the device is in the van.
A still, quiet body is the only praised outcome in group.

blocks.body: Next: the evidence of who gets compliance-trained — and whose communication never makes the plan.

blocks.alt: A communication tablet in use, staff sitting beside not talking over.
blocks.caption: Ask who never gets a usable conversation: device users, people of color, people whose stim is called aggression.

blocks.body: Compliance training and missed communication are not evenly distributed. People with more support needs, people who do not use speech, people of color, people in greater Minnesota, and people whose autism is read as “behavior” are more likely to get a plan that trains their face and less likely to get a device, an interpreter, or a quiet room they asked for. If your “success stories” are all people who already look ready in a meeting, your practice has a queue you have not named.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows

blocks.body: This lesson is the chair test for neurodiversity — who is missing while the compliance goal is still soft, and who never gets their words on the page.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Map who gets compliance-trained and who gets under-heard.
Treat communication access as the first health and planning tool.
See how race, language, and disability stack in the note.
Name the harm of writing a stim as aggression without context.

blocks.body: If only the “easy to have in group” get a community life, you do not have inclusion. You have a sorting hat.

items.body: A device left at home is a missed plan and a missed “that hurts.” Meetings without the device are not meetings. They are guesses we write as goals.
items.title: People who do not use speech the way we do

items.body: A flap in a crowded room, a bolt from fluorescent light, a shout when touched without warning. If the first tool is a hold, we will miss the sensory story and punish the signal.
items.title: People whose stim is called aggression

items.body: Autism in Black and brown people is still under-identified or over-policed. An English-only social-skills goal and a clinic that will not wait for an interpreter are equity decisions dressed as clinical ones.
items.title: People of color and people who need another language

items.body: How a family talks about difference, ceremony, and support may not match a metro clinic script. Do not write a social-skills curriculum onto a Tribal citizen without the person and the Nation.
items.title: Tribal citizens and Urban Indian communities

blocks.alt: A staff person listens while a young man explains how he wants to work, laptop closed.
blocks.caption: The people we call “not ready for a meeting” are often the people we have not listened to in a format they can use.

blocks.body: When you start with people who already sit still in group, your notes look better and your culture learns who can have a walk. Reverse the test: who would we usually keep out of the meeting? Design their communication first this month. If your staffing cannot support a device and a quieter room, the staffing is the finding — not their neurology.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: last-asked is a method

cards.back: The meeting happens without their words. Staff answer. The note says “uncooperative.” Access failed before the question.
They flap when the room gets loud. We write aggression. We do not turn down the lights or shorten the meeting.
They say autistic. We say “person with autism” over them. Or the reverse. Their word is the word. Ask once. Use it.
Greater Minnesota has libraries, quiet rooms, and people. Distance is a design problem. It is not proof that affirming support pauses at the metro belt.
cards.front: Rural = no specialists, so no support

blocks.heading: Reading the same caseload three ways

tabs.body: Who had a “behavior” this year. Useful. Blind to who never got a device, and who never got a quiet offer.
tabs.label: Behavior map

tabs.body: Who had their words in the room — speech, device, typing, extra time. This is the map that predicts a real plan.
tabs.label: Communication map

tabs.body: Who can set a goal the person did not ask for: clinician, guardian, night supervisor, “program.” Those voices matter. They do not replace the person’s informed choice about their own brain.
tabs.label: Power map

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A quiet group is not inclusion if the people who talk on devices wait in the hall.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Complexity is a room-design problem. A specialist can help. It cannot be the reason you stop offering the meeting.

options.text: That is how group works. Stay the course.
Device users are safer in 1:1, so group is optional forever.
The people who need communication access are missing from the room. Change the group — noise, pace, device — do not change the presumption they belong.
Wait for a specialist vendor that handles “complex communication.”

blocks.question: Your “great groups” are mostly people who already sit still. Your device users wait in the hallway. What does the empty-chair test say?

blocks.heading: How to check your map without a consultant

items.body: Not five already easy in group. Five you would usually skip. If you cannot name them, you do not have a caseload picture. You have a comfort zone.
items.title: Name five people who have not had a usable conversation this month

items.body: Device, interpreter, extra time, a staff person who waits. If the meeting happened without their words, it was not informed planning.
items.title: Ask who had their words

items.body: Night supervisor, guardian, “social skills.” Bring it into the plan with the person’s yes or no. Do not let a curriculum happen in the hallway.
items.title: Ask who can set a goal they did not choose

items.body: A chair test will not replace maltreatment reporting, a medical order, or Tribal consultation. It will stop you from being surprised that only one kind of person got a quiet room.
items.title: Limits of this scan

items.text: A person with high support needs who has not been in a meeting they can use in six weeks.
A planning meeting without the communication device.
A Tribal member whose way of naming difference was overwritten as “lack of insight.”
Stimming written only as a behavior without sensory context.
A greater-Minnesota adult whose only offer is “drive to the metro for social skills.”

blocks.alt: Fluorescent open office — a room that could be changed before a person is.
blocks.caption: Fix-the-person ends at “try harder.” Change-the-environment designs the hour after you dim the lights.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either we accept everything and never teach a skill, or we train people to look typical and call it care. Neurodiversity is neither. Some skills a person asks for are real. Some “goals” are our meeting manners with a form attached. Change-the-environment names the lights, the noise, the time, and the device. Fix-the-person names our discomfort and puts it on their body.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters

blocks.body: This lesson compares those frames so you can pick the right one — without using “they’ll never make it in the real world” as a way to skip a room you still owe.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Tell a skill they asked for from a performance we demanded.
Keep support real when a guardian or a prior incident is loud.
Hold clinical care without making typical the destination.
Know when maltreatment, licensing, or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: A hard skill does not cancel the person. It changes the teaching. A real clinical path still requires their informed yes.

items.body: Lead with what looks wrong to us. Train the face, still the body, require group. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a life. Use teaching when they asked for the skill. Do not use it as the only plan forever.
items.title: Fix-the-person

items.body: The life is on the table first. The room is named in plain language. Device, headphones, extra time, a quieter offer stand next to the goal. You will still teach skills. That is not the same as designing a performance.
items.title: Change-the-environment

items.body: Maltreatment, a 245D rights process, an EIDBI authorization, emergency hold, and Tribal consultation are not “team vibes.” Use the proper door. Do not workshop a duty that belongs to licensing, a clinician, or a government-to-government path.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

blocks.alt: A quiet community room: two people working side by side, not performing a group.
blocks.caption: Change-the-environment is visible: they are working. The lights are bearable. Nobody is being trained to look at a face.

blocks.body: If you only watch for compliance, you will miss a person who already communicated on a device. If you only watch for choice, you may miss a skill they asked for. If you only watch for the people already “easy,” you will call the rest unready.
blocks.heading: Frameworks shape what you notice

tabs.body: An adult wants a job. They stim, use a device, and leave noisy rooms. The guardian wants social-skills group first. Staffing is thin on Saturdays.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: No job until group looks better. Device stays home “to work on talking.” Fear of looking different wins because it was the only expert in the room.
tabs.label: Fix-the-person

tabs.body: Device comes. A quieter job-site try. Headphones allowed. Guardian is in the conversation, not the only voice. Social skills only if the person asked for them.
tabs.label: Change-the-environment

tabs.body: If a rights restriction is actually being used, use the 245D process. If maltreatment is suspected, report. If a Tribal program is involved, ask consultation leads. Do not “engage” your way around those doors.
tabs.label: Formal path

cards.back: Should make a life possible. If the only outcome is “look typical in group,” it is compliance with better branding.
Needs information, experience, and a chance to try. A no from a guardian is not the same as the person’s informed no.
The smallest change that actually works. Dim the lights before you add a goal about sitting still.
Ask. Use their word. Do not make the style guide more important than the person in the chair.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The ADA-shaped world includes headphones. Withholding the tool is not preparation. It is practice at being unsupported.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not erase the job. Do not erase the tool. “The real world” is not a reason to run a nervous system without what works.

options.text: Agree. Practice without tools so they get used to it.
Ignore work altogether until the world changes.
The real world includes accommodations. Practice with the tool, name the job they want, and stop using “the real world” as a reason to withhold support.
Write “family declined accommodations” and close the goal.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “The real world will not give them headphones, so we should not either.” What is the strongest response?

blocks.body: Teams disagree about how much teaching is useful, how fast to fade a support, and when a clinical hour is truly wanted. Disagreement about pacing is allowed. Never offering the device, because it would be inconvenient, is not a professional debate.
blocks.heading: Where people of good faith disagree
Real disagreements — and the line they may not cross

items.body: If you cannot name a skill they asked for, you are teaching our manners. Put their goal on the plan. You can still teach. You cannot hide a compliance curriculum in “readiness.”
items.title: How much teaching?

items.body: A social story is not community experience. A supported hour in a real place is closer to informed choice than a brochure about “being ready.”
items.title: When is a try enough?

items.body: The person. Autistic or person with autism. ADHD or person with ADHD. Write what they want. Do not workshop their name.
items.title: Who decides the words?

blocks.body: Fact: people cannot choose a communication method they were never offered. Prescription: whether you use a device, extra time, or a quieter room this month. Argue about the prescription. Do not argue about the fact.
blocks.heading: Facts versus prescriptions

items.text: Bring the device and dim the lights for the meeting.
No community until they stop stimming.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of “handling it in-house.”
Assume a Tribal citizen will not want identity-first language.
Use the 245D process if you are actually restricting a right.

blocks.alt: A quiet room that had to be designed, not hoped for.
blocks.caption: The method has to survive a Tuesday meeting. If it needs a 40-page sensory binder, the old group will win.

blocks.body: Staff need a loop that survives a full caseload. Not a neurodiversity manual. Six moves: ask how they communicate and what they call themselves; match that in the room; change the environment before the goal; teach only a skill they want; document both columns; review every compliance goal on a dated calendar.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?

blocks.body: This lesson is the job-aid underneath the job aid — why each step exists, and what “good enough” looks like.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Run the environment-first loop on one person you already serve.
Write the communication, the room, and the skill — not only the face.
Use questions that invite a real yes or a real no.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one noisy group, a standing social-skills goal, and a frozen “noncompliant.”

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write it down so Tuesday-you still offers a usable room.

items.body: Open with their words and their tools. Device, typing, extra time, a walk while talking. Ask autistic or person with autism. If they have been trained to perform, say you are asking again because the performance is not the person.
items.title: 1. Ask — how they communicate, what they call themselves

items.body: The device in the bag. The interpreter. The extra ten minutes. If you cannot match it today, that is a finding — not “they would not engage.”
items.title: 2. Match communication

items.body: Light, noise, surprise, length, number of voices. The least change that actually works. A quieter offer is a first tool, not a last one.
items.title: 3. Change the room

items.body: A bus. A job. Cooking. Sleep. If the goal is only eye contact, it is our manners. Skill-building is real. Put their destination on the page.
items.title: 4. Teach only what they want

items.body: What they want. What the room did. What communication worked. What compliance goal remains, if any. If a provider in the room sells stillness as easier staffing, write that conflict down too.
items.title: 5. Document — both columns

items.body: A skill goal can be real. An undated “sit still” is a lifestyle. Put the next look on the plan. The person can still want a skill. You cannot hide from the calendar.
items.title: 6. Review — the compliance goal has a date

blocks.alt: Listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like a med pass. If it is not on the plan, the old group will win at 10 a.m.

blocks.body: You do not need a perfect neurodiversity plan to start. You need a door: “Here is how you communicate. Here is what we changed in the room. Here is the skill you asked for. Here is any compliance goal and when we will look at it again. Here is how you say stop.” Then mean it.
blocks.heading: A usable status line

tabs.body: A checkbox that says “communication discussed.” A group they cannot stand. A social-skills goal copied from last year. Leaders learn about harm from a licensing visit they cannot explain.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: Their words first, the device in the room, the lights named, a skill they asked for, both columns written, a dated review.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page sensory profile nobody opens on Saturday. If the method takes longer than the meeting, the old group will win. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

cards.back: If “they had a behavior” is the whole story, you have not looked. Specific environment gets specific change.
cards.front: Name the room in one sentence

cards.back: Planning without their words is staff planning. Access is part of step 1.
Do not cheer only stillness. A documented stop that we honor is success of process. A coerced group is a later crisis.
cards.front: Protect the yes and the stop

cards.back: If you cannot write a review date, you are not ready to train the face. You are ready to hope no one asks.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. They named an environment. You have a life to design. The sentence they gave you is data, not a closed file and not a void.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named a room that does not work. Your job is environment design, not a social-skills override and not a pep talk.

options.text: Refuse. Group is how we socialize people.
Thank them, name the noise, offer a quieter way to get the same life (a job, a club, a walk), write both columns, and date any remaining group goal — honor stop as far as the real need allows.
Cancel all community to honor neurodiversity.
Ask them to present their feelings in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A person says, “I don’t want group.” They stim and leave noisy rooms. Best next step?

blocks.body: The hardest part is not the loop. It is delaying a convenient group until the person has a usable hour. That pause is neurodiversity. Installing the old group on time is not.

items.body: Ask how they talk, what they call themselves, and wait. A shy yes after a power meeting is not a reliable sample.
items.title: Pitfall: “Any communication needs?” as the whole offer

items.body: Write the review date into the plan. Memory is not a control.
items.title: Pitfall: “We’ll remember next quarter.”

items.body: If the conversation is unusable, there was no conversation. Devices, extra time, and a quieter room are part of step 1.
items.title: Pitfall: treating the device as a later translation

items.body: “Before we keep this social-skills goal — have we named their words, the room, the skill they want, and the date?” That sentence changes more behavior than a branded campaign.
items.title: Better: close in the room

items.text: Ask whether they say autistic or person with autism.
Dim the lights and allow headphones.
Write the social-skills goal and a review date on the same page.
Teach bus riding because they asked for it.
Bring the tablet instead of “working on talking.”

blocks.alt: The meeting from the start of the course: mixed brains, mixed tools, everyone fully in frame.
blocks.caption: The course ends when one compliance goal that outlived the person gets a date — or comes off.

blocks.body: You now have a definition of both duties, a pattern for how we treat difference as deficit, a chair test, two frames, and a six-move loop. This lesson turns that into one person you already serve — not a special “neurodiversity project.”
blocks.heading: From evidence to Tuesday

blocks.body: Pick someone you would usually keep out of group or keep without a device: high support, a frozen social-skills goal, a stim-as-aggression file, a language you have not used. Small and complete beats a strategy deck with no name.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Choose one person and run the chair test.
Practice a repair that does not blame them for our room.
Set a seven-day practice transfer.
Know the job aid and the formal doors you must not skip.

blocks.cite: Lesson 1, to take with you
blocks.text: If we measure success by eye contact, stillness, and looking ready, we did not support a person. We made them perform our comfort.

items.body: Apply the job aid to one person. Ask, match communication, change the room, teach what they want, document, review. Small and complete.
items.title: Fix the next meeting

items.body: The unit’s planning agenda or social-skills log. If the template asks for their words, the room, a skill they want, and a date, every future meeting inherits the method.
items.title: Fix one template

items.body: If people who stim are called disruptive, interrupt it. If a still group is praised as good care, stop praising it. Culture is what gets applause.
items.title: Fix the culture tell

blocks.alt: A quiet community room — the destination of change-the-environment.
blocks.caption: Return to the room. The question is whether the people we serve get this kind of hour before we congratulate ourselves for a quiet group.

blocks.body: You will have left compliance goals on too long. Repair is: name the miss, offer the communication now in a format they can use, change the room, put a date on what remains, change the agenda so their words come first from now on, and skip the speech that makes them manage your embarrassment. “We should have brought the device months ago. I am bringing it now. Here is the quieter offer. You can say stop. We will write it down and come back on a date we name.”
blocks.heading: Repair without theater

tabs.body: Caseloads and thin shifts are real. Many “no time for a quieter offer” notes are late starts. When time is short, shorten the loop; do not delete the device.
tabs.label: Time

tabs.body: EIDBI, medical orders, 245D, and maltreatment law are real. They shape how you teach. They do not cancel a review date or a supported try while you wait on a door.
tabs.label: Orders and licensing

tabs.body: Providers, clinics, counties, and Tribal programs have their own calendars. DHS still sets the tone for the balance in meetings we host. Do not lower the bar because a partner is used to the still group.
tabs.label: Partners

tabs.body: If every stim is an emergency hold, you are choosing calm over the person. Write the room in one sentence. Change it. Then teach only what still needs it — with a date.
tabs.label: Urgency theater

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Repair is the goal restored plus a method change. It is not a sharing circle they did not ask to lead.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Contentment after a skipped life is not informed choice. Restore the real goal. Date what remains. Do not make them the trainer for your miss.

options.text: Ask them to tell the team how it felt, as a learning moment, then move on.
Name the miss, put their real goal on the page, drop eye contact as the measure, and change the agenda so communication and the room come before our manners.
Leave it — they seem content, so neurodiversity does not apply.
Add a poster about acceptance in the hallway.

blocks.question: You realize a social-skills goal has been “maintain eye contact” for two years. The person is not angry. What is the strongest repair?

blocks.body: Do these four things in the next seven calendar days. They are small enough to finish and large enough to count as Neurodiversity and Cognitive Difference.
blocks.heading: Seven-day transfer
Your seven-day list
items: Pick one person you would usually keep out of group or keep without a device. Write a half-page: how they communicate, what they call themselves, what compliance goal sits in the file.
Ask in a format they can use — device, extra time, quieter room — or schedule that access now.
Date one compliance goal. If you cannot defend the date, drop it or replace it with a skill they asked for.
Tell your team that a still group is not the applause line — then follow it when the first quieter offer is inconvenient.

blocks.heading: Principles to keep when the week gets loud

items.body: The undated eye-contact goal, the skipped device, or the fluorescent room is. The person who said stop, or who never heard the question, gave you information.
items.title: The person is not the problem

items.body: Do not call it choice if the device was never in the bag. Brief with dignity instead of a checkbox.
items.title: The support has to be real

items.body: Maltreatment, 245D restrictions, EIDBI, medical orders, and Tribal paths are not “extra comms.” Use the right door.
items.title: Formal doors are not optional

items.body: What they want. What the room did. What we will try. When we look again. That note is the product.
items.title: Review the compliance goal or you taught them not to want the life

blocks.alt: The fluorescent office — the old default when the room is unnamed.
blocks.caption: The noisy room can stay as a real place to practice with support. It cannot be the first option we never change.

blocks.body: Intention → who was offered a usable conversation → who had their words → what room we named → what we changed → what compliance goal remains, dated → revision. If you never ask who was offered a usable conversation, you will congratulate yourselves for groups that only worked for people already easy to keep still.

Report suspected maltreatment instead of handling it as a house issue.
Ban headphones because a meeting ran long.
Bring the communication device to the next meeting.
Write a stim as aggression without naming the room.

course.scope: DHS-wide staff practice with Disability Services, EIDBI, lead agencies, and 245D providers in view. Applies to case managers, supervisors, clinicians, and anyone who writes “noncompliant” into a note. Not a substitute for clinical evaluation, EIDBI authorization, maltreatment reporting, or Tribal consultation. How a person names themselves — autistic, person with autism, ADHD — is theirs.

jobAid.quote: If we measure success by eye contact, stillness, and looking ready, we did not support a person. We made them perform our comfort.

sections.heading: Ask (their words first)
items: How do you communicate — speech, device, typing, extra time, a walk while talking?
What do you call yourself — autistic, person with autism, ADHD, something else?
Bring the device, extra time, a quieter room. An unusable conversation is not consent.
If they have been trained to perform, say you are asking again because the performance is not the person.

sections.heading: Change the room, then teach
items: The real environment in one sentence — lights, noise, surprise, length — not “they had a behavior.”
Least change that actually works: headphones, dimmer, shorter meeting, one voice at a time.
Teach only a skill they asked for. Eye contact is not a life.
A stim can be joy, thinking, or regulation. Do not make stillness the only allowed body.

sections.heading: Document and review
items: Write both columns: their words, the room, the skill, any compliance goal.
A skill goal is allowed. An undated “sit still” is a lifestyle. Put the next look on the calendar.
Name conflicts (easier group vs. the person’s nervous system).
Honor stop. Coerced group is a later incident.

sections.heading: Repair if the goal outlived the person
items: Name the miss. Offer the device and the quieter room now. Do not make them lead a sharing circle.
Change the agenda so communication and the room come before our manners from now on.
If a social-skills goal froze after one incident, say so, and still design the support — their choice, dated.

sections.heading: Use the formal door — do not workshop these
items: Maltreatment reporting — Minn. Stat. §626.557. Do not handle it as a house issue.
245D rights and restriction process — a restriction has to be justified, not merely convenient.
EIDBI and clinical paths — chosen, not a mandate to look typical.
Positive supports — respect and feeling safe as the floor.
Tribal consultation — DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations.
When in doubt, ask the proper office before you freeze a compliance goal.

course.introTranscript: Safety that shrinks a life is not wellness. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, health, wellness, and safety are one job, not three competing posters. If we lock the kitchen and call it care, we did not keep someone well. We made them smaller. This course is a staff guide: hold the duty to keep people safe, and the duty to let them live. Name the real risk. Support around it. Watch for trauma. And review every restriction until it earns its place — or comes off.

learning.appliedNextStep: Bring one live work object into the application workspace. Name who it was built for, who may carry the burden, and one change or formal escalation.
evidence: Make and reconsider scenario decisions without being assigned a score.
Complete the practical activities and record a one-minute transfer commitment.
Apply the learning to a live work object in the Equity Analysis Toolkit.
objectives: Identify how health, wellness, and safety affects a DHS decision, service, or workplace process.
Use the course concepts and evidence to examine one live policy, form, meeting, service, hire, budget, or engagement plan.
Choose and document one defensible change, the person who owns it, and the date the team will review it.

blocks.alt: A Black man cooks at the stove while a Somali woman support worker spots beside him and a white woman sits at the table. All heads fully in frame.
blocks.caption: Wellness looks like a person doing a real thing. Safety is the person beside them, not the locked door.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: the same restriction for everyone, called safety. Adaptation: hold important-to and important-for at once. This course does not assign a score.

Minnesota person-centered practice asks staff to balance what is important to someone — the life they want — with what is important for them — health and safety. Teams often treat those as a fight that safety always wins. A locked kitchen, a cancelled outing, a standing order that never gets reviewed: those can be documented as “keeping them safe” while the person gets smaller, sicker of being managed, and further from a community life.

If wellness is only the absence of an incident report, we will keep writing restrictions. This course is the staff job: hold both duties at once.
blocks.heading: Why this is a leadership course

blocks.body: This lesson names the terms. Later lessons show how we shrink people in the name of safety, whose body gets overprotected, two honest frames, and a method that fits ordinary work — the well-and-safe loop.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Separate a supported life from a managed one.
Name dignity of risk without dropping the safety duty.
Spot when “important for” has eaten “important to.”
Own the staff job: you cannot delegate the balance to a form.

blocks.body: If we lock the kitchen and call it care, we did not keep someone well. We made them smaller.
Government pages are evidence, not the staff-facing deliverable. These are the terms this course uses on purpose.
blocks.heading: Terms used with care

cards.back: What makes a life worth living for this person: cooking, a walk, a late night, a job, a relationship, a faith practice. If it is not on the page, safety will fill the page.
Health, safety, and what keeps a person well enough to have that life. Medication, a seizure plan, a real risk named. Necessary. Not a veto of the life.
Adults get to try, fail, and try again with support. Risk that is named, understood, and supported is not the same as neglect. A life with no risk is often a life with no choice.
Assume control, surprise, and being done-to can re-injure. Ask what happened to this person, not what is wrong with them. Our procedures can be the next injury.

blocks.body: Nurses own clinical orders. Licensing and 245D own the floor for rights and restrictions. Maltreatment reporting is a legal door. Culture of Safety reviews systems after a critical incident. None of that removes the person in the planning meeting from asking, first, “What does a good day look like — and what would actually keep it possible?”
blocks.heading: Who holds which part
What sits with you versus specialists

items.body: You decide whether a restriction is a time-limited support or a lifestyle, whether “they’ll get hurt” is allowed to stand without a plan to try, and whether the person was in the conversation in a language they can use.
items.title: You own the balance

items.body: Use nursing, positive supports, trauma-informed clinicians, Culture of Safety, and guardianship / supported decision-making paths. Bring them in early. Do not hand them a person who was never asked what they want.
items.title: Specialists support the path

items.body: Wellness that has to be deserved after compliance is not wellness. It is a token economy with better letterhead.
items.title: The person should not have to earn a walk

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Both duties at once: the stove stays in the life, and the risk gets a support, not a lock that never comes off.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Dignity of risk is not neglect. A lock without a supported try and a review date is not safety. It is a smaller life.

options.text: Lock the kitchen. Safety first. Cooking can be a goal later.
Name the real burn risk, put cooking on the page, design support at the stove, and date a review of any restriction — do not let last year’s scare become a lifestyle.
Let them cook unsupervised to honor dignity of risk.
Wait for nursing to decide. Planning does not touch kitchens.

blocks.question: A team is writing a plan. The person wants to cook. Staff want the kitchen locked after a near-burn last year. What is the Health, Wellness, and Safety move?

blocks.alt: A planning table with a support plan, a risk worksheet, a pill organizer, a house key, and a bus pass.
blocks.caption: The page has to hold the key and the medication. If only the pill box survives the meeting, the life did not.

blocks.body: Move from “how do we prevent anything from happening?” to “what life are we trying to make possible, and what support makes the real risk survivable?” Zero incidents can be a success metric for a locked unit. It is a poor metric for a human life.
blocks.heading: The shift this course asks for

blocks.body: Person-centered protocol, the HCBS toolkit on discussing risk, Positive Supports, and Culture of Safety are public evidence. They are not the staff course. Minnesota DHS work also lands on lead agencies, 245D homes, clinics that talk over communication devices, and people whose trauma was caused in care. That is the practice context.
blocks.heading: DHS-wide, not a vendor script

tabs.body: They hear “safety plan” and lose the outing. They are not asked what wellness is. Pain and mood get written as behavior.
tabs.label: The person

tabs.body: Missed dental, skipped preventive care, no interpreter at the clinic. “They don’t like appointments” becomes a health disparity with a nickname.
tabs.label: Health

tabs.body: A restriction written after a scare, never reviewed. Direct support is blamed after an incident instead of the system that left them alone with an impossible rule.
tabs.label: Safety

tabs.body: A hold, a surprise search, a new staff every week. We call it protocol. Their body calls it the next injury.
tabs.label: Trauma

blocks.body: Choose a statement, then choose the bucket. The point is not to attack safety. It is to stop hiding a smaller life inside a risk form.
blocks.heading: Sort these statements
Life, support, or a smaller life?

items.text: Cooking dinner because they want to.
A staff person at the stove after a prior burn.
Kitchen locked for all meals, no review date.
A walk in the park they asked for.
Cancelling all community outings “until we hire.”

blocks.body: Next: the pattern — how Minnesota still makes people smaller after promising a community life.

blocks.alt: A closed, latched kitchen door in a residential hallway, late afternoon.
blocks.caption: A latch can be a time-limited support. Without a review, it is the floor plan of a smaller life.

blocks.body: Minnesota wrote person-centered practice, HCBS rights, and positive supports into the work. Homes still lock food. Clinics still skip people who use devices. Teams still treat a prior incident as a lifetime ban. Direct support still gets blamed when the system left them with a rule that could not be followed on a Tuesday night.
blocks.heading: The pattern is older than the protocol

blocks.body: This lesson is the history and the habit — so you can see your own plan in it.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Name restriction-as-lifestyle as a practice, not a one-off.
See how trauma repeats inside “protocol.”
Separate a real medical order from a house rule with letterhead.
Spot the three usual shrinks: lock, delay, and blame.

blocks.body: “For their own good” is often “for our own calm.”

events.body: Living in the community includes the ordinary risks of a community life. A building that never has an incident can still be segregation.
events.title: Community is the point

events.body: Licensing expects rights, dignity, and limits on coercive practices. A restriction has to be justified, not merely convenient.
events.title: Rights and restrictions

events.body: DHS protocol: planning is not driven by professional opinion or the services we already run. Balance the life and the safety.
events.title: Important to / important for

events.body: Minnesota positive supports work treats respect, choice, and feeling safe as the floor — not after compliance.
events.title: Not a hold as the plan

events.body: After a critical incident, learn the system. Do not only redesign the worker. The same lens belongs before the incident: does this rule even work at 10 p.m.?
events.title: Culture of Safety

items.body: A restriction after a scare. No fade-out, no skill-building, no date. The plan still says “person-centered.” The door says otherwise.
items.title: The lock that never comes off

items.body: “After we hire.” “After the psych eval.” “After they show they can.” Some assessments are real. Using them as a queue is how a walk becomes next year.
items.title: The delay dressed as assessment

items.body: A direct support professional improvised at 10 p.m. because the plan was unworkable. The review starts with their character. Culture of Safety says start with the system. So does this course, before anyone gets hurt.
items.title: The blame after the incident

blocks.alt: A clinic waiting room: a woman sits with a young adult using a communication device; staff sits beside them.
blocks.caption: Health equity is also this room: who gets an interpreter, a device, and a clinician who waits.

blocks.body: If you do not put the life on the paper, the restriction will. If you do not name trauma, protocol will. If you do not date a review, last year’s scare becomes the house. Shrinks are usually omissions, not villains.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: calm fills the vacuum

cards.back: It may mean they were not allowed to try. Wellness includes movement, relationships, food they chose, and care they can actually use.
cards.front: No incidents means they are well

cards.back: No. It means we step in with support, information, and a plan — and we do not confuse a lock with a plan.
cards.front: Dignity of risk means we step back

cards.back: Pain, constipation, dental infection, trauma reminders, and no way to say “stop” get written as behavior. Health first, then the clipboard.
If new staff still enter without knocking, if holds are still the backup plan, the certificate did not land. Practice is what the body meets.

blocks.heading: Myths that still sit in the room

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Eighteen months without a review is not a health plan. It is a smaller kitchen.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Weight and safety can be real. An undated lock is still a lifestyle. Review it. Support around it. Do not freeze last year’s scare.

options.text: It is working if there have been no incidents.
Health requires the lock. Review would be unsafe.
An undated lock is a lifestyle. Put food and health on the same page, design support, and date a review — do not let a scale run the house.
Wait for the person to ask for the key.

blocks.question: A home locked the snack cupboard after weight gain. The restriction has been in place 18 months with no skill-building. Strongest read?

tabs.body: “They got burned. Lock it. Document it. Train staff on the lock.” The life after the incident is not in the sentence.
tabs.label: Incident

tabs.body: “When they follow the meal plan for 90 days, we can talk about cooking.” Wellness as a prize.
tabs.label: Compliance

tabs.body: “Cooking matters to them. The burn was real. Here is support at the stove, a dated review, and what we will try before we ever lock the room.”
tabs.label: Well and safe

items.text: Community outings cancelled “until we are fully staffed,” month after month.
A door latch with no fade-out and no review date.
A DSP is written up after an unworkable night plan fails.
“After the eval” is the only wellness step on the plan.
Snacks locked for the whole house because of one person’s diet.

blocks.alt: Clinic waiting room with a communication device in use and staff sitting beside, not talking over.
blocks.caption: Ask who never gets a usable health conversation: device users, people of color, people whose pain is called behavior.

blocks.body: Restrictions and missed care are not evenly distributed. People with more support needs, people who do not use speech, people of color, people with mental health labels, and people in greater Minnesota are more likely to be “kept safe” at home and less likely to get a dentist, an interpreter, or a walk they asked for. If your incident-free success stories are all the same kind of person in a quiet house, your practice has a queue you have not named.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows

blocks.body: This lesson is the chair test for wellness — who is missing while the restriction is still soft, and who never gets into the clinic.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Map who gets overprotected and who gets under-cared-for.
Treat communication as health access, not a nicety.
See how race, language, and disability stack in the exam room.
Name the harm of writing pain as behavior.

blocks.body: If only the “compliant” get a community life, you do not have wellness. You have a sorting practice that decides who counts.

items.body: A device left at home is a missed appointment and a missed “that hurts.” Health conversations without the device are not conversations. They are guesses we write as plans.
items.title: People who do not use speech the way we do

items.body: Dental infection, constipation, headache, trauma reminder. If the first tool is a behavior plan, we will miss the abscess and punish the signal.
items.title: People whose pain is called behavior

items.body: Minnesota HCBS work has named racial and ethnic disparities. An English-only wellness plan and a clinic that will not wait for an interpreter are health decisions. They are also equity decisions.
items.title: People of color and people who need another language

items.body: Health, ceremony, food, and family obligation may look different. Do not write a metro house rule onto a Tribal citizen without the person and the Nation. Consultation is not a stakeholder workshop.
items.title: Tribal citizens and Urban Indian communities

blocks.alt: A support worker listens while a man with a walker explains what he wants this week.
blocks.caption: The people we call “unsafe in the community” are often the people we have not listened to long enough to design the outing.

blocks.body: When you start with people who already “do well” in the house, your incident numbers look better and your culture learns who can have a walk. Reverse the test: who would we usually keep home? Design their outing first this month. If your staffing cannot support it, the staffing is the finding — not their disability.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: last-asked is a method

cards.back: The clinic visit happens without their words. Staff answer. The note says “patient was uncooperative.” Access failed before the exam.
They push staff away at bath time. We write a behavior. We do not check the skin, the water temperature, or the last time someone they trust did this care.
A guardian says no walks. The adult is not asked separately. Protection without the person’s voice is still a smaller life. Use supported decision-making. Do not disappear the person.
Greater Minnesota has clinics, trails, and faith communities. Distance is a design problem. It is not proof that wellness pauses at the metro belt.

blocks.heading: Reading the same caseload three ways

tabs.body: Who had a report this year. Useful. Blind to who never got to try, and who never got a dentist.
tabs.label: Incident map

tabs.body: Who cooked, walked, worked, worshipped, dated, or saw a clinician they could use. This is the map that predicts wellness.
tabs.label: Life map

tabs.body: Who can say no for the person: guardian, provider, family, night supervisor. Those voices matter. They do not replace the person’s informed choice about their own body.
tabs.label: Power map

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A quiet house is not a wellness outcome if the people inside never get a sidewalk.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Complexity is a support design problem. A specialist can help. It cannot be the reason you stop offering a life.

options.text: That is how risk works. Stay the course.
High-support people are safer at home, so outings are optional.
The people with more support needs are missing from wellness. Design their outing and their clinic access first — change the support, not the presumption they get a life.
Wait for a specialist vendor that handles “complex” community time.

blocks.question: Your “safe” homes are mostly high-support people who never leave. Your community outings are mostly people who already speak up. What does the empty-chair test say?

blocks.heading: How to check your map without a consultant

items.body: Not five already on the outing list. Five you would usually keep home. If you cannot name them, you do not have a caseload picture. You have a comfort zone.
items.title: Name five people who have not had a community hour this month

items.body: Device, interpreter, extra time, a clinician who waits. If the exam happened without their words, it was not informed care.
items.title: Ask who had a usable health conversation

items.body: Night supervisor, guardian, “house rule.” Bring it into the plan with a date. Do not let a veto happen in the hallway.
items.title: Ask who can restrict without being in the room

items.body: A chair test will not replace maltreatment reporting, a medical order, or Tribal consultation. It will stop you from being surprised that only one kind of person got a walk.
items.title: Limits of this scan

items.text: A person with high behavioral support who has not left the house in six weeks.
A clinic visit without the communication device.
A Tribal member whose food and ceremony were written as “noncompliance with diet.”
Pain during personal care written only as a behavior plan.
A greater-Minnesota adult whose wellness plan is “stay on site until we have a driver.”

blocks.alt: A latched kitchen door in a residential hallway.
blocks.caption: Restrict-to-protect ends at the latch. Support-to-live designs the hour after you open it.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either we lock everything, or we ignore risk and call it dignity. Health, wellness, and safety are neither. Some restrictions are medically required and time-limited. Some are the team’s anxiety with a form attached. Support-to-live names the real risk and puts a person next to it. Restrict-to-protect names our fear and puts a door in front of it.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters

blocks.body: This lesson compares those frames so you can pick the right one — without using “they’ll get hurt” as a way to skip a life you still owe.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Tell a real restriction from a house rule with letterhead.
Keep support real when a guardian or a prior incident is loud.
Hold trauma without making protocol the next injury.
Know when maltreatment, licensing, or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: A hard medical risk does not cancel the life. It changes the support. A real restriction still requires a date.

items.body: Lead with the worst day. Lock, cancel, delay. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a life. Use a restriction when the risk is real and the support is not yet in place. Do not use it as the plan forever.
items.title: Restrict-to-protect

items.body: The life is on the table first. The risk is named in plain language. Support stands next to the stove, the sidewalk, the clinic. You will still have incidents. That is not the same as designing a cage.
items.title: Support-to-live

items.body: Maltreatment, a 245D rights restriction process, a physician order, emergency hold, and Tribal consultation are not informal team judgments. Use the proper door. Do not workshop a duty that belongs to licensing, a clinician, or a government-to-government path.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

blocks.alt: Two people walking and talking on a Minnesota park path.
blocks.caption: Support-to-live is visible: they are outside. Someone is with them. The risk was not imaginary. It was designed around.

blocks.body: If you only watch for incidents, you will miss a person who wanted a walk. If you only watch for choice, you may miss a medical risk you are required to name. If you only watch for the people already closest to the default, you will call the rest unsafe.
blocks.heading: Frameworks shape what you notice

tabs.body: An adult wants to walk to the store. They have gotten lost before. The guardian is afraid. Staffing is thin on Saturdays. They use a communication device.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: No store. “Too risky.” The device stays home. Fear wins because it was the only expert in the room.
tabs.label: Restrict-to-protect

tabs.body: Device comes. A staff person walks with them, then a fade toward more independence. A simple check-in plan. Guardian is in the conversation, not the only voice. Review date on any extra support.
tabs.label: Support-to-live

tabs.body: If a rights restriction is actually being used, use the 245D process. If maltreatment is suspected, report. If a Tribal program is involved, ask consultation leads. Do not “engage” your way around those doors.
tabs.label: Formal path

cards.back: Should make a life possible. If the only outcome is “stay home,” it is a restriction with better branding.
Needs information, experience, and a chance to try. A no from a guardian is not the same as the person’s informed no.
The smallest support that actually works. A lock on the whole house is rarely the least. A person at the stove often is.
Not “be nicer.” It is: no surprise, no extra force, predictable people, the device in the room, a way to say stop that we will honor.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. History is data for support design. It is not a lifetime stay-home order.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not erase the incident. Do not let it freeze a life. Design around the actual risk.

options.text: Agree. Prior incidents cancel community life.
Ignore the incident and send them alone this afternoon.
Name the real getting-lost risk, put community time on the page with support and the device, and date a review — do not let two-year-old fear run the calendar.
Write “family declined” and close the wellness goal.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “We had a missing-person incident two years ago, so community time is off the table.” What is the strongest response?

blocks.body: Teams disagree about how fast to fade a support, how much risk a guardian will allow, and when a medical order is truly required. Disagreement about pacing is allowed. Never offering the sidewalk, because it would be uncomfortable, is not a professional debate.
blocks.heading: Where people of good faith disagree
Real disagreements — and the line they may not cross

items.body: If you cannot name a date, it is already a lifestyle. Put the date on the plan. The person can still need the support. They cannot get free of a restriction you never reopen.
items.title: How soon to review a restriction?

items.body: A social story is not community experience. A supported outing is closer to informed choice than a brochure about “staying safe.”
items.title: When is a try enough?

items.body: The person, after information, with supported decision-making if needed. Not the loudest night supervisor, and not the lock we already installed. Write what they want, what we tried, and what restriction remains — with a date.
items.title: Who decides it is good enough?

blocks.body: Fact: people cannot choose a walk they were never offered. Prescription: whether you use a supported outing, a fade plan, or a clinic with an interpreter this month. Argue about the prescription. Do not argue about the fact.
blocks.heading: Facts versus prescriptions

items.text: Walk to the store with staff and the communication device.
Cancel all outings because of a two-year-old incident.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of “handling it in-house.”
Assume a Tribal citizen will not want community food practices.
Use the 245D process if you are actually restricting a right.
