blocks.alt: Two people on a park path — a community hour that had to be designed, not hoped for.
blocks.caption: The method has to survive a Tuesday meeting. If it needs a binder, the lock will win.

blocks.body: Staff need a loop that survives a full caseload. Not a 40-page wellness manual. Six moves: ask what a good day is; name the real risk, not the team’s anxiety; support around it; watch for trauma in our procedure; document important-to and important-for on the same page; review every restriction on a dated calendar.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?

blocks.body: This lesson is the job-aid underneath the job aid — why each step exists, and what “good enough” looks like.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Run the well-and-safe loop on one person you already serve.
Write the life, the risk, and the support — not only the lock.
Use questions that invite a real yes or a real no.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one scare, a standing order, and a frozen restriction.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write it down so you still offer a life.

items.body: Open with the life. Cooking, a walk, a clinic they can use, sleep, food they chose, people they want. If they have been restricted before, say you are asking again because the life still counts.
items.title: 1. Ask — what a good day is

items.body: Not “anything could happen.” The actual harm: burn, getting lost, missed medication, a seizure on a bus. If you cannot name it in one sentence, you are writing anxiety, not a plan.
items.title: 2. Name the real risk

items.body: A person at the stove. A device in the clinic. An interpreter. A check-in text. The least support that actually works. A lock is a last tool, not a first one.
items.title: 3. Support around it

items.body: Surprise, force, new staff every shift, being done-to. Ask what this procedure feels like in their body. Change the procedure before you change their “behavior plan.”
items.title: 4. Watch for trauma

items.body: Important to. Important for. What we tried. What restriction remains. Who can say stop. If a provider in the room sells the restriction as easier staffing, write that conflict down too.
items.title: 5. Document — both columns

items.body: A restriction can be real. An undated restriction is a lifestyle. Put the next look on the plan. The person can still need it. You cannot hide from the calendar.
items.title: 6. Review — the restriction has a date

blocks.alt: A support worker listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like a med pass. If it is not on the plan, the lock will win at 10 p.m.

blocks.body: You do not need a perfect wellness plan to start. You need a door: “Here is the life you want. Here is the risk we actually see. Here is the support. Here is any restriction and when we will look at it again. Here is how you say stop.” Then mean it.
blocks.heading: A usable status line

tabs.body: A checkbox that says “safety discussed.” A lock. A restriction copied from last year. Questions go to a generic inbox. Leaders learn about harm from a licensing visit they cannot explain.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: Life first on the agenda, a named risk, a person-level support, trauma checked, both columns written, a dated review.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page risk matrix nobody opens on Saturday. If the method takes longer than the meeting, the latch will win. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

cards.back: If “the community” is the whole risk, you have not looked. Specific harm gets specific support.
cards.front: Name the risk in one sentence

cards.back: Health and safety conversations without the person’s words are staff conversations. Access is part of step 1.
Do not cheer only compliance. A documented stop that we honor is success of process. A coerced outing is a later crisis.
cards.front: Protect the yes and the stop

cards.back: If you cannot write a review date, you are not ready to restrict. You are ready to hope no one asks.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Privacy plus a named fall risk. The sentence they gave you is data, not a closed file and not neglect.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named a dignity issue and you have a real risk. Your job is support design, not a lock and not a pep talk.

options.text: Refuse. Falls mean we stay in the room forever.
Thank them, name the fall risk, design the least support that works (check-ins, grab bars, a call button), write both columns, and date a review — honor stop as far as the real risk allows.
Leave them fully alone today to honor dignity of risk.
Ask them to present their feelings in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A person says, “I don’t want staff in the bathroom.” There was a fall last year. Best next step?

blocks.body: The hardest part is not the loop. It is delaying a convenient lock until the person has a supported try. That pause is wellness. Installing the latch on time is not.

items.body: Ask what a good day is, what has hurt before, and wait. A shy yes after a power meeting is not a reliable sample.
items.title: Pitfall: “Any safety concerns?” as the whole offer

items.body: Write the review date into the plan. Memory is not a control.
items.title: Pitfall: “We’ll remember next quarter.”

items.body: If the wellness conversation is unusable, there was no conversation. Devices, interpreters, and extra time are part of step 1.
items.title: Pitfall: treating access as a later translation

items.body: “Before we keep this restriction — have we named the life, the real risk, the support, and the date?” That sentence changes more behavior than a branded campaign.
items.title: Better: close in the room

items.text: Open the meeting with what a good day looks like.
Put a staff person at the stove instead of locking the kitchen.
Write the restriction and a review date on the same page.
Stop a surprise search that re-triggers trauma.
Name “getting lost on Saturday” instead of “the community is unsafe.”

blocks.caption: The course ends when one restriction that outlived the scare gets a date — or comes off.

blocks.body: You now have a definition of both duties, a pattern for how we shrink people, a chair test, two frames, and a six-move loop. This lesson turns that into one person you already serve — not a special “wellness project.”
blocks.heading: From evidence to ordinary work

blocks.body: Pick someone you would usually keep home or keep locked out of a room: high support, a frozen restriction, a pain-as-behavior file, a language you have not used. Small and complete beats a strategy deck with no name.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Choose one person and run the chair test.
Practice a repair that does not blame them for our lock.
Set a seven-day practice transfer.
Know the job aid and the formal doors you must not skip.

blocks.cite: Lesson 1, to take with you
blocks.text: If we lock the kitchen and call it care, we did not keep someone well. We made them smaller.

items.body: Apply the job aid to one person. Ask, name the risk, support, watch for trauma, document, review. Small and complete.
items.title: Fix the next meeting

items.body: The unit’s planning agenda or restriction log. If the template asks for important-to, a one-sentence risk, a support, and a date, every future meeting inherits the method.
items.title: Fix one template

items.body: If people who keep asking for outings are called unrealistic, interrupt it. If a quiet house is praised as good care, stop praising it. Culture is what gets applause.
items.title: Fix the culture tell

blocks.alt: A community walk — the destination of support-to-live.
blocks.caption: Return to the path. The question is whether the people we serve get this kind of hour before we congratulate ourselves for zero incidents.

blocks.body: You will have left restrictions on too long. Repair is: name the miss, offer the life now in a language they can use, design the support, put a date on what remains, change the agenda so important-to comes first from now on, and skip the speech that makes them manage your embarrassment. “We should have reviewed this lock months ago. I am reviewing it now. Here is the support. You can say stop. We will write it down and come back on a date we name.”
blocks.heading: Repair without theater

tabs.body: Caseloads and thin shifts are real. Many “no time for a walk” notes are late starts. When time is short, shorten the loop; do not delete the life.
tabs.label: Time

tabs.body: Medical orders, 245D, and maltreatment law are real. They shape how you restrict. They do not cancel a review date or a supported try while you wait on a door.
tabs.label: Orders and licensing

tabs.body: Providers, clinics, counties, and Tribal programs have their own calendars. DHS still sets the tone for the balance in meetings we host. Do not lower the bar because a partner is used to the lock.
tabs.label: Partners

tabs.body: If every scare is an emergency lock, you are choosing calm over the person. Write the risk in one sentence. Support it. Then restrict only what still needs it — with a date.
tabs.label: Urgency theater

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Repair is the life restored plus a method change. It is not a sharing circle they did not ask to lead.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Contentment after a skipped life is not informed choice. Restore the cooking. Date the restriction. Do not make them the trainer for your miss.

options.text: Ask them to tell the team how it felt, as a learning moment, then move on.
Name the miss, put cooking back on the page with support at the stove, date any remaining restriction, and change the agenda so important-to comes before the latch.
Leave it — they seem content, so dignity of risk does not apply.
Add a poster about wellness in the hallway.

blocks.question: You realize a kitchen has been locked for two years after a burn. The person is not angry. What is the strongest repair?

blocks.body: Do these four things in the next seven calendar days. They are small enough to finish and large enough to count as Health, Wellness, and Safety.
blocks.heading: Seven-day transfer
Seven-day list
items: Pick one person you would usually keep home or keep out of a room. Write a half-page: the life they want, the real risk in one sentence, what restriction sits in the file.
Ask what a good day is in a language they can use — device, interpreter, extra time — or schedule that access now.
Date one restriction. If you cannot defend the date, start the fade or the supported try.
Tell your team that a quiet house is not the applause line — then follow it when the first outing is inconvenient.

blocks.heading: Principles to keep when the week gets loud

items.body: The undated lock, the unnamed risk, or the skipped clinic is. The person who said stop, or who never heard the question, gave you information.
items.title: The person is not the problem

items.body: Do not call it choice if the walk was never on the paper. Brief with dignity instead of a checkbox.
items.title: The support has to be real

items.body: Maltreatment, 245D restrictions, medical orders, and Tribal paths are not “extra comms.” Use the right door.
items.title: Formal doors are not optional

items.body: What they want. What we fear. What we will try. When we look again. That note is the product.
items.title: Review the restriction or you taught them not to want the life

blocks.alt: The latched kitchen door — the old default when risk is unnamed.
blocks.caption: The latch can stay as a time-limited support. It cannot be the first option we never review.

blocks.body: Intention → who was offered a life → who heard it in a usable way → what risk we named → what support we put beside it → what restriction remains, dated → revision. If you never ask who was offered a life, you will congratulate yourselves for houses that only worked for people already close to the default.
blocks.heading: The feedback loop

items.text: Date one restriction or start the supported try.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of handling it as a house issue.
Lock a kitchen for the whole house because a meeting ran long.
Bring the communication device to the next clinic visit.
Write pain as a behavior without a health check.

blocks.cite: Lesson 2, to take with you
blocks.text: “For their own good” is often “for our own calm.”

blocks.body: Open the Well-and-Safe Job Aid and keep it beside your next planning meeting. This course is original One DHS instructional content for staff practice. For maltreatment, licensing restrictions, medical orders, and Tribal consultation, use those formal doors. This is not a substitute for them.

course.scope: DHS-wide staff practice with Disability Services, lead agencies, and 245D providers in view. Applies to case managers, supervisors, direct support professionals, nurses, and anyone who writes a restriction into a plan. Not a substitute for maltreatment reporting, licensing, medical orders, or Tribal consultation. Dignity of risk is the person’s. The duty to keep people safe is still yours.

sections.heading: Ask (the life first)
items: Open with a good day: cooking, a walk, sleep, food, people, a clinic they can use.
Bring the device, interpreter, extra time. An unusable conversation is not consent.
If they have been restricted before, say you are asking again because the life still counts.
Important to and important for share the page. If only safety survives the meeting, start over.

sections.heading: Name the risk and support around it
items: The real harm in one sentence — not “the community” as a whole.
Least support that actually works: a person at the stove, a check-in, grab bars, a fade plan.
A lock is a last tool, not a first one. Trauma: no surprise, no extra force, a way to say stop.
Pain is health until proven otherwise. Do not open with a behavior plan.

sections.heading: Document and review
items: Write both columns: the life, the risk, the support, any restriction.
A restriction is allowed. An undated restriction is a lifestyle. Put the next look on the calendar.
Name conflicts (easier staffing vs. the person’s life).
Honor stop as far as the real risk allows. Coerced compliance is a later incident.

sections.heading: Repair if the lock outlived the scare
items: Name the miss. Offer the life now. Do not make them lead a sharing circle.
Change the agenda so important-to comes before the latch from now on.
If a house rule froze after one incident, say so, and still design the support — their choice, dated.

sections.heading: Use the formal door — do not workshop these
items: Maltreatment reporting — Minn. Stat. §626.557. Do not handle it as a house issue.
245D rights and restriction process — a restriction has to be justified, not just convenient.
Medical orders, positive supports, and Culture of Safety reviews after a critical incident.
Tribal consultation — DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations.
When in doubt, ask the proper office before you freeze a lock.

course.introTranscript: Competitive, integrated work is the first and expected option in Minnesota — not a prize for looking ready. At the Department of Human Services, Employment First is a practice, not a poster. If the people we serve only hear about day programs, we did not offer a choice. We offered a default. This course is a staff guide: presume people can work, including people with complex support needs. Name the fear about benefits. Use informed choice without a conflict of interest. And review the no until the person says stop.

blocks.alt: A coworker and a woman using a wheelchair stock produce together in a grocery store.
blocks.caption: First means a real job, a real wage, real coworkers. Not a simulated workplace and not a prize.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: a day program first because it is the same for everyone. Adaptation: competitive integrated employment as the first option. This course does not assign a score.

Minnesota is an Employment First state. Statute says working-age Minnesotans with disabilities can work, want to work, and can achieve competitive integrated employment — and that they be offered the chance to earn a competitive wage before other supports. Policy is not the staff-facing deliverable. The deliverable is what you say in the planning meeting when someone looks “not ready.”

If the first option on the table is a day program, a sheltered schedule, or “let’s wait until they are more stable,” you did not implement Employment First. You implemented a queue.
blocks.heading: Why this is a leadership course

blocks.body: This lesson names what “first” means in the room. Later lessons show how we still sideline people, who gets asked last, two honest frames, and a method that fits ordinary work — the first-option loop.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Separate a real job from a placement that only looks like work.
Name the presumption: people can work, including people with complex support needs.
Spot the difference between informed choice and a steered default.
Own the staff job: you cannot delegate the first question.

blocks.body: If work was never on the table, that was not a choice. That was a default.
Government pages are evidence, not the staff-facing deliverable. These are the terms this course uses on purpose.
blocks.heading: Terms used with care

cards.back: A real job in the competitive labor force, on a real payroll, paying at least minimum wage and not less than coworkers without disabilities doing similar work. Full-time, part-time, or self-employment, with or without supports. Community coworkers. Not a simulated workplace.
Work is the opening offer, not the reward after someone proves they are “ready.” Other services can sit beside work. They do not have to come first.
The person has community-based experience, knows how work can change life and benefits, and can say yes, no, or not yet without being steered by our convenience or our fear.
The starting point is that this person can work. Support needs, disability type, and past “failure” do not cancel the question. They shape the support, not the offer.

blocks.body: Vocational Rehabilitation finds and supports jobs. Waiver employment services use Engage, Plan, Find, Keep. Benefits planners name the money fear. Schools prepare youth. DHS, DEED, and MDE share the E1MN path. None of that removes the person in the planning meeting from asking, first, “What work do you want?”
blocks.heading: Who holds which part
What sits with you versus specialists

items.body: You decide whether work is on the agenda before other day supports, whether “they’re not ready” is allowed to stand, and whether a no is documented as an informed no or as your relief.
items.title: You own the first question

items.body: Use VR, employment providers, Disability Hub MN, DB101, and benefits counseling. Bring them in early. Do not hand them a person who was never asked about work.
items.title: Specialists support the path

items.body: People should not have to guess that a job is allowed, or that they can work and keep essential benefits with a plan. “They didn’t ask, so they must not want it” is a leadership statement about whose curiosity you are willing to skip.
items.title: The person should not have to decode the system alone

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. First means first — in the conversation, not as a footnote after the slot is filled.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: An available slot is not an informed choice. Work has to be offered before other supports, not after they “do well.”

options.text: Take the slot. Work can be discussed later if they do well.
Ask about work first, including with supports; use the day program only if it is the person’s informed choice after a real offer, and write down why.
Mention work once so it is on the notes, then fill the slot.
Wait for Vocational Rehabilitation to bring it up.

blocks.question: A lead-agency meeting is planning supports for an adult with significant disability. The team opens with a day-program slot that has an opening next month. What is the Employment First move?

blocks.alt: A case manager sits with a young man and his mother looking at job listings and a one-page plan.
blocks.caption: The first-option conversation looks like this: work on the paper, not only a day-program brochure.

blocks.body: Move from “where can we place them so they are busy and safe?” to “what work do they want, and what support makes that possible?” Busy and safe can be a day program. They are not the same as economic inclusion.
blocks.heading: The shift this course asks for

blocks.body: E1MN, the Employment First Policy, and the statute are public evidence. They are not the staff course. Minnesota DHS work also lands on lead agencies, 245D providers, eleven Tribal Nations, immigrant families who fear benefits cliffs, and people whose support needs used to get them parked. That is the practice context.
blocks.heading: DHS-wide, not a vendor script
Where teams drop the first option

tabs.body: They hear “program” and “schedule.” They never hear “job.” Or they hear “job” once, with a look that says we already know the answer is no.
tabs.label: The person

tabs.body: Fear about losing Medical Assistance, housing, or a known routine. If we do not name benefits and natural supports, the family will protect the person from a risk we never explained.
tabs.label: Families

tabs.body: A full day-program roster is easier to staff than a job site. Convenience is not a person-centered plan. Name the conflict of interest out loud.
tabs.label: Providers

tabs.body: Subminimum or token pay is not competitive employment. If the paycheck would embarrass a coworker without a disability, it is not the first option.
tabs.label: The public wage

blocks.body: Tap a statement, then tap the bucket. The point is not to attack day supports. It is to stop hiding the first option inside a full calendar.
blocks.heading: Sort these statements
First option, other support, or not employment?

items.text: Stocking produce at a grocery, on the store payroll, at the same wage as coworkers.
A community day program for skills and preferred activities, not a paycheck.
A workshop paying below minimum wage among only disabled peers.
Job coaching at a cafe while the person is on the cafe payroll.
“Let’s try the day program first and see if they’re ready.”

blocks.body: Next: the pattern — how Minnesota still sends people to the sideline after promising work first.

blocks.alt: An empty day-program craft room with folding tables and a circle of unused chairs.
blocks.caption: Empty chairs are not rest. They are people who were never asked about work, or who were asked after the slot was filled.

blocks.body: Minnesota wrote Employment First into policy and then into statute. Dashboards still show how few people in disability services hold competitive jobs. The gap is not a mystery. Teams protect people from work they were never supported to try. Providers fill the services they already run. Benefits fear goes unnamed. “Ready” becomes a test no one passes.
blocks.heading: The pattern is older than the policy

blocks.body: This lesson is the history and the habit — so you can see your own Tuesday in it.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Name readiness culture as a gate, not an assessment.
See how a full roster becomes the plan.
Separate day programs from jobs — they are not paid work.
Spot the three usual sidelines: too complex, too risky, too soon.

blocks.body: “Not ready” is often “we are not ready to support them.”

events.body: Advocates and agencies start treating competitive wages in typical workplaces as the goal, not a specialty track.
events.title: Employment First Coalition

events.body: DHS, DEED, and MDE commit: integrated, competitive employment is the first and expected service option, including for people with complex disabilities.
events.title: State Employment First Policy

events.body: Minnesota’s Olmstead work treats work in the community as part of living in the community. A building full of only disabled workers is not integration.
events.title: Community, not segregation

events.body: Law says offer the chance to earn a competitive wage before other supports. Policy became a duty, not a slogan.
events.title: Statute

events.body: DHS, DEED, and Education share a path. The dashboards still ask the only question that counts: who actually has a job?
events.title: E1MN and the dashboards

blocks.heading: How Minnesota named the first option

items.body: Social skills first. Sobriety first. “Let’s get stable.” Some conditions need care. Care can sit beside work. Using readiness as a locked door is how people age out of the question.
items.title: Readiness as a gate

items.body: A day-program opening next month is a real resource. It is also a conflict. If it is easier to fill than a job development referral, the calendar will beat the policy. Name the conflict. Do not pretend the slot is the person’s dream because it was available.
items.title: The open slot

items.body: High support needs, behavioral history, dual diagnosis, limited English, or a Tribal community far from a metro job board. Complexity is a support design problem. It is not evidence they cannot work.
items.title: Too complex

blocks.alt: A table with a paycheck stub, a benefits worksheet, glasses, a bus pass, and a pen.
blocks.caption: The money fear is real. Leaving it unnamed is how families vote no for the person.

blocks.body: If you do not put work on the paper, the known program will. If you do not name Medical Assistance, housing, and SSI, fear will. If you do not schedule a review of a no, the no becomes a lifetime. Sidelines are usually omissions, not villains.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: default fills the vacuum

cards.back: They are not. Minnesota is clear: day programs support community life and skills. They are not focused on earning money. Calling them work teaches the wrong wage.
cards.front: Day programs are a kind of job

cards.back: No. Employment First is the offer and the presumption. The person can decline after informed choice. Document the no, remove barriers, and review. Do not coerce. Do not skip the offer to avoid the paperwork.
Often false, and always in need of a planner, not a rumor. DB101 and benefits counseling exist so work can be part of the plan without terror. “You’ll lose everything” is not counseling.
A bad job match is data. It is not a career closed. Review, change the support, try again. People without disabilities get more than one job.

blocks.heading: Myths that still sit in the room

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. One short job is a design note, not a lifetime verdict.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Employment First includes people who already “tried.” Review the no. Do not freeze a two-year-old match.

options.text: Three weeks proves they cannot work. Close the file.
Happiness in a program means Employment First does not apply.
A short job is information about match and support. Ask again, name what failed, and offer work with a different design — unless the person makes an informed no now.
Wait until the person brings it up.

blocks.question: A team says, “We tried a job two years ago. It lasted three weeks. They’re happier in the day program.” What is the strongest read?

tabs.body: “When they can handle a full day without support, then we’ll talk jobs.” The bar is set at independence the job could have provided with a coach.
tabs.label: Readiness

tabs.body: “We have a Monday–Friday opening. Let’s lock that so they don’t lose it.” The program’s capacity became the person’s plan.
tabs.label: Roster

tabs.body: “What kind of work interests you? Who already knows you? What support would make a real payroll job possible this season — and what else do you want besides work?”
tabs.label: First option

items.text: “Let’s wait until they’re more stable.”
“Take the opening before someone else does.”
“If they work they will lose their Medical Assistance.”
“They aren’t job-ready until they can ride the bus alone.”
“Families in our culture don’t talk about benefits cliffs, so we skip it.”

blocks.body: Next: the evidence of who is usually asked last — and who never hears the offer in their language.

blocks.alt: Unused chairs in a day-program room late in the afternoon.
blocks.caption: Ask who is not in the employment conversation: high support needs, Tribal citizens, people with mental health labels, youth, immigrants.

blocks.body: Employment outcomes are not evenly distributed. People with more support needs, people of color, people whose first language is not English, people with mental health disabilities, and people in greater Minnesota are more likely to be “placed” in unpaid or segregated days. If your successful job stories are all the same kind of person, your practice has a queue you have not named.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows

blocks.body: This lesson is the chair test for economic inclusion — who is missing while the plan is still soft.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Map who usually gets asked last.
Treat Tribal employment paths as government-to-government, not a vendor list.
See how language, race, and disability stack.
Name the harm of using “family doesn’t want it” as a closed file.

blocks.body: If only the people closest to the labor market get the first option, you do not have Employment First. You have a sorting practice that decides who counts.

items.body: Customized jobs, job carving, and high-intensity coaching exist. If your mental picture of “a job” is unsupervised full-time retail, you will screen these people out before the conversation.
items.title: People with complex support needs

items.body: Job offers in English-only meetings, uncaptioned work webinars, and forms that cannot be used with a screen reader are not offers. They are performances of offers.
items.title: People who need another language or access

items.body: Work, land, and family obligation may look different. Tribal employment programs and consultation paths are not a stakeholder workshop. Do not park a Tribal citizen in a metro vendor default without asking the Nation and the person.
items.title: Tribal Nations and Urban Indian communities

items.body: E1MN wants paid competitive work experience before a diploma. If transition still means “day program after graduation,” we spent 18 years practicing the sideline.
items.title: Youth becoming adults

blocks.alt: An employment specialist listens and takes notes while a job seeker talks, laptop closed.
blocks.caption: The people we call hard to employ are often the people we have not listened to long enough to carve a job.

blocks.body: When you start with people already close to the labor market, your numbers look better and your culture learns who “counts.” Reverse the test: who would we usually skip? Ask them first this month. If your tools cannot support them, the tools are the finding — not their disability.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: last-asked is a method

cards.back: The work conversation happens in English. The interpreter is for the waiver paperwork. The person never got the offer in a language they can use.
A parent says no because of benefits or safety. The adult is not in the room, or is in the room and is not asked separately. Protection without the person’s voice is still a sideline.
“When they’re stable.” Stability is treated as a finish line instead of a support alongside a job that might be part of getting well.
Greater Minnesota has employers. It also has distance, transportation, and thin provider networks. Distance is a design problem. It is not proof that Employment First pauses at the metro belt.

blocks.heading: Reading the same caseload three ways

tabs.body: Who is in day services, who is in employment services, who is in neither. Useful. Blind to who was never asked.
tabs.label: Placement map

tabs.body: Who heard a real first-option conversation this year, in a usable language, with benefits named. This is the map that predicts economic inclusion.
tabs.label: Offer map

tabs.body: Who can say no for the person: guardian, provider, family, team. Guardianship and family matter. They do not replace the person’s informed choice process.
tabs.label: Power map

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A lopsided success list is a practice finding, not a labor-market law.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Employment First includes people with complex needs. A specialist vendor can help. It cannot be the reason you stop asking.

options.text: That is how the labor market works. Stay the course.
Day programs are culturally appropriate for the rest, so offers are optional.
The people with more support needs, people of color, and people outside the metro are missing from the first option. Ask them first, and change the support — not the presumption.
Wait for a new vendor that “specializes” in hard-to-serve clients.

blocks.question: Your successful job placements this year are mostly white, metro, mild-support adults. Your day-program roster is everyone else. What does the empty-chair test say?

blocks.heading: How to check your map without a consultant

items.body: Not five already in job development. Five you would usually skip. If you cannot name them, you do not have a caseload picture. You have a comfort zone.
items.title: Name five people you have not asked this year

items.body: If the offer needs an interpreter, captions, plain language, or extra time, those are part of the offer — not a sequel.
items.title: Ask who heard it in their language

items.body: Guardian, provider, family. Invite them into informed choice. Do not let a veto happen in the hallway.
items.title: Ask who can veto without being in the room

items.body: A chair test will not replace VR eligibility, waiver rules, or Tribal consultation. It will stop you from being surprised that only one kind of person got a job.
items.title: Limits of this scan

blocks.heading: Who is missing from the offer?

items.text: An adult with high behavioral support who has never had a job-carving meeting.
A Somali-speaking family who only received English job flyers.
A Tribal member whose plan used a metro vendor without asking the Nation.
A person who needs ASL and was invited to an uncaptioned “work info” night.
A youth in greater Minnesota whose transition plan is “day program after graduation.”

blocks.alt: A planning table with job listings in front of a young man, his mother, and a case manager.
blocks.caption: Presume-and-offer puts work on the paper. Protect-from-work puts a program on the paper and calls it safety.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either we push everyone into jobs, or we protect people from a cruel labor market. Employment First is neither. It is a presumption plus informed choice. Some people will say no. Some jobs will be the wrong match. Protection without an offer is still a sideline. Pressure without information is still harm.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters

blocks.body: This lesson compares those frames so you can pick the right one — without using “they’re fragile” as a way to skip a duty you still have.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Tell a real no from a steered default.
Keep the offer real when benefits fear is loud.
Hold family disagreement without erasing the person.
Know when VR, benefits planning, or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: A hard support need does not cancel the offer. It changes the support. A real no still requires an offer you can document.

items.body: Lead with risk: benefits, failure, behavior, transportation. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a life. Use caution inside a plan. Do not use it as the plan.
items.title: Protect-from-work

items.body: Work is on the table first, with community experience, benefits facts, and a support design. You will hear no sometimes. That no is only honest if the yes was possible.
items.title: Presume-and-offer

items.body: VR eligibility, waiver authorization, benefits counseling that can bind a household, guardianship, and Tribal consultation are not informal team judgments. Use the proper door. Do not workshop a duty that belongs to another agency or government.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

blocks.alt: A paycheck stub and a benefits worksheet on an office table.
blocks.caption: Name the money. A rumor about losing everything is not informed choice.

blocks.body: If you only watch for safety, you will miss a person who wanted a job. If you only watch for placements, you may miss a coerced yes. If you only watch for the people already close to work, you will call the rest unmotivated.
blocks.heading: Frameworks shape what you notice

tabs.body: An adult on Medical Assistance wants to try stocking at a store. The parent is afraid of a benefits cliff. The provider has a day-program opening. The person has limited English.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: Take the program slot. Tell the person “maybe later.” Never call a benefits planner. The fear wins because it was the only expert in the room.
tabs.label: Protect-from-work

tabs.body: Interpreter in the room. Work on the paper. Benefits counseling this month. Day supports can sit beside a part-time job if the person wants both. Document what they choose.
tabs.label: Presume-and-offer

tabs.body: If waiver employment services or VR must be authorized, start that path now. If a Tribal program is involved, ask consultation leads. Do not “engage” your way around enrollment rules.
tabs.label: Formal path

cards.back: Not the same as picking among the programs we already run. Choice needs experience, information, and a chance to try work.
Real. Dignity of risk is also real. A risk you never explained is not a safety plan. It is a veto.
Skills can be built on a job. Requiring them first is often protect-from-work in professional clothing.
The agency that runs the day program is in the planning meeting. Say so. The person still needs an independent picture of work.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Culture and family are in the conversation. They are not a silent veto of the first option.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not erase family. Do not let family, or our idea of their culture, replace the person’s informed choice.

options.text: Agree. Culture cancels Employment First.
Ignore the family and enroll VR today.
Keep the presumption, bring the person and family into informed choice with an interpreter and benefits facts, and document the person’s decision — not the team’s relief.
Write “family declined” and close the employment goal.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “Families in this community don’t want work for their adult children, so we don’t push it.” What is the strongest response?

blocks.body: Teams disagree about how hard to press after a no, how soon to try again, and how much risk a guardian will allow. Disagreement about pacing is allowed. Never asking, because it would be uncomfortable, is not a professional debate.
blocks.heading: Where people of good faith disagree
Real disagreements — and the line they may not cross

items.body: Policy asks for regular review. A no is not a personality. Put a date on the calendar. The person can say no again. They cannot say yes if you never return.
items.title: How soon to review a no?

items.body: A video is not community experience. A tour, a work tryout, or a short paid experience is closer to informed choice than a brochure.
items.title: When is exploration enough?

items.body: The person, after information. Not the loudest parent, and not the provider with the open slot. Write what they heard, what they tried, and what they chose.
items.title: Who decides it is good enough?

blocks.body: Fact: people cannot choose a job they were never offered. Prescription: whether you use a work tryout, a discovery process, or a VR referral this month. Argue about the prescription. Do not argue about the fact.
blocks.heading: Facts versus prescriptions

items.text: Ask about work before filling a day-program slot.
Skip the offer because a parent looks worried.
Refer for benefits counseling before a payroll start date.
Assume a Tribal citizen will not want a community job.
Ask whether Tribal consultation or a Tribal employment program applies.

blocks.alt: Coworkers at a warehouse break table going over a shift huddle together.
blocks.caption: The method has to survive a Tuesday meeting. If it needs a binder, it will lose to the open slot.

blocks.body: Staff need a loop that survives a full caseload. Not a 40-page employment manual. Six moves: ask about work first; try work in the community; name the money and the fear; connect to Engage / Plan / Find / Keep and the right partners; document the choice without a conflict of interest; review the no on a dated calendar.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?

blocks.body: This lesson is the job-aid underneath the job aid — why each step exists, and what “good enough” looks like.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Run the first-option loop on one person you already serve.
Write what they want, what they fear, and what they tried.
Use questions that invite a real yes or a real no.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one mention, a brochure, and a frozen no.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write it down so you still offer work first.

items.body: Open with work. “What kind of work interests you?” not “We have a Monday opening.” If they have said no before, say you are asking again because the offer stands.
items.title: 1. Ask — work before the other slot

items.body: A brochure is not experience. A visit, a short tryout, a conversation with a worker who does the job. Discovery and job carving belong here for people who will not fit a posted listing.
items.title: 2. Community experience — not only on paper

items.body: Say that work can change benefits, and that a planner can show the numbers. Point to DB101 and Disability Hub. Do not give hallway tax advice. Do not let a rumor close the file.
items.title: 3. Name the money — benefits and wage

items.body: Match the phase. Curious but not sure: Engage. Ready to design a path: Plan. Looking: Find, including VR and employment services. Hired: Keep, including natural supports and transportation. Do not dump everyone into Find.
items.title: 4. Connect — Engage, Plan, Find, Keep

items.body: What they heard. What they tried. What they chose. Why, in their words if you can. If a provider in the room sells the alternative service, write that conflict down too.
items.title: 5. Document — the person’s choice, not the team’s relief

items.body: A no is allowed. An undated no is a sideline. Put the next ask on the plan. The person can stop you. You cannot stop yourselves from offering.
items.title: 6. Review — the no has a date

blocks.alt: An employment specialist listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like an authorization or a start date. If it is not on the plan, the default will win.

blocks.body: You do not need a perfect employment plan to start. You need a door: “Work is the first option. Here is what we know about what you want, what we don’t know about benefits, and when we’ll know more. Here is who can help. Here is how you say no without disappearing from the next review.” Then mean it.
blocks.heading: A usable status line

tabs.body: A checkbox that says “employment discussed.” A flyer. A no copied from last year. Questions go to a generic inbox. Leaders learn about under-employment from a dashboard they cannot explain.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: Work first on the agenda, a community experience, a benefits appointment, a named phase in Engage / Plan / Find / Keep, a written choice, a dated review.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page career binder nobody opens. If the method takes longer than the meeting, the open slot will win. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

cards.back: Engage, Plan, Find, or Keep. If “the team” owns employment, no one does.
Benefits, transportation, failure, family. Unnamed fear writes the plan in invisible ink.
Do not cheer only the yes. A documented no after a real offer is success of process. A coerced yes is a later crisis.
cards.front: Protect the yes and the no

cards.back: If you fill the day-program slot first, you are choosing. Write that you chose. Better: pause the slot until the offer is real.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Fear plus facts. The sentence they gave you is data, not a closed file.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named the classic barrier. Your job is a planner, not a rumor and not a pep talk.

options.text: Agree that work is too risky and close employment.
Thank them, name the fear as legitimate, book benefits counseling / DB101 support, and keep work on the table until they have numbers — then document their choice.
Tell them most people are fine and they should try anyway this week.
Ask them to present their feelings in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A person says, “I don’t want to lose my benefits.” Best next step?

blocks.body: The hardest part is not the loop. It is delaying a convenient slot until the person has heard a real offer. That pause is Employment First. Filling the slot on time is not.

items.body: Ask what kind of work, who they already know, what a good day looks like, and wait. A shy no after a power meeting is not a reliable sample.
items.title: Pitfall: “Any interest in work?” as the whole offer

items.body: Write the review date into the plan. Memory is not a control.
items.title: Pitfall: “We’ll remember next year.”

items.body: If the offer is unusable, there was no offer. Interpreters, captions, and plain language are part of step 1, not a sequel.
items.title: Pitfall: treating access as a later translation

items.body: “Before we fill another service — have we offered work, named benefits, and written the choice?” That sentence changes more behavior than a branded campaign.
items.title: Better: close in the room

items.text: Open the meeting with the job question before the day-program slot.
Book a benefits counseling appointment.
Write the person’s no in their words and set a review date.
Match them to Find and make a VR referral.
A community tryout at a real workplace.

blocks.body: Last lesson: practice on one person already on your caseload, and how to repair a skipped offer without making them the show.

blocks.alt: A mixed crew at a real workplace huddle — the destination of the first option.
blocks.caption: The course ends when one person who was never asked gets a real offer this week.

blocks.body: You now have a definition of first, a pattern for how we sideline people, a chair test, two frames, and a six-move loop. This lesson turns that into one person you already serve — not a special “employment project.”
blocks.heading: From evidence to ordinary work

blocks.body: Pick someone you would usually skip: high support, a frozen no, a family veto, a language you have not used. Small and complete beats a strategy deck with no name.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Choose one person and run the chair test.
Practice a repair that does not blame them for our skip.
Set a seven-day practice transfer.
Know the job aid and the formal doors you must not skip.

blocks.cite: Lesson 1, to take with you
blocks.text: If work was never on the table, that was not a choice. That was a default.

items.body: Apply the job aid to one person. Ask, try work in the community, name money, connect, document. Small and complete.
items.title: Fix the next meeting

items.body: The unit’s planning agenda, ISP prompt, or transition checklist. If the template asks about work before other day supports, every future meeting inherits the method.
items.title: Fix one template

items.body: If people who keep asking about jobs are called unrealistic, interrupt it. If filling slots fast is praised as good casework, stop praising it. Culture is what gets applause.
items.title: Fix the culture tell

blocks.alt: The grocery job from the start of the course: a real payroll, real coworkers.
blocks.caption: Return to the store. The question is whether the people we serve get this kind of option before we fill something else.

blocks.body: You will have skipped people. Repair is: name the miss, make a real offer now in a language they can use, book the benefits conversation, change the agenda so work comes first from now on, and skip the speech that makes them manage your embarrassment. “We should have asked you about work before we filled the other service. I am asking now. Here is who can help with benefits. You can say no. We will write it down and come back on a date we name.”
blocks.heading: Repair without theater

tabs.body: Caseloads are real. Many “no time to try work” notes are late starts. When time is short, shorten the loop; do not delete the first question.
tabs.label: Time

tabs.body: Waiver rules, VR eligibility, and 245D licensing are real. They shape how you connect. They do not cancel the offer while you wait on a door.
tabs.label: Authorization

tabs.body: Providers, schools, counties, and Tribal programs have their own calendars. DHS still sets the tone for the first option in meetings we host. Do not lower the bar because a partner is used to the sideline.
tabs.label: Partners

tabs.body: If every opening is an emergency, you are choosing the roster over the person. Write the list. Offer work. Then fill what they actually want.
tabs.label: Urgency theater

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Repair is the offer restored plus a method change. It is not a sharing circle they did not ask to lead.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Contentment after a skipped offer is not informed choice. Restore the offer. Change the agenda. Do not make them the trainer for your miss.

options.text: Ask them to tell the team how it felt, as a learning moment, then move on.
Name the miss, make the offer now with an interpreter, book benefits support, put work first on the next plan, and date a review if they say no.
Leave it — they seem content, so Employment First does not apply.
Add a poster about jobs in the day-program hallway.

blocks.question: You realize a person has been in a day program for two years and was never offered work in their language. They are not angry. What is the strongest repair?

blocks.body: Do these four things in the next seven calendar days. They are small enough to finish and large enough to count as Employment First.
blocks.heading: Seven-day transfer
Seven-day list
items: Pick one person you would usually skip. Write a half-page: what work might interest them, what was offered before, what fear sits in the file.
Ask about work first in a language they can use — or schedule the interpreter now.
Name the money: send or sit with DB101 / Disability Hub / a benefits planner, and write the appointment.
Put a review date on any no, and tell your team that filling a day slot before the offer is no longer the applause line.

blocks.heading: Principles to keep when the week gets loud

items.body: The skipped offer, the unnamed fear, or the convenient slot is. The person who said no, or who never heard the question, gave you information.
items.title: The person is not the problem

items.body: Do not call it choice if work was never on the paper. Brief with dignity instead of a checkbox.
items.title: The offer has to be real

items.body: VR, benefits counseling, waiver employment services, and Tribal paths are not “extra comms.” Use the right door.
items.title: Formal doors are not optional

items.body: What they heard. What they tried. What they chose. When you will ask again. That note is the product.
items.title: Review the no or you taught them not to want it

blocks.alt: The empty day-program room — the old default when work is not offered.
blocks.caption: The room can stay as a support people choose. It cannot be the first option we never named.

blocks.body: Intention → who was offered work → who heard it in a usable way → what they chose → what wage they hold → revision. If you never ask who was offered work, you will congratulate yourselves for programs that only worked for people already close to a job.
blocks.heading: The feedback loop

items.text: Ask one skipped person about work in their language.
Refer for benefits counseling before a payroll start.
Fill a day-program slot so you do not “lose it,” then mention jobs next year.
Put a review date on a no.
Tell a family their culture means work is off the table.

blocks.cite: Lesson 2, to take with you
blocks.text: “Not ready” is often “we are not ready to support them.”

items: Open with work. What kind of job, what kind of day, who they already know.
Presume they can work, including with complex support needs.
If they have said no before, say you are asking again because the offer stands.
Access: interpreter, captions, plain language, time. An unusable offer is not an offer.

sections.heading: Community experience and the money
items: Community experience beats a brochure: visit, tryout, conversation with a worker.
Job carving and discovery for people who will not fit a posting.

Wage test: would this paycheck embarrass a coworker without a disability? If yes, it is not the first option.

sections.heading: Connect, document, review
items: Name the phase: Engage, Plan, Find, or Keep. Match VR and waiver employment services to the phase.

sections.heading: Repair if you skipped them
items: Name the miss. Make the offer now. Do not make them lead a sharing circle.
Change the agenda so work comes before other day supports from now on.
If a slot was filled first, say so, and still offer work beside or instead — their choice.

sections.heading: Use the formal door — do not workshop these
items: Vocational Rehabilitation Services (DEED) for eligibility and job supports.
Waiver employment services and 245D / MHCP enrollment rules.
Benefits counseling and Disability Hub MN / DB101.
Tribal consultation and Tribal employment programs — DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations.
When in doubt, ask the proper office before you freeze a no.

course.introTranscript: A signed policy can still fail in the building. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, change lands on staff, county partners, Tribal Nations, providers, and the people who use services. If the people who will live with the change find out last, you did not bring anyone along. You announced. This course is a practice guide for leaders: name the loss, invite people early enough to change the design, treat resistance as information, and close the loop.

Choose and document one defensible change, the person who owns it, and the date the team will review it.

blocks.alt: A mixed DHS team at a conference table. The supervisor is listening, not performing a pep talk.
blocks.caption: Bringing people along looks like a working conversation, not an all-staff banner.

blocks.body: Minimization in this work: people find out after the memo. Adaptation: they find out with the work. This course does not assign a score.

When a policy is signed, a system go-live is dated, or a reorg chart is posted, leaders often feel the change is “done.” Staff still have to stop doing the old work, learn the new work, and face the public who did not get the memo. Counties, Tribal Nations, and providers may hear it after the press release. People who use services may hear it from a letter they cannot use.

That gap is not a communications glitch. It is a design choice about whose time and trust count. Specialists can help with a rollout plan. They do not own whether people were treated as passengers or as partners.
blocks.heading: Why this is a leadership course

blocks.body: This lesson names what you actually move when you sponsor a change. Later lessons show how rollouts usually fail here, who finds out last, two honest frames, and a method that fits ordinary work — the along-loop.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Separate an announcement from bringing people along.
Name what a change costs in work, identity, and trust.
Spot the difference between buy-in theater and real influence.
Own the sponsor job: you cannot delegate being present for the loss.

blocks.body: If they find out last, you did not manage the change. You mailed it.
Corporate change language is evidence, not the staff-facing deliverable. These are the terms this course uses on purpose.
blocks.heading: Terms used with care

cards.back: People who will live with the change can influence the design early enough that the design can still move. Example: county eligibility staff see the new form before it is locked, and one field is cut because it will fail at the counter.
Information after the decision, with no path to change it. Necessary sometimes. Not the same as leadership. Example: an all-staff email the morning of a go-live.

The inner process of ending the old way, walking a gap, and beginning the new. The org chart can change on Monday. People are still in the gap on Thursday. Name the ending or they will keep the old work alive in secret.
Pushback is often information: a missed partner, an unworkable step, a trust debt. Some resistance is self-protection. Treat it as a signal first, not a character flaw.

blocks.body: Project managers schedule. Communications writes. HR and labor relations handle the formal workforce path. Tribal and Urban Indian Relations supports consultation. None of that removes the sponsor’s job: stay in the room for the people the change will land on.
blocks.heading: Who holds which part
What sits with leaders versus specialists

items.body: You decide whether the old way is named as a real loss, whether front-line staff hear it from you or from a client, and whether “we don’t have time to engage” is allowed to stand. Culture is set by who gets a draft and who gets a directive.
items.title: Leaders own the ending

items.body: Use project, communications, training, labor relations, and consultation experts. Bring them in early. Do not hand them a finished decision and ask for “buy-in slides.”
items.title: Specialists support the path

items.body: Staff, county partners, and the public should not reverse-engineer a change from a rumor, a leaked slide, or a letter with no contact. “They’ll figure it out” is a leadership statement about whose time you are willing to burn.
items.title: People who do the work should not have to decode it alone

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Influence has to be real. Tone on an email cannot replace a chance to change the work.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A warmer announcement is still an announcement. If the people who live with the template cannot change it, you are not bringing them along.

options.text: Send the email Friday. Training can catch whoever is confused.
Hold the lock. Show the draft to people who use it weekly, change what you can, name what you cannot change and why, then send the notice with a named owner.
Ask communications to make the email warmer so people feel included.
Call it a technical change so engagement is not required.

blocks.question: Your administration is changing a reporting template that county and Tribal partners use weekly. The template is locked. A staff email will go out Friday. What is the leadership move?

blocks.alt: A supervisor listens and takes notes while a staff member speaks. The laptop is closed.
blocks.caption: Presence is operational: closed laptop, notes, a chance that the design can still move.

blocks.body: Move from “how do we get them to accept this?” to “who has to live with this, and how early can they still change it?” Acceptance is a lagging measure. Design access is a leading one.
blocks.heading: The shift this course asks for

blocks.body: Kotter, ADKAR, and other models are public evidence that under-communication and skipped coalitions fail. They are not the One DHS deliverable. Minnesota DHS change also lands on a county-supervised, state-administered system, on eleven Tribal Nations, on unions, and on people whose benefits and safety can move when we move. That is the practice context.
blocks.heading: DHS-wide, not a vendor script

tabs.body: Supervisors learn in a meeting. The people who answer the phone learn from the first angry call. Hybrid staff miss the hallway version. Night and weekend coverage is an afterthought.
tabs.label: Staff

tabs.body: A memo after the decision. No time to change local procedure, staffing, or notices. Partners are treated as a distribution list, not a design partner.
tabs.label: Counties & providers

tabs.body: Consultation is not a stakeholder workshop. If a change affects Tribal citizens or Tribal programs, “we cc’d the list” is not consultation. Use the DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations path early.
tabs.label: Tribal Nations

tabs.body: A letter, a website update, or a news item. If the notice is English-only, untagged, or arrives after the rule is already in force, people did not get a change. They got a surprise.
tabs.label: The public

blocks.body: Choose a statement, then choose the bucket. The point is not to make communications the villain. It is to stop hiding sponsor work inside a send button.
blocks.heading: Sort these statements

categories: Someone else owns the formal path
blocks.heading: Announcement or bringing along?

items.text: All-staff email the morning a new script goes live.
Front-line staff mark up the script two weeks earlier and one step is cut.

items.category: Someone else owns the formal path
items.text: A change in hours that may affect a bargaining agreement.
County partners see the draft notice and flag a date that collides with their peak week.
A press release before supervisors have talking points.

blocks.alt: A government corridor bulletin board with a dense memo. Staff walk past. Someone reads a long email alone.
blocks.caption: The memo can be accurate and still fail. Accuracy without a path is still a drop.

blocks.body: Human services staff have lived through stacked initiatives: new eligibility rules, new systems, new vendors, new equity commitments, new reporting, often with the old work still on their desk. When leaders say “this one is different,” people hear a pattern, not a promise. That skepticism is often earned.
blocks.heading: How the past shows up on Monday

blocks.body: You do not need a history degree. You do need to stop diagnosing the pattern as “they don’t like change.”

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Place common failure modes in working order.
Separate change (the event) from transition (the human gap).
See why counties, Tribal Nations, and the public are not a last chapter.
Reject “we already told them” as proof that they could act.

blocks.body: People are not tired of change. They are tired of being the last to know and the first to absorb it.
These dates are not a trivia quiz. They are answers to “who already named this problem?”
blocks.heading: A working timeline of ideas — used as evidence

events.body: The event can be scheduled. The inner ending, gap, and beginning cannot. Leaders who skip the ending get shadow systems — the old way kept alive in a folder.
events.title: Bridges: change vs. transition

events.body: Public evidence, not our playbook: under-communicating, skipping a coalition, declaring victory early. If your plan has one email and a training video, you are in that evidence.
events.title: Kotter: why transformations fail

events.body: Awareness and desire are not created by a slide. They describe whether someone can even see the change and whether they have a reason to move. Treat the words as a check, not a product to buy.
events.title: ADKAR as a common language

events.body: Minnesota human services often moves through 87 counties and Tribal partners. A St. Paul decision that ignores local procedure is not a rollout. It is a collision scheduled in advance.
events.title: County-supervised, state-administered work

events.body: People will not name the hole in your plan if the last person who did that paid for it. Edmondson’s research is evidence: silence is a design outcome.
events.title: Psychological safety as an operating condition

events.body: Pandemic rules, system replacements, budget shocks, and equity commitments landed on the same desks. Sequence is a leadership duty. “Everything is priority one” is how nothing is.
events.title: Stacked initiatives after crisis years

blocks.heading: Ideas that still bind the work

items.body: Training teaches a tool. It does not repair a decision people did not get to influence. If the only “engagement” is a required module after go-live, you are teaching compliance, not bringing people along.
items.title: The training-as-engagement trap

items.body: A steering committee of central office leads will miss the counter, the night shift, the county, and the Tribal program. Empty chairs are data.
items.title: The coalition of people already in the room

items.body: Launch is the start of the gap, not the end of the work. The first two weeks of tickets, workarounds, and public confusion are the real report.
items.title: Declaring victory at launch

items.body: “They are change-resistant” is often a way to avoid saying “we designed this without them.” Ask what they are protecting: a client, a legal duty, a workaround that actually serves.
items.title: Naming people instead of the pattern

blocks.alt: At a public counter, a staff member hears about a benefits change from a member of the public. A supervisor in the background realizes the team was not briefed.
blocks.caption: If the public is your briefing channel for staff, the sequence is backwards.

blocks.body: Communities that use DHS programs have already lived through changes they did not choose: rule cuts, form changes, closed offices, new portals. When staff feel done-to, they are tasting a smaller version of what the public already knows. Humility here is accuracy, not guilt theater.
blocks.heading: From protest to procedure — a different kind of history
What each era still asks of a DHS leader

tabs.body: What stops? Who loved the old way because it protected a client or a legal duty? Say it out loud. Unnamed endings become sabotage, then we call it culture.
tabs.label: Endings

tabs.body: Who must be able to act before the public does? Supervisors, then staff who meet the public, then partners, then notices. Invert that order and you donate your credibility.
tabs.label: Sequence

tabs.body: If the last three rollouts were late, confusing, or punitive, this one starts in a hole. Extra time and extra honesty are not softness. They are the cost of prior design.
tabs.label: Debt

tabs.body: Who can say no? Union contracts, Tribal sovereignty, federal rules, and county capacity are not “noise.” They are the field you are playing on.
tabs.label: Power

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Character diagnoses are cheap. Design diagnoses take a conversation.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A completed training roster does not prove people could influence the work, or that the work is usable.

options.text: They are right. Training is the engagement. Complaints after that are attitude.
Complaints after training are usually a union issue only.
Training is not the same as influence. Complaints may be data about sequence, loss, or an unworkable step. Investigate the pattern before you diagnose character.
Only communications can interpret complaints.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “We trained them. If they are still complaining, they resist change.” What is the accurate frame?

cards.back: Change is the event (new form, new boss, new system). Transition is the inner ending, gap, and beginning. You can calendar the first. You have to lead the second.
Leaders who live in the change for months forget that staff met it this morning. One email is not a campaign. Repeating is not nagging if the work is new.
The new change arrives on top of the old change that never finished. Ask what you will stop, delay, or staff up — or you are asking for unpaid overtime as a strategy.
A quiet staff meeting after a big announcement is not buy-in. It may be fear, exhaustion, or people waiting to see if you mean it.

blocks.body: Every era added a model. Agencies often responded by hiring a change manager. Change managers matter. The pattern that fails is using them as a place to park the sponsor’s job while the decision stays closed.
blocks.heading: Persistent pattern

items.text: The old report is still required “in case we still need it,” plus the new dashboard.
Clients arrive with a letter staff have not seen.
Three go-lives in one quarter, same unit, no work taken off the plate.
A reorg chart posts before anyone says what job is ending.
A press call happens the same hour supervisors get the FAQ.

blocks.alt: A planning meeting with a blurred whiteboard and two empty chairs at the table.
blocks.caption: The empty chairs are the lesson: who is not here while the design is still soft?

blocks.body: Stakeholder maps often list offices, not people who will absorb the hit. “Internal” hides the night shift. “Partners” hides a Tribal Nation with a government-to-government relationship. “Customers” hides a person who needs an interpreter to read the notice. If your map is a logo collage, it will fail at the counter.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows

blocks.body: This lesson is the evidence of practice — who is usually missing, and how that missing shows up as “resistance” later.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Map who lives with the change, not who owns the slide.
Treat Tribal consultation and labor relations as paths, not checkboxes.
See how language and disability access travel with every rollout.
Name the harm of using the public as the staff briefing.

blocks.body: If they are not in the draft, they will be in the incident report.

items.body: Eligibility workers, contact-center staff, facility staff, investigators, and county colleagues. They know where the form will snag. They are often invited to “review” after lock. That is decoration.
items.title: The people who meet the public

items.body: Staff and members of the public who need captions, plain language, interpreters, or extra time. A rollout webinar without captions is a change meeting some people cannot attend. Access is part of bringing people along.
items.title: People who cannot use the default channel

items.body: Minnesota DHS has a Tribal and Urban Indian Relations function to support ongoing consultation. Tribal Nations are governments. Do not park them in a stakeholder list next to a vendor. If you are unsure whether consultation applies, ask early — not after the date is printed.
items.title: Tribal Nations

items.body: Every old system had unofficial experts. If you do not invite them, they will keep the old way alive because it is how they still help clients. Bring them in as designers, not as obstacles.
items.title: The people who will lose unofficial power

blocks.alt: A member of the public at a human-services counter with a letter about a change.
blocks.caption: The public is not your quality-assurance team. If they are teaching staff the change, the map failed.

blocks.body: When you brief leadership first, then comms, then supervisors, then staff, then counties, then the public, you are not being careful. You are concentrating information at the top until it is too late to use. Reverse the test: who has to act first on Monday morning? Brief them while the design can still move.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: last-in is a method

cards.back: Staff hear it from a Facebook comment or a client. Trust drops before you have said a word. Speed without a named owner still loses to rumor.
Households with limited English proficiency meet the change as a denial or a missed deadline. Outreach then looks like “low engagement.”
A statewide date ignores local peak weeks, staffing, or another system outage. Partners spend their credibility calming people you did not warn.
The person who flags a hole is labeled negative. Next time the room is quiet. You have trained silence.

blocks.heading: Reading the same rollout three ways

tabs.body: Administrations, divisions, named directors. Useful for approvals. Blind to the counter, the county, and the night shift.
tabs.label: Org-chart map

tabs.body: Who touches the case, the phone, the notice, the building, the data. This is the map that predicts failure.
tabs.label: Work map

tabs.body: Who can delay you legally or politically: labor, Tribal governments, federal partners, advocates, the press. Ignoring them is not bravery. It is a later, worse meeting.
tabs.label: Power map

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Representation by title is not the same as the people who do the keystrokes.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A technical label does not cancel partnership or consultation. If they enter the data, they are in the change.

options.text: Six weeks is enough if the FAQ is thorough.
Counties can be informed at go-live; Tribal consultation can wait until after launch because it is a technical change.

The people who enter the data — including county and Tribal partners — are missing while the design is still supposed to be movable. Put them in now, and ask whether consultation is required before you lock the date.
Empty chairs are normal; the steering group represents everyone.

blocks.question: A system change will alter how counties and a Tribal human-services program enter the same data. The steering group is all central-office leads. Go-live is in six weeks. What does the empty-chair test say?

blocks.body: When a rollout “surprises” the front line, do not start with “we have a communications problem.” Start with the chairs. You will often find a closed design, a backwards sequence, and a map of offices instead of work.
blocks.heading: From observation to explanation
How to check your map without a consultant

items.body: Not five directors. Five actual roles. If you cannot name them, you do not have a rollout plan. You have a hope.
items.title: Name five people who will touch it Monday

items.body: That person should have seen the notice, the script, and the exception path before the public did.
items.title: Ask who hears it from the public first

items.body: If the only people who can delay go-live are already committed to the date, the map has no brake.
items.title: Ask who can say this is not ready

items.body: A chair test will not replace formal consultation, labor notice, or a civil-rights review. It will stop you from being shocked that the missing people did not cheer.
items.title: Limits of this scan

items.text: Night-shift facility staff who will use the new handoff.
A Tribal Nation whose members will get the new notice.
ASL users who cannot use the uncaptioned launch webinar.
County eligibility supervisors in a peak SNAP week.
The bargaining path for a change in work hours.

blocks.body: Next: two honest frames — announce-and-hope versus design-with — and when each is actually required.
